author: Priyanka Sharma
title: Africa on the Map, But Still Off the Table
content:
On 4 September 2026, the United Nations General Assembly adopted a non-binding resolution that might initially appear to belong to the relatively technical world of cartography. The resolution, “Correct the Map: Rebalancing Global Cartographic Representation and Promoting Equitable Representation of the World’s Regions, Particularly Africa,” was introduced by Togo on behalf of the African Group and adopted by 164 countries, with one country voting against and six abstaining.


In presenting the resolution, Togo’s Foreign Minister Robert Dussey argued that maps are not merely technical tools: their repeated use in schools, the media and digital platforms shapes how people understand and visualise the world. The African Group argued that the Mercator projection, designed for specific purposes—especially maritime navigation—had become a general-purpose image of the world that visually minimises Africa and other regions near the Equator.


The delegation framed the initiative around scientific and educational accuracy, cognitive justice, historical memory and the equal dignity of peoples. It also stressed what the resolution would not do: condemn the Mercator projection, impose a single map for every use, alter borders or take a position on territorial claims. Instead, it encouraged the use of projections such as Equal Earth when comparing the relative areas of continents, alongside better teaching about the strengths and limitations of different projections.


The resolution encourages the use of equal-area map projections, including Equal Earth, particularly when the relative size of regions matters. It also highlights the implications of existing representations for geographical and cartographic literacy. Importantly, however, it does not replace the Mercator projection, redraw international borders or alter the legal status of any territory. So why does a map matter? And why now?


These questions are more significant than the technical debate over which projection should be used. The UN resolution opens a much larger question about who has historically possessed the authority to represent the world, whose knowledge becomes universal knowledge, and what happens when previously marginalised actors begin to challenge that authority.


Mercator Map versus Equal Earth (wikicommons)


The map is not the territory—but it shapes how the territory is imagined


Gerardus Mercator’s famous projection was first published in 1569. It was developed primarily as a tool for maritime navigation, as its preservation of angles and constant compass bearings made it particularly useful for sailors plotting routes across oceans. The projection was never intended to provide an accurate comparison of the relative size of continents. Its distortion, however, has had a long afterlife.


Because the Mercator projection increasingly enlarges landmasses as they move away from the Equator, Greenland can appear comparable in size to Africa, despite Africa being approximately fourteen times larger.There is therefore an important distinction to make. Mercator was not invented as a deliberate attempt to make Africa smaller. Its original purpose was navigational. The political question emerges from what happened afterwards: how a projection designed for a particular technical purpose became normalised as a general image of the world.


A cartographic choice made for navigation became, through repetition, an educational and cultural convention. Maps entered classrooms, atlases, newspapers, television graphics, websites and digital platforms. In doing so, they did more than provide geographical information. They participated in producing a particular visual imagination of the world. This is where cartography becomes political. Can a two-dimensional map ever be neutral?


From geographical distortion to cognitive hierarchy


The significance of the new

UN resolution

 therefore lies less in replacing one map with another than in recognising that representation itself has consequences. The resolution’s language is striking. It connects cartographic representation to education, perception and collective understanding, framing the correction of historical distortions as a matter of equitable representation. The UN Office of the Special Adviser on Africa has presented the initiative as an African-led effort to challenge the symbolic minimisation of the continent. But the tension remains.


If representation contributes to how societies imagine the world …

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Western Cape hit with tighter water restrictions
content:
The water and sanitation department has issued a warning to residents and businesses in the Western Cape that it will implement a 7% reduction in domestic and industrial water allocations as well as a 15% reduction in water for irrigation. Addressing the media on Monday, Minister of Water and Sanitation, Pemmy Majodina said that the current water in storage in the province is below the preferred operational threshold of 80%.


“While the major dams remain at acceptable levels overall, some key components of the system have recorded significant declines compared to the previous year. Storage levels remain significantly above those experienced during the severe drought period of 2016-2017; yet, the current water storage is below the preferred operational threshold of 80% and approximately 11.9 % points below the ten-year average of 84.49%,” Majodina said.


According to the minister, the decline in stored water resulted from below-average winter rainfall in the province while the looming El Niño event is increasing temperatures and evaporation.


Municipalities are expected to restrict water supply to residents and can impose further restrictions, but by no more than the 7% that the national government has imposed. The department is expected to write a submission to the director general who will approve the restriction and get it gazetted.


“Modelling undertaken by water resource specialists reveals that if water users continue to utilise their full allocations without intervention, the risk of water shortages and mandatory restrictions will increase substantially from 2027 onwards,” said Majodina.


The City of Cape has announced that it will introduce level 1 water restrictions from 1 December 2026.


Rural taps already dry


The Kannaland Local Municipality that covers Ladismith, Calitzdorp and Zoar are already on level 4 water restrictions. Water in the municipality is available for human consumption only.


Carmelitta Juries lives on a farm near Ladismith. While the farm dam is full, the water isn’t safe to drink without first disinfecting it with bleach. Carmelitta said they have no choice but to rely on the unsafe dam water as the municipality offers no alternative. “The municipality promised that they would put up water tanks. One tank could sustain a couple of homes. For example, 10 homes can use one tank, but to date we haven’t heard anything further,” she said.


Zoar resident, Irene Isaacs said that it is harder for the village to access water in summer. Community members without water storage tanks must wait for municipal trucks to deliver water. Elderly residents are especially vulnerable in these circumstances, she said, and depend on members of the community to carry water in buckets to their homes.


Kannaland Municipality is already on level 4 restrictions. File photo by Mandla Mnyakama


Bergriver, Swartland and Saldanha Bay municipalities have been flagged as key areas where water scarcity and aging infrastructure pose significant constraints to future growth unless supply and bulk infrastructure are urgently upgraded. Hendrix Van Wyk from Vredenburg, which falls under Saldanha Bay Municipality, told

Elitsha

 that in poor neighbourhoods like Hopland, Louwville, Selbou and Yskor, the water pressure in the taps is low. “It takes up to 30 minutes to fill up a 5-litre bucket and a 20-litre bucket takes about 2 hours to fill up,” he said.


According to Majodina, construction of the Clanwilliam Dam, which will increase water availability for the West Coast District Municipality, is 40% complete.


Partnership, not privatisation of water

 insists DWS


A

new amendment to the Water Plan

 states that if a municipality is not delivering a clean, safe supply of water, the national government can hand that function over to the private sector. The government has already implemented this in the City of Tshwane where a public-private partnership is taking effect. According to

BusinessTech

, Coca-Cola has partnered with the government to invest R500-million in municipal water infrastructure to stop service delivery from collapsing.


During Cape Town’s severe drought between 2015 and 2018, marked by the

Day Zero Campaign

, water rights groups protested against water guzzlers, and the soft drink manufacturer was one of their targets. At the time, Coca-Cola drew about 530-million litres of water annually from the City of Cape Town to manufacture its products. A litre of Coke requires about 2 litres of …

author: Abahlali_3
title: Socialism or Barbarism?
content:
Keynote address at the Third National Conference of the Aotearoa New Zealand Federation of Socialist Societies held in Ōtepoti Dunedin, on Saturday, 14 November 2026.

Comrade Programme director, thank you for welcoming me to Aotearoa once again. May I express my sincere gratitude to the New Zealand Federation of Socialist Societies and Palestine Solidarity Network Aotearoa for inviting me to speak here today, and across the country. I bring greetings from Abahlali baseMjondolo, our movement in South Africa which now has more than 200,000 members.

I want to begin with the words of a song, a song about socialism, that is often sung in the struggles of the left in South Africa.

Yini iSocialism? Umhlaba wonke ezandleni zabantu Akunamuntu, akunamuntu ongaphatha umhlaba ngayedwa Ayayesaba bo, ayesaba amabhujwa, nongxiwa Ngoba bona, ngobabona befuna ukusetshenzelwa ngabantu

The song asks, ‘What is socialism?’ It answers that socialism is the whole world in the hands of the people. It goes on to say that no one person can own the world on their own. It concludes that the bourgeoisie are afraid of socialism, because they want the people to work for them.

Comrades, as you will all know, in 1915, during the mass slaughter of the First World War, Rosa Luxemburg wrote from a prison cell in Germany that humanity stood at a crossroads. Either it would move towards socialism, towards global justice and peace, or it would collapse into further barbarism. She was writing as millions of workers were being sent to kill each other in the trenches for the profits of their rulers. Four years later she was murdered.

In our movement we have our own version of this choice. Lindokuhle Mnguni, the gifted young chairperson of one of our branches, the eKhenana Commune in Durban, introduced the slogan ‘Socialism or Death’ into our movement. For Lindokuhle, socialism was not something that would come one day in the future, after a revolution, or after an election. Socialism had to be lived now, in the way we occupy land, ensure that it is not bought and sold, manage it democratically, grow food together, ensure that nobody goes hungry, care for each other, build and manage social infrastructure like halls, creches and kitchens, and make decisions together.

For us, like urban and rural movements elsewhere in the world, building socialism from below means building communes, connecting them and building wider forms of democratic popular power from these communes. In the same way that the liberated zones were the bases for anti-colonial movements in countries like Mozambique and Guinea-Bissau, communes – from South Africa to Brazil, Venezuela and elsewhere – are the strongest bases for our movements to build socialism. As Ruthie Wilson Gilmore says, ‘Freedom is a place’.

The price for challenging oppression can be very high. Many comrades around the world have given their lives. On 20 August 2022, Lindokuhle was shot dead in his home. He was the third leader of the eKhenana Commune to be assassinated in less than six months.

Frantz Fanon taught that ‘Each generation must, out of relative obscurity, discover its mission, fulfill it, or betray it.’ Comrades like Rosa Luxemburg and Lindokuhle Mnguni understood the mission of their generation, and gave their lives to it. Our generation also has a mission. We are living in a time of genocide, of wealth beyond imagination for a few and hunger for millions, of the far right and fascist forces rising and of the poor being turned against each other. We have to decide whether we will fulfil our mission or betray it. In our movement we have often used Fanon’s words. When people find themselves pushed to the margins of the city and of life, they have the opportunity to discover their mission and to decide whether they want to fulfil it or betray it.

I want to speak today about the barbarism that we see around us, in South Africa and around the world, and about the work of building socialism from below, as we have tried to do it in our movement.

When Luxemburg wrote about barbarism she was thinking of the slaughter of the First World War. Today we are witnessing another mass slaughter of human beings. We have all watched the genocide in Gaza. We have watched children being starved, hospitals and schools being bombed, and whole families being buried under the rubble of their homes. We have watched the most powerful governments in the world supply the weapons and protect Israel at the United Nations. We …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Eight Years in Prison for Fighting Anti-Black Racism in Tunisia: Free Saadia Mosbah!
content:
For years, Saadia Mosbah has been one of the leading voices against anti-Black racism in Tunisia. As president of the anti-racism organisation Mnemty, she has stood up for Black Tunisians and Black migrants alike. When


violence against Black migrants escalated

 after President Kais Saied’s February 2023 statement against African migrants, she became a target of online hate campaigns.


On May 6, 2024, she was arrested. On March 19, 2026, she was sentenced to eight years in prison and a heavy fine on charges of money laundering and illicit enrichment. On June 23, the Tunis Court of Appeals upheld her conviction, along with those of five Mnemty colleagues and associates. A final appeal, filed on June 29, is now before the Court of Cassation.


Human rights movements and organisations,


including Amnesty International

, have denounced the irregularities in the proceedings and the lack of evidence for the alleged offences. They have also raised the alarm over the racist treatment and violence Saadia has reportedly suffered in detention.


Saadia’s case sits within a wider pattern of repression. Since President Kais Saied seized sweeping powers in July 2021, Tunisia has slid back into authoritarian rule. Since May 2024, the month of Saadia’s arrest, the authorities have waged

a systematic crackdown on civil society

: activists prosecuted, organisations suspended, independent voices jailed. Throughout, the European Union has kept its

2023 migration deal with Tunisia

 in place, funding the country to stop people crossing to Europe and outsourcing its borders to a government that imprisons those who defend Black migrants. In this climate of repression and European complicity, Saadia’s voice and her freedom matter more than ever.


Saadia is more than a case file. Below, three activists tell their stories of the woman they know and the movement she helped build. Read them, then join the call for her immediate and unconditional release and for the convictions to be overturned. Keep fighting for those who fight for us in an anti-Black world.


 


Saadia’s Imprisonment Inseparable from Criminalisation of Black Organising and Solidarity


I first met Saadia Mosbah shortly after the 2011 Tunisian Revolution, when she was active in feminist organisations. Over the years that followed, I witnessed her unwavering commitment to the struggle for Black dignity, justice, and liberation in Tunisia. I watched her organisation, Mnemty, grow. And I watched a dream grow alongside it: the dream of a Tunisia where racism would no longer be denied, normalised, or left unpunished. 


A Tunisia with a law explicitly criminalising racial discrimination. Saadia was determined to bring together as many voices as possible around this struggle. She openly confronted a reality that many preferred to ignore: a significant part of Tunisia’s supposedly progressive and activist civil society remained silent on racism. Even within movements claiming to fight for equality and justice, Black people were too often expected to fight their battles alone.


Saadia refused that silence. She refused to make racism a secondary issue, or to soften her political demands to make others more comfortable.


But through years of persistence, political courage, and collective organising, she helped build a movement strong enough to achieve a historic victory: the adoption of Tunisia’s law against racial discrimination in 2018.


Years later, in 2023, I had the privilege and honour of working alongside Saadia to organise a march against state racism. Following the Tunisian presidency’s disgraceful statement targeting sub-Saharan African migrants, she was there, standing with us on the anti-fascist front line, organising, mobilising, supporting, and defending Black people and migrants in Tunisia. Saadia knew the risks. She understood what it meant to confront state racism in an increasingly authoritarian political climate. Yet she refused to retreat.


Today, Saadia est en prison. Her imprisonment is inseparable from the criminalisation of Black political organising, anti-racist resistance, and solidarity with migrants.


Saadia’s story is also a reminder that political victories are never irreversible.


A law can be adopted while the structures of domination it was meant to challenge remain intact. Rights written into legislation mean little when those who fought for them are deprived of their freedom.


But Saadia’s struggle is bigger than her imprisonment. It …

author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

The post

Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

.

author: Sara Connors
title: Yukon court dismisses wrongful death lawsuit against Whitehorse shelter operator
content:
The Supreme Court of Yukon has dismissed a wrongful death lawsuit against the operator of the Whitehorse emergency shelter.

Chief Justice Suzanne Duncan said in a Nov. 6 decision that the lawsuit was brought after the one-year limitation period under the Yukon’s Fatal Accidents Act.

Josephine Hager, 38, a Selkirk First Nation citizen, died at the shelter on Feb. 1, 2023. Her father, Dale Joe, filed the lawsuit last October.

An inquest in April 2024 heard that Hager, who lived in a supportive housing unit at the shelter, died from a lethal mix of morphine and alcohol.

The lawsuit claims Connective, the non-profit organization operating the shelter, and five unnamed staff members were negligent in Hager’s death.

However, Connective argued in an application that Joe, who filed the suit more than two years after his daughter’s death, missed the one-year deadline under the act.

According to the decision, Joe said he wasn’t aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death and its potential wrongful nature until shortly after the 2024 inquest, more than a year after she died.

The decision also notes that his mother and brother died within a year of each other, adding to his grief.

An affidavit from Selkirk Elder and former chief Lucy McGuinty also states that traditional Northern Tutchone laws prevent those who follow them from interfering with matters of the deceased until a headstone potlatch is held, which she said typically takes one to two years.

The decision also notes that other jurisdictions, such as Alberta and Saskatchewan, give courts some discretion to consider personal circumstances.

Connective, meanwhile, argued that the act stipulates that the limitation period begins on the date of death, regardless of a plaintiff’s knowledge of the matter.

The organization also argued that even if Joe’s argument were allowed to proceed, the lawsuit was still filed more than a year after he became aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death.

The organization further contended that Indigenous customs or traditions provide no legal basis to extend or eliminate limitation periods.

It also noted that a headstone potlatch had not yet been held for Hager or Joe’s brother, which it said contradicts McGuinty’s statement that cultural tradition requires a headstone potlatch before the deceased’s affairs may be addressed.

Duncan said there was merit to Joe’s argument that the one-year limitation could begin when he became aware of the circumstances surrounding his daughter’s death.

However, she found that nothing in Yukon’s act allows a plaintiff’s personal circumstances to be considered grounds for an extension.

Duncan granted Connective’s application, effectively dismissing the lawsuit.

A spokesperson for Connective said in an email statement to APTN News that it was aware of the dismissal but had no comment.

Father disappointed lawsuit dismissed

Mark Wallace, Joe’s lawyer, said his client filed the lawsuit seeking justice for his daughter and was disappointed it was dismissed.

“(Joe) had really hoped that Justice Duncan would agree and let this go forward,” he said, noting his client was “quite upset by it.”

Wallace acknowledged that they knew there was a “reasonable chance” Connective would move to strike the lawsuit based on the limitation period, but said they hoped Duncan would agree with their arguments.

However, he said he didn’t disagree with the decision and that Joe wouldn’t be appealing.

“I think her interpretation of the law is correct,” he said.

Wallace said that while the outcome wasn’t what they wanted, Joe is hopeful the lawsuit will help raise awareness of the act’s limitation period for people in similar situations who might not be aware of it.

He also said he would like to see more flexibility under the act to account for personal circumstances, such as adopting wording similar to that in other jurisdictions.

The lawsuit is the 4th filed in recent years involving deaths at the shelter.

Two were settled last year, while another is still before the courts.

Sara Connors is originally from Nova Scotia and has a journalism degree from the University of King’s College in Halifax. After graduation she worked in South Korea for two years as an English language teacher and freelance journalist. After she returned home in 2019 she worked behind the scenes at CTV Atlantic in Halifax before joining APTN's Yukon bureau in July 2020.

author: Dominique Gené - Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Nunavik communities elect new school board commissioners
content:
Nunavik communities have elected representatives to Kativik Ilisarniliriniq’s council of commissioners, with the new council set to serve a three-year term.


The election results were announced Wednesday. Representatives were elected in 13 of the region’s 14 communities, a press release issued Wednesday by Nunavik’s school board said.


The election in Kangiqsujuaq was postponed to Thursday for logistical reasons, communications director Jade Duchesneau-Bernier said in an email.


Several candidates were elected by acclamation, including Adamie Alayco in Akulivik, Nancy Palliser in Inukjuak and Sarah Aloupa in Quaqtaq.


Ten commissioners were elected in contested races, including Charlie Akpahatak (Aupaluk), Evie Mark Kalingo (Ivujivik), McCombie Annanack (Kangiqsualujjuaq), Peter Annahatak Timmons (Kangirsuk), Eva Kauki (Kuujjuaq), Jeannie Aragutak (Kuujjuaraapik), Jacqueline Amamatuak (Puvirnituq), Patsy Cameron (Salluit), Mary Berthe (Tasiujaq) and Noah Inukpuk (Umiujaq).


The newly elected commissioners will meet for the first time from Nov. 30 to Dec. 4. During that meeting, they will elect a president and members of the executive committee from among themselves.


Aloupa, who was re-elected by acclamation as Quaqtaq’s commissioner, is eligible to serve another term as president. She will remain in the role of immediate past president until the new council makes its selection.

author: Mike Ludwig
title: GOP Rams Through Trump FCC Nominee Opposed by Free Speech Groups
content:
Democrats boycotted the vote as Trump’s other lame duck nominees caused headaches for the Senate GOP.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

As Democrats plan investigations into corruption and abuses of power, Republicans are working to shore up the president’s influence over the federal bureaucracy while they still can. But Senate Republicans are having mixed success as they attempt to speed through the federal nomination process for as many GOP-approved officials as they can.

Despite a boycott of the confirmation hearing by Democrats, Republicans on the Senate Commerce Committee voted on November 18 to advance President Donald Trump’s nomination of Danielle Thumann Severs to serve on the Federal Communications Commission (FCC). Thumann Severs is senior counsel to FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, and Democrats had called for an additional hearing to question her about internal records suggesting that she helped Carr pressure cable news outlets to change their content on Trump’s behalf.

“Today, Senator [Ted] Cruz greenlit a vote for an FCC nominee who not only provided false testimony to his committee, but did so to cover up her role in FCC Chairman Carr’s ongoing efforts to pressure and punish broadcasters that anger the president,” said Jessica J. González, co-CEO of the digital rights group Free Press, in a statement on Wednesday.

González pointed to internal FCC documents recently released to watchdogs under the Freedom of Information Act that show Thumann responding to emails about Trump and Carr’s jawboning of cable news outlets, including pressuring ABC to temporarily pull comedian Jimmy Kimmel off of late-night TV last year. Jawboning is the use of informal public pressure and veiled threats by government officials to cajole or coerce private actors, and the Senate Commerce Committee has advanced bipartisan legislation to rein it in.

Thumann is one of multiple Trump nominees that Republicans are attempting to ram through the confirmation process before Democrats regain majorities in Congress next year. Other high-profile Trump nominees failed to gain traction in the GOP-controlled Senate on Wednesday, including Jim O’Neill, a venture capitalist who is not a scientist but was nominated to run the National Science Foundation, despite vocal opposition from actual scientists.

Senate health committee Chairman Bill Cassidy (R-Louisiana) abruptly blocked a vote on O’Neill, citing a nasty shakeup over childhood vaccines at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, where Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. installed O’Neill as acting director after firing public health expert Susan Monarez. Monarez later testified that she was pushed out after resisting Kennedy’s efforts to fire career scientists and change public vaccine recommendations to align with anti-vax ideology.

The U.S. faces a severe measles outbreak and has officially lost its measles elimination status due in part to lower childhood vaccination rates. Senator Cassidy has said he now regrets casting a deciding vote last year to confirm Kennedy, a longtime leader of the anti-vaccine movement who regularly spreads misinformation from his perch at the Department of Health and Human Services.

“I like Jim personally, but this time requires leadership and fortitude and standing up for what is right,” Cassidy said as he blocked O’Neill’s confirmation.

Additionally, the White House dropped its nomination of physician and abortion opponent Heidi Overton for Food and Drug Administration commissioner. The move came as a disappointment to some Republicans, including Cassidy, who suggested on Wednesday that the nomination had enough GOP votes to pass. Reproductive health advocates feared Overton would undermine access to medication abortion, which she has baselessly asserted is “dangerous to women.” Overton also controversially played a role in the White House’s overhaul of the childhood vaccination schedule, and infamously stood behind Trump as he falsely stated that the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine could be “quite lethal.”

Unlike O’Neill and Overton, however, Thumann Severs’s nomination will advance to a full Senate vote, and free speech advocates are urging lawmakers to reject it. Chris Lewis, president and CEO of the non-partisan group Public Knowledge, said Thumann Severs’s testimony during a November 10 hearing failed to assure …

author: Savannah Peters, The Associated Press
title: As Deb Haaland elected first Indigenous woman governor in ‘US,’ other Pueblo women still face hurdles
content:
Prior to her election as Governor of ‘New Mexico,’ Democratic nominee Deb Haaland answers questions during an interview at her campaign headquarters in ‘Albuquerque’ on Oct. 9.

Photo by Susan Montoya Bryan/AP


This story is published through the

Global Indigenous Reporting Network

 at The Associated Press, and appears here with permission and minor style edits.


On the morning of Kawaika (

Laguna Pueblo

)’s annual Feast Day, Ashley Sarracino knelt in her family home holding clothespins between her teeth. 


She straightened her niece’s black cotton manta, a traditional one-shouldered dress, and tied a sash around her waist. 


On these days, Sarracino is a caretaker, dressing relatives for the harvest dance and helping feed up to 150 guests. And as a former member of the Pueblo Council, she knows how to balance those traditional responsibilities with official duties. 


“To me, those things aren’t in conflict at all,” she said. 


Yet even as another Kawaika woman, former “U.S.” Interior Secretary Deb Haaland, is set to become the first

Indigenous woman state governor

, women with leadership aspirations such as Sarracino say they are swimming upstream in their Pueblo communities. 


READ MORE:


In Nevada, Indigenous land protectors face off with a Canadian mining company


Sarracino said she was forced off the council after alleging she was paid less because she was a woman, a claim Pueblo officials deny. 


In some of the

19 Pueblos

 in “New Mexico,” including Kawaika, tribal law and customs do not allow women to hold top government positions. 


Haaland told The Associated Press she was once nominated to serve on her Pueblo council but did not make it past a primary. She quipped it was “easier to raise $1 million and run for Congress” than succeed in Pueblo politics. 


“It’s still a man’s world in a lot of Pueblo communities, and certainly in mine,” she said. 


Ashley Sarracino, right, and her sister Lindsay Sarracino prepare food for the annual Feast Day celebration on Oct. 17 in Paraje, a village within Kawaika (Pueblo of Laguna), ‘New Mexico.’

Photo by Roberto E. Rosales/AP


A fight over women’s place in tribal leadership 


Sarracino was offered a road map familiar to ambitious young Indigenous people: Leave the reservation to get an education, then return home to serve your community. 


She built a career in non-profit work and political organizing, including as chair of her county’s Democratic Party. 


In 2022, Sarracino was nominated by a Pueblo Elder to run for council secretary. She finished second but was appointed to the post after a resignation. 


“Finally, I had an opportunity to use my skills to help my own community,” she said. 


While reviewing budget documents, Sarracino discovered she was being paid US$14,000 less than her male predecessor. She asked the Pueblo governor for an explanation, sparking a bitter dispute that would end her tenure on council. 


The council says Sarracino was paid less because she lacked experience and that she abandoned her post. 


But Sarracino insists she was ousted and that the pay discrepancy reflects sexist attitudes embedded in tribal law. 


Since 1996, the Pueblo’s election code has allowed women to run for council treasurer and secretary, but it does not explicitly allow them to serve as governor or lieutenant governor. 


Its constitution, last amended in 2012, refers to the governor as “he” and “him.” 


READ MORE:


Across the border, Indigenous fears spike amidst ‘U.S.’ immigration crackdown


Sarracino’s dispute landed in tribal court but was dismissed this year on sovereign immunity grounds and she’s exhausted her appeals. 


The case took a toll on her mental health. She said it’s been bittersweet to watch Haaland make political history. 


“We all know she would never have the same opportunity here,” she said. 


Yet Haaland’s ascent could help change attitudes at home. 


Emily Hunt, who became Kawaika’s first woman elected official in the late 1990s with legal help from Haaland, believes the Pueblo will someday nominate a woman governor. 


“Whether I’ll see it in my lifetime, I don’t know,” Hunt said. 


Ashley Sarracino poses at her home on Oct. 17 in Paraje.

 Photo by Roberto E. Rosales/AP


Pueblo governance is varied and complex 


Some Pueblos retain traditional theocracies, with government roles appointed by ceremonial Elders and reserved for men.

author: Valerie Anne
title: LGBTQ+ Representation in Television Hits Devastating Lows
content:
As I’m sure you’ve noticed, LGBTQ+ representation in media is at the lowest it’s been in over a decade.

GLAAD’s latest Where We Are in TV study showed some bleak results that reflect the state of the country due to the hateful administration we live under and the wealthy conservatives who own most of the media conglomerates. Trans representation took the biggest hit, going from 33 characters to a measly SEVEN, and since three of them were on shows that were cancelled and four are from limited series, none of those seven will be returning next season. NONE. Devastating.

Twenty-five percent of LGBTQ+ characters have left our screens since last year, which brings the stats to their lowest point in over a decade. Cable television hit a 16-year low. BLEAK.

Streamers have more queer representation than cable and broadcast characters put together, but we have lost almost 100 characters from streamers as well, so even that isn’t great news. And combining streaming, cable, and broadcast, of all LGBTQ+ characters, 44% of them are characters of color, which is the lowest percentage since GLAAD’s 2017-2018 report.

Pride points out that it seems wild to imagine because some of the buzziest shows of the last few years feature queer characters: The Hunting Wives, Hazbin Hotel, Pluribus, Stranger Things, Heated Rivalry. I don’t think this show made it into the count, but we also have Sterling Point and now The Body. Queer people show up for shows that feature them, and queer people are great at telling unique stories. Alas, too many higher-ups lean on outdated Christian ideals and won’t invest in us in an effort to silence us.

This is especially wild because, while it reflects what the political times want you to believe (that queer people are outsiders, among other things), it doesn’t reflect the actual statistics. Every generation reports identifying as gayer than the last, so representation should also be at a steady increase to reflect reality, not a drastic decrease.

The actual numbers of LGBTQ+ characters on broadcast and cable shows are harrowing to look at. There are dozens of characters on any given TV show, and dozens of shows on each network, and yet the highest number among them is HBO with 15 characters. The second-highest is a big drop down, with Fox and Starz coming in with 10 characters each.

The numbers start off a little more promising for streaming, with 116 on Netflix, but then they also start dropping dramatically, with 68 on Prime Video and then again a steep drop to Hulu with 24.

I’m sure you, like I have, felt the shift even before you saw these numbers. Here at Autostraddle, we used to have to have a weekly TV roundup because there were so many queer characters on cable and broadcast shows that we couldn’t keep up with individual recaps. We used to do Pop Culture Fix twice a week to keep up with the news coming at us from all angles. And now there aren’t enough recurring characters for a weekly roundup and barely enough news for 10-15 links a week in a pop culture roundup.

It’s disheartening to see these numbers go down more and more every year when we were in such a steady incline for so long, but the fact is: We’re still here. We’re still out here writing well-rounded characters and telling our stories and watching and supporting the LGBTQ+ characters we DO still have on TV. We will not go quietly into the night. We will keep shouting and keep showing up for the queer shows doing it right until these numbers make sense again.

More queer pop culture news (that’s less depressing)

+ Phoebe Bridgers was the musical guest on this weekend’s SNL

+ Former wee lesbian (on Derry Girls) Nicola Coughlan doubles down on her pro-trans, anti-Harry Potter stance and we love her for it

+ Beanie Feldstein had nothing but lovely things to say about working with Ariana Grande on Focker-In-Law

+ Kate McKinnon and Queen Latifah are among those listed to be part of the NBC100 Live Celebration next month

+ Sarah Paulson and Holland Taylor have no plans to marry; Sarah Paulson doesn’t even like the idea of someone calling her a “wife”

+ The Hunting Wives stars Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman play fuck, U-Haul, kill in an interview, which eventually devolves into them complimenting each other’s past performances

+ Kate Berlant is going to co-host next year’s Spirit Awards

+ Rapper Young Miko has been dubbed the “Sexiest Lesbian Alive” by Curve magazine

+ Aspyn Ovard exposes fellow ex-Mormon socialites to the …

author: Gaurav Kumar
title: How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline
content:
This article

How India’s Cockroach movement maintains nonviolent discipline

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


On Nov. 7, the eve of Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, the leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, or CJP, including founder Abhijeet Dipke, were not at home. They were marching in Kochi, a port city in the southern state of Kerala, nearly 1,300 miles from Delhi. 


The march echoed the two demands the movement had been shouting in Delhi’s streets since the first week of October: Scrap the nationwide recheck of voter rolls that began in June 2025, and sack the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar. 


The Cockroach movement came into being in May of this year and won its first victory in July, pushing India’s education minister out of office over a leaked national medical entrance exam. The open question then was whether

a movement with no one leader and no office

 would still be around after winning its first fight. It is, and while it still has no office, it has picked a much bigger fight. Not an exam this time, but the vote itself.


The Election Commission, which runs India’s elections, is rechecking every one of India’s nearly one billion voters. In the name of clearing the rolls of the dead, the duplicated, people who have moved and what its

June 2025 order

 called “foreign illegal immigrants,” it has

purged more than 130 million

 voters. In Delhi alone, the cleanup has knocked 4.76 million people, nearly a third of the city’s electorate, off the voter list. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, or BJP, strongly backs the recheck, saying that it’s necessary to strike undocumented migrants from neighboring Bangladesh, particularly Muslims, who have slipped onto the rolls. Amit Shah, Modi’s home minister and most powerful lieutenant, has defended the recheck as a way to “detect, delete, deport” what he calls infiltrators.

But critics charge

 that the rolls are being manipulated to benefit the BJP. They say the recheck shifts the burden of proof onto voters, and that the people least likely to have the required documents are the ones being dropped. 


Human Rights Watch found

 that the purge has disproportionately affected women, the poor and Muslims; in one area of West Bengal that is nine percent Muslim, more than 92 percent of those deleted were Muslim.

Opposition leaders

 have called the recheck a backdoor version of the National Register of Citizens, a citizenship list the BJP promised in 2019 to extend across India.


Presiding over it all is Kumar, whose commission both referees India’s elections and runs the recheck. He was handpicked by Modi in February 2025 under a new law giving Modi more power over the selection, in a decision announced late at night over the written dissent of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi.


In late September, the national daily

The Indian Express


reported

 that two of the election commission’s three members, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had objected on record at least 14 times in 10 months to decisions and orders tied to the recheck that they say were issued in the commission’s name without their knowledge. (In an official statement, the commission maintained that all of its decisions on the recheck were unanimous.) 


Previous Coverage


What India’s Cockroach Party won — and what’s next


The Cockroach movement, which had been pressuring the government since July over broken promises, responded by calling Kumar the biggest threat to India’s democracy and giving him 48 hours to resign.


When Kumar ignored the movement’s deadline, it took to the streets of Delhi and other cities on Oct. 2, the birthday of Mahatma Gandhi, who led India’s nonviolent struggle for independence.


Unlike most Indian police forces, Delhi’s police do not answer to the city’s elected government but to the federal Home Ministry, run by Shah. It answered the protests the way it did in July, only harder. On Oct. 10 police detained more than 2,000 people in Delhi, opposition leaders and journalists among them, while about 600 were detained in Mumbai, India’s financial capital, and mobile internet went dark in the heart of Delhi.


Two days later

, Jantar Mantar — a square just a short walk from Parliament that has been Delhi’s main protest site for decades and was occupied by the movement for five weeks this summer — was …

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Supreme Court Rejects Trump Administration’s Bid to Restrict Gender Affirming Care for Incarcerated People
content:
On October 21, 2026, the Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration’s request to restrict medical treatment and accommodations for transgender people in federal prisons. The decision allows a lower court order blocking the policy to remain in place while the legal challenge proceeds. The ruling is an important development in the ongoing debate over transgender rights, access to healthcare, and the federal government’s authority over incarcerated people.

The dispute began after President Donald Trump issued an executive order restricting federal funding for certain medical treatments for transgender people in government custody. In response, the Bureau of Prisons introduced a policy that would end hormone therapy and gender-affirming surgeries for incarcerated people with gender dysphoria. The policy also sought to restrict certain accommodations for transgender prisoners.

Gender dysphoria is the distress some people experience when their gender identity does not align with their sex assigned at birth. The administration argued that these gender-affirming treatments were not necessary and that restricting them was justified by security and administrative concerns within federal prisons.

However, the policy faced legal challenges from three transgender people incarcerated in federal prisons, including one transgender woman and two transgender men. Their attorneys argued that the new restrictions would force the end of treatments that the Bureau of Prisons had provided to people with gender dysphoria since 1992.

The policy could affect nearly 1,000 incarcerated people in federal custody. The lawsuit raises questions about whether the government can discontinue established medical treatments for incarcerated people and what constitutional protections apply to people in its custody.

A lower federal court blocked the administration from enforcing the policy. The Justice Department then appealed to the Supreme Court, asking the justices to pause that ruling and allow the restrictions to take effect while the case continued. On October 21, the Supreme Court rejected the emergency request in an unsigned order. Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas stated that they would have granted the request. The decision leaves the lower court’s order in place, preventing the administration from immediately enforcing the restrictions.

However, the Supreme Court’s decision does not resolve the underlying lawsuit or determine whether the administration’s policy is constitutional. The legal challenge will continue in the lower courts.

The case highlights the challenges transgender people face when seeking health care in settings where the government controls their medical decisions. Incarcerated people depend on prison authorities for access to doctors, medication, and other necessary services so when a policy restricts particular treatment, people in custody may have limited options for obtaining care independently.

Although the ruling does not end the case, it prevents the Trump administration from immediately implementing the restrictions while the legal proceedings continue. The outcome of the lawsuit will have important consequences for transgender people in federal prisons if the restrictions are placed and as the case moves forward, it shows the importance of questioning how government policies affect vulnerable populations and how government decisions apply to people whose freedom and access to healthcare are already limited.

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .

author: Joshua Davis, Whitney K. Taylor
title: Federal Government Is Targeting Officials Who Are Trying to Hold ICE Accountable
content:
This story was co-published with


Truthout

.


In the months leading up to the 2026 midterm elections, congressional Republicans and federal prosecutors have targeted dozens of local officials in cities and counties across the country that have adopted some sanctuary policies. The investigations have increasingly focused on prosecutors and law enforcement officers, many of whom have publicly announced plans to go after Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents who commit crimes in their jurisdictions or refuse demands to cooperate with federal immigration policing.


In total, 65 officials in 16 states have been targeted since January, according to a review of documents released by the

House Judiciary


Committee

 and the

Department of Justice

 (DOJ), as well as interviews with senior officials who have direct knowledge of individual investigations. The House Judiciary Committee has issued subpoenas and other demands for testimony, documents, and records to more than 40 officials, 15 of them local prosecutors. Alongside that, the DOJ has initiated investigations into 50 local or state officials since 2025, including five involving local prosecutors. In all, 17 local prosecutors have been swept up in House Judiciary or DOJ investigations and lawsuits related to immigration policies.


House Judiciary Committee Chair Rep. Jim Jordan said in a recent

report

 that “Democrats’ open-borders policies at the federal level and sanctuary policies at the state and local level allow millions of illegal aliens to pour into the country and ensure that criminal aliens, after encountered by local law enforcement, are released back into American communities,” echoing language the committee has commonly used in its investigations.


Many experts describe these investigations as unprecedented, and view the move as retaliation against local officials who refuse to cooperate with federal immigration agents or threaten legal action against ICE officers.


“These [prosecutors] are being intentionally intimidated by congressional and federal authorities,” said Mona Sahaf, the director of the Reshaping Prosecution initiative at the Vera Institute of Justice. “The use of [the] DOJ to target perceived political opponents is new. It’s busting norms, and it’s highly dangerous.”


The targeting of local prosecutors appears to be a matter of policy in the second Trump administration. “

Sanctuary Jurisdictions Directives

” issued by the attorney general’s office on February 5, 2025, held that the DOJ Civil Rights Division should “identify state and local laws, policies, and practices that facilitate violations of federal immigration laws or impede lawful federal immigration operations,” and “where appropriate, take legal action to challenge such laws, policies, or practices.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


The DOJ, in a June 18

press release

 announcing an investigation into local officials in Philadelphia — including District Attorney Larry Krasner — concerning a policy prohibiting federal agents from wearing masks, said that its “series of lawsuits brought by the Civil Division” targeted “illegal policies designed to thwart federal law enforcement across the country.”


Rebecca Roiphe, the Joseph Solomon Distinguished Professor of Law at New York Law School, said the investigations into local prosecutors represented “a wholesale abandonment” of the principle of separation between the DOJ and the political branches of government. “This administration has pretty openly suggested that it is normal and appropriate and even laudable for the political branches to have some degree of control over the Department of Justice,” she said.


Referring to the DOJ investigations, Roiphe said, “The bottom line is that these federal prosecutions can end up threatening local prosecutors to fall in line with federal priorities, and that’s illegitimate in our system.”


These overlapping investigations, reports, and the DOJ directives follow the Heritage Foundation’s

Project 2025 threat to “initiate legal action against” prosecutors

 who refuse to adhere to the priorities of the Trump administration. For many of the targeted prosecutors, the political influence has become impossible to ignore.


Among the targeted is Parisa Dehghani-Tafti, the top prosecutor in Arlington, Virginia, who drew the ire of Representative Jordan’s …

author: Fraser Needham
title: Outgoing Green Party leader says Carney is the most ‘opaque, unaccountable person in politics’
content:
Elizabeth May says Prime Minister Mark Carney is perhaps the most challenging party leader she has had to work with in more than four decades in politics.


“Accountability is really important and Mr. Carney is the most opaque, unaccountable person in politics I think I have ever seen,” the Green Party MP said.


May stepped down as Green Party leader earlier this month, making way for former Kitchener, Ontario MP Mike Morrice to take over the party’s reins.


She will continue on as the MP for the riding of Saanich-Gulf Islands in British Columbia.


One of the reasons May voted in favour of the 2025 budget was Carney’s pledge to respect Canada’s Paris commitments on climate change.


With the Liberal government’s continued backing of oil and gas projects, it is now highly unlikely Canada will meet these commitments.


Carney, a former governor of both the Bank of Canada and Bank of England, has often been touted as the right leader at the right time due to the country’s ongoing trade issues with the Trump administration in the U.S.


However, May said his credentials may not be as suitable as they seem.


“He comes with a very impressive resume and a lot of people assume he’s an economist and a banker,” she said. “He’s really a banker. Economists are capable of saying let’s take a project like pipelines and before we throw billions of public dollars at it, can we do a cost/benefit analysis?


“Is there a market for diluted bitumen in other countries around the world? Is there a reason we want to violate Indigenous rights and bulldoze these things through with bills like C-5 and C-39? He’s not held to account very much.”


In spite of it all, Carney and the Liberals continue to ride high in the polls. May has a theory of why this is the case.


“It’s like when you are on a highway and all the traffic slows down because you are rubbernecking an accident over there. If we keep our eyes on the road in Canada, we can see some flaws with Mr. Carney but if we’re rubbernecking and looking at, ‘Oh my God, the White House,’ it’s really easy for Mr. Carney not to be held to the same standards that previous prime minsters would have been for their actions.”


‘There needs to be a guarantee that the accountability does fall with the government,’ says AMC Grand Chief Kyra Wilson. Photo: Todd Lamirande/APTN.


First Nations water


The head of the Assembly of Manitoba Chiefs says the organization has a number of issues with the Carney government’s First Nations Clean Water Act (Bill C-37) including the fact that it does not include access to clean drinking water as a human right.


“There needs to be a guarantee that the accountability does fall with the government,” Grand Chief Kyra Wilson said. “We always need to ensure that government is upholding the treaties. First Nations signed treaties with the Crown. It’s Canada’s duty and obligation to uphold those treaties. So, when we’re talking about safe drinking it’s not up to First Nations people to prove the case. It’s Canada’s obligation to uphold all of that.”


Wilson was in Ottawa this week to serve as witness before the House of Commons Indigenous and Northern Affairs Committee on Bill C-37.


She also said AMC takes issue with the fact the legislation was drafted without sufficient consultation from First Nations.


Arctic drilling


The minister of Northern and Arctic Affairs said oil and gas exploration off the coast of the Arctic will not move forward without the necessary consultation with Inuit organizations and environmental safeguards.


“We will be working hand-in-hand with the Indigenous groups in the north to understand whether we should move the Tariuq Accord (2023 co-management and revenue-sharing agreement for offshore petroleum resources signed between Canada, Inuvialuit Corporation and the Government of the Northwest Territories) forward,” Rebecca Chartrand said. “The governance is there, there’s still much work to do on making decisions.


“So, the decisions will rest on whether we have sound environmental assessments ensuring that we’re protecting the marine ecosystems and this comes directly from the early engagement meetings that I have held with the leadership in the north.”


The 2026 federal budget pledges $11 million over four years to support Arctic offshore governance which has led some to question whether or not the Carney government is going to lift the moratorium on offshore oil and gas activity signed between the previous Trudeau government and …

author: Esperanza
title: Danzar con la cámara: “A 26 pixeles de distancia” llega al 7º FestivalPICNIC de Valdivia
content:
Hacer de la boca una escena expandida por la medialidad es uno de los imaginarios posibles de Tecnocorporeidades, proyecto de creación artística liderado por Nirvana Sepúlveda y Loreto García, quienes trabajan la relación cuerpo-tecnología combinando danza contemporánea, performance y proyección en tiempo real. “No es nuestro propósito instalar un mensaje de cómo nos relacionamos con la tecnología, sino más bien provocar en torno a esta relación”.


Por Morín Ortiz.


Un proyector, una pantalla, un notebook, tres cámaras web, un micrófono, un foco led, dos aros de luz y tres cuerpos que producen movimientos y voces expandidas, componen el universo de “A 26 pixeles de distancia”. Obra de danza contemporánea de Tecnocorporeidades que, en 40 minutos, “produce ciberespacios eróticos, lúgubres y lúdicos, donde el cuerpo físico se disuelve en un cuerpo digitalizado que desborda los límites de lo real”, dice la sinopsis de esta obra para mayores de 18 años. 


Dirigida por Nirvana Sepúlveda y Loreto García, quienes se conocieron en el Centro de Danza Espiral para luego seguir su formación en danza en la Academia de Humanismo Cristiano, en Santiago. Desde entonces, se sintieron atraídas. Por el afán de investigar de Loreto García, quien además es socióloga, y por la desinhibida creatividad de Nirvana Sepúlveda, quien danza desde pequeña y practica burlesque. Entonces comenzaron a crear en contextos sociales marcados por las tomas feministas, la revuelta social chilena y la pandemia. Hoy la tecnología media la mayor parte del tiempo esta relación creativa y afectiva, porque Loreto vive en Temuco y Nirvana en Barcelona.


Pero el nacimiento de esta experimentación escénica tuvo lugar en Casa Varas de Temuco el año 2021, y luego en el centro cultural Ceina de Santiago, donde las investigaciones en torno a la proyección de danza en tiempo real devinieron en una performance, que hoy se convirtió en la primera de tres escenas que componen la obra. Recuerdan que por estos años las habitaban reflexiones pandémicas del cómo hacer contacto e insistir en el encuentro pese a las pantallas. “La danza, que piensa el cuerpo, tiene que pensar en este cuerpo que ya no es solo físico, sino que está expandido en múltiples redes imaginarias y virtuales”, señala Nirvana.


El nombre de “A 26 pixeles de distancia” es una cita del texto “Realidad virtual” del libro “Enciclopedia del amor en los tiempos de porno” (Editorial Cuarto Propio, 2014) de Lucía Egaña Rojas y Josefa Ruiz-Tagle. Esta y las oraciones finales “No soy real. Ya no me queda nada de humanidad, solo el deseo”, hicieron eco en Tecnocorporeidades por propiciar una visión expandida del cuerpo.


“Desarrollamos interacciones del cuerpo con la imagen desde una propuesta

cyborg

, que entiende el cuerpo como una figura híbrida que desdibuja los límites entre lo humano y lo más que humano y crea alianzas políticas basadas en el deseo por lo otro», comparte Loreto.


Más que una búsqueda discursiva, este trabajo escénico explora las operaciones técnicas mediante las cuales “producimos afectos y efectos con la tecnología. Un lugar experimental a partir de la relación cotidiana que tenemos con ella”. Proceso que les llevó a pensar “en el binarismo como mecanismos de producción de subjetividades y desde ese lugar, el proyecto Tecnocorporeidades nos permite construir otros imaginarios en torno a la sexualidad, al género, a las posibilidades que tiene un cuerpo”.


El equipo de “A 26 pixeles de distancia” lo componen Nirvana Sepúlveda y Loreto García en la dirección e interpretación, Yoko Pérez y Tiwa Labastida también como intérpretes, Nicolette Michael en diseño integral e iluminación, Samuel Martínez en asistencia técnica e iluminación, Carlos Contreras como realizador audiovisual y fotógrafo, Álvaro Núñez en composición musical, Matías Vergara en operación técnica, Lukas Julio en producción y Morín Ortiz en comunicaciones.


Con casi una decena de presentaciones autogestionadas en Santiago, Temuco y Collipulli


Tecnocorporeidades está en pleno desarrollo de un proyecto de Circulación Nacional financiado por el Fondo Nacional de Fomento y Desarrollo de las Artes Escénicas, convocatoria 2026. Con el que se presentaron en el Festival LOFT de Concepción y les tendrá en el Festival PICNIC de Valdivia y en la Carpa Trashumantes en Temuco.


Con un espacio de formación y una exhibición, llegarán hasta el 7º Festival PICNIC del Centro Cultural Bailarines de los Ríos, el jueves 19 de noviembre …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Lesbicidios nunca más: Emoción por la sentencia y deuda con Sofía
content:
La condena a Barrientos contempló por primera vez en la Justicia la orientación sexual de las víctimas. La sentencia provocó emoción, es un punto de partida para los derechos de las mujeres lesbianas y deja deudas. La reparación que falta.


Por Maby Sosa. Fotos: Ariel Gutraich. Edición: María Eugenia Ludueña.


Fue un crimen de odio.

Lo confirmó la justicia

 este miércoles 18 de noviembre cuando en la sentencia del juicio contra Justo Fernando Barrientos lo condenó por “homicidio agravado con ensañamiento y alevosía por odio a la orientación sexual de las víctimas”. Barrientos las mató por lesbianas, y la cantidad de pruebas (muchas menos de las que se evaluaron) así lo demostró en los seis meses que duró el proceso judicial.


La noticia, en las afueras de Tribunales, fue recibida bajo una intensa lluvia que se desencadenó casi a la misma hora que se conociera la condena. Lágrimas, gritos, sonrisas, abrazos y cánticos se multiplicaron entre les activistas que esperaban desde primeras horas de la mañana por el ingreso de Tucumán al 1300.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Presentes (@presenteslatam)


“Lo que le hicieron a ellas nos lo hicieron a todes”


La ultima jornada del juicio arrancó con las palabras finales del asesino de las tres mujeres. En la pequeña sala donde se desarrolló el debate oral, la defensa integrada por Ricardo Richiello y Florencia Díaz Cantón -que días antes habían pedido la absolución de Justo Fernando Barrientos por falta de pruebas-, le acercó el micrófono. El acusado habló: “Me siento inocente”.  Sus palabras no fueron más que la confirmación de que existe un contexto de odio hacia las diversidades sexuales. De acuerdo a los últimos informes, las agresiones aumentaron con la llegada del gobierno de Javier Milei. El ataque en el hotel de Barracas, en mayo de 2024, fue diez días después de que Nicolás Márquez, el “biógrafo” del actual presidente,

difundiera un marcado mensaje de odio

 en una entrevista realizada por Ernesto Tenembaun en Radio con Vos.


Ayer al mediodía, luego de que se cortara el segmento entre las calles Talcahuano y Uruguay, se realizaron las diversas actividades planeadas para esperar la resolución del tribunal integrado por los jueces Adrián Pérez Lance, Juan Manuel Grangeat y Cinthia Oberlander. El nerviosismo previo a la lectura de la sentencia se convirtió en una celebración catártica

cuando se leyó el veredicto

 del Tribunal Oral en lo Criminal Correccional N°5 que condenó a Barrientos como autor de los lesbicidios de Pamela Cobbas, Roxana Figueroa y Andrea Amarante, y en grado de tentativa en relación al ataque de Sofía Castro Riglos.


Sin embargo, quedó el sabor amargo del rechazo a las

medidas de reparación para Sofía Riglos Castro

, la única sobreviviente del ataque, que la querella encabezada por Luciana Sánchez había solicitado.


Bajo una incesante lluvia, Samanta Pedrozo quien encabezó la querella colectiva por parte de la Federación Argentina de Lesbianas, Gays, Bisexuales y Trans (FALGBT) salió del edificio de justicia entre aplausos y lágrimas. Frente a la carpa de la Coordinadora Lesbicidios Nunca Más donde sobre un papel brillante se leía “Pamela, Roxana, Andrea, ¡presentes!” la abogada abrió una pequeña conferencia de prensa.


“Fue un proceso muy difícil y complejo, hace dos años venimos acompañando este caso”, dijo Pedrozo. Ayer recordó que se enteró del caso por una amiga que le escribió preocupada. “Mataron a tres lesbianas y están tirando todas las cosas de ellas a la calle. ¿Qué podemos hacer?”, recuerda que le dijo. Desde entonces, se acercó a las asambleas que, en ese entonces, se convocaban para pedir justicia. Tiempo después, desde la FALGBT la llamaron para llevar adelante la querella.


“Fueron meses de escuchar testimonios, de poder descubrir ese elemento que era tan difícil de probar: el odio. Fuimos escarbando, interrogando y pudimos demostrar que la muerte de estas chicas no fue un hecho aislado, fue un hecho que ocurrió en un contexto de odio y discriminación”, destacó la abogada querellante. “Lamentablemente está pasando,  sigue pasando y va a seguir pasando porque tenemos un gobierno que nos discrimina. Y cuando los discursos de odio vienen de allá arriba, es muy difícil para las diversidades, para las mujeres y también para las infancias sobrevivir a esta ola de odio.”
