author: Thiago Domenici
title: PL Samuel Klein é aprovado no Senado e vai à sanção presidencial
content:
No mesmo plenário em que encaminhou o ajuste fiscal do governo, o Senado também aprovou, em votação simbólica, nesta quarta-feira, 18 de novembro, um projeto que nasceu de uma reportagem da

Agência Pública

.


O

PL 4186/2021

, conhecido como PL Caso Klein ou PL Samuel Klein, amplia de três para 20 anos o prazo para que vítimas de crimes sexuais sofridos na infância ou na adolescência recorram à Justiça e sejam indenizadas.


No Senado, o projeto recebeu apenas uma emenda de redação, que não altera seu conteúdo principal. O texto segue agora para o presidente Lula (PT), que terá 15 dias úteis, contados a partir do recebimento, para sancioná-lo. Como o projeto prevê vigência imediata, o novo prazo de 20 anos passará a vigorar na data da publicação da lei. 


O texto foi apresentado a partir da investigação na qual a

Pública

 revelou, há mais de cinco anos, denúncias de exploração sexual de meninas e mulheres envolvendo Samuel Klein, fundador das Casas Bahia. “A série de reportagens da

Pública

 foram fundamentais para que o Brasil conhecesse esse problema e nos inspirou muito para que a gente pudesse protocolar esse projeto de lei”, afirmou um das deputadas autoras, Sâmia Bomfim (PSOL-SP). 


A deputada conta que também foi procurada pela vereadora Bruna Biondi (PSOL-SP), que acompanhava os desdobramentos do caso em São Caetano do Sul, a cidade-sede da rede varejista. A partir desse contato e das informações reunidas pela investigação, as parlamentares apresentaram a proposta em novembro de 2021, que também contou com a participação de Fernanda Melchionna (PSOL-RS). 


O que prevê o texto aprovado 


Pelo texto aprovado, o prazo de 20 anos começará a contar quando a vítima completar 18 anos – ou seja, ela poderá, em regra, ajuizar a ação até os 38 anos. A mudança limita-se à reparação dos danos e não altera as regras de responsabilização criminal dos agressores. “Não foi um prazo que a gente tirou da cabeça. A gente quer equiparar à legislação da esfera criminal”, explicou Sâmia Bomfim.


Na esfera criminal, a prescrição varia conforme a pena prevista para cada delito e pode chegar a duas décadas. Nos casos de violência sexual contra crianças e adolescentes, a contagem, em regra, só se inicia na maioridade. 


O projeto busca aproximar as condições oferecidas nos dois campos: enquanto o processo criminal trata da punição do agressor, a ação civil permite à vítima pleitear indenização. A intenção é que ela tenha mais tempo para recorrer a ambos os caminhos e não perca tão cedo a possibilidade de obter reparação.


“Mesmo para mulheres adultas, a gente demora às vezes anos para se dar conta da gravidade da violência que a gente vivenciou. Imagina para uma menina de 14, de 16 anos”, disse a deputada. Segundo ela, muitas vítimas só conseguem reconhecer a violência sofrida e buscar ajuda quando já são adultas, o que torna o prazo atual insuficiente. Se a vítima tem menos de 16 anos, a contagem só começa quando ela atinge essa idade. Na prática, quem sofreu abuso na infância pode, em regra, ter apenas até os 19 anos para pedir reparação. Em algumas situações, a existência de uma investigação ou de um processo criminal pode adiar esse limite. Ainda assim, quando o prazo começa a correr, pode se esgotar antes que a vítima tenha condições e entendimento para recorrer à Justiça.


Uma conquista para as mulheres


Para Sâmia, a aprovação é uma resposta às dificuldades enfrentadas pelas mulheres que denunciaram o empresário, mas pode beneficiar também vítimas de outros casos de violência sexual. “Eu acho que é uma reparação para as vítimas do Caso Klein, para as vítimas dos demais casos, mas também é uma reparação simbólica e fundamental para todas as mulheres brasileiras”, disse.


No plenário, a votação do projeto foi acompanhada pelas autoras do projeto e também pela vereadora Bruna Biondi. Eleita em 2020 pelo mandato coletivo Mulheres por Mais Direitos, Bruna passou a atuar em defesa das vítimas de Samuel Klein depois da publicação das denúncias da

Pública

. Em São Caetano do Sul, a vereadora mobilizou o mandato para cobrar justiça e questionar as homenagens públicas ao empresário, conhecido como “rei do varejo”.


“A

Pública

 deu luz a um tema que a elite política de São Caetano sempre soube, mas nunca levou a público e nunca debateu com seriedade”, afirmou a vereadora. Além de ter participado da articulação do PL, ela integra desde 2021 as mobilizações para retirar o nome de Samuel Klein de espaços públicos da …

author: Nahuel Lag
title: La economía agroecológica avanza en América: lecciones desde los movimientos
content:
Por Nahuel Lag


Desde Perú


¿Qué economías agroecológicas queremos? Es la pregunta que se instaló en Pisco (Perú), en el encuentro de "Intercambios de Aprendizajes de las Américas sobre Economías de la Agroecología", que reunió a 60 organizaciones de 15 países, con el respaldo de Agroecology Fund. El análisis partió de lo que está en marcha: mercados locales, Sistemas Participativos de Garantías (SPG), comercialización, financiamiento, agregado de valor y cooperativismo. 


La anfitriona fue la Asociación Nacional de Productores del Perú (

ANPE

), una organización con economía propia: 281 agrupaciones territoriales, una marca de alimentos certificados y ferias locales. A lo largo de una semana, las diferentes experiencias expusieron el rumbo de las economías agroecológicas, advirtieron los desafíos en un contexto regional amenazado por gobiernos de ultraderecha y evidenciaron la necesidad de profundizar las políticas de fomento en una economía que continúa promoviendo el agronegocio para la exportación de materias primas. El aprendizaje e intercambio fueron profundos y dejaron lecciones e inspiración para el desarrollo de las economías agroecológicas de las Américas. 


“Hay que hacer sinergia e integración entre todas las organizaciones para generar el cambio del sistema convencional”, convocó Moises Quispe, director ejecutivo de la ANPE, y propuso continuar buscando aliados estratégicos para incidir en las políticas públicas y “convencer desde el estómago”. 


Economías agroecológicas: una experiencia continental  


La puerta de entrada del encuentro fue la visita a la

Agroferia Campesina

 de Lima que, con 90 productores de 23 regiones del Perú, ofrece una diversidad de alimentos disruptiva con la uniformidad de las góndolas de los supermercados. 


“El agricultor tiene el conocimiento de cómo cultivar y cocinar los alimentos. La gente valora que quien produce la tierra esté en los puestos y agradecen el acceso a alimentos más nutritivos y sanos”, destaca Jorge Panta, presidente de la Coalición Campesina, que hace 13 años sostiene la feria a la que asisten 6.000 personas por domingo. 


“El comercio es algo que está presente desde siempre, desde las culturas precolombinas los pueblos indígenas tenían intercambios, pero en la modernidad se ha transformado en algo muy concentrado. Entonces, cuando hablamos de agroecología no hablamos sólo de prácticas y técnicas de producción sino de otras cosas como la economía”, señaló Ángela Cordeiro, co-directora del Agroecology Fund, sobre el eje que atravesó los intercambios en Pisco.


Foto: Agroecology Fund


La experiencia de la Agroferia Campesina, en la que participan productores integrantes de la ANPE, no es ajena a las miles de organizaciones que promueven la agroecología desde sus territorios. Los mercados locales son la base de las economías agroecológicas en toda América, el punto de encuentro de “productor a consumidor”. La Red de Mercados Agroecológicos Campesinos del Valle del Cauca (

Redmac

), Colombia, lleva 17 años y reúne 21 mercados. María Fernanda Palacios Salcedo, integrante de la Redmac, compartió su experiencia sobre esos espacios en los que no ocurre solo una relación comercial: quienes se acercan son un “amigo consumidor”.  


Los productores de la Redmac se favorecen de los circuitos cortos de comercialización evitando intermediarios y largas distancias, lo que les permite ofrecer un precio anual por los alimentos. “No competimos con los precios de mercado; establecemos precios justos y fomentamos el valor de los alimentos sanos”, señala María Fernanda e indica también cómo la red transforma la comercialización en un acto solidario de organización, cuidado del territorio y construcción de soberanía alimentaria. Experiencias de mercados locales en Guatemala, Panamá, México, Honduras, Brasil y Perú ratificaron el camino virtuoso de estos mercados y los desafíos para ampliar el abastecimiento y la llegada a más consumidores.  


Los Sistemas Participativos de Garantía (SPG) son una herramienta construida por el movimiento agroecológico para saltar los altos costos en dólares de las certificaciones orgánicas y construir nuevas lógicas de relación. “Por un lado fortalecen el modelo de producción agroecológica con reglas comunes y, por otro, la confianza de los consumidores”, valoró Alfredo Patricio Robles, representante del

Colectivo Agroecológico del Ecuador

 en Pisco. El colectivo sostiene seis sistemas de SPG autónomos y colaborativos en …

author: Andrés
title: «La noche de las ollas»: 25 asociaciones civiles exigen el cese de hostigamientos a Jorge Macri
content:
Foto: Andrés Manrique


Después de la noche de los museos, de los teatros, de las librerías y tantas otras noches promovidas por y para las clases a las que les queda resto económico y mental para el ocio, llega a la Ciudad de Buenos Aires La Noche de las Ollas. Más de 25 organizaciones, ollas y espacios que acompañan a personas en situación de calle en la Ciudad de Buenos Aires realizarán “La Noche de las Ollas”. Bajo el lema “Dejen de hostigarnos”, entre el lunes 23 y el domingo 29 de noviembre, las organizaciones “destaparán la olla” para mostrar el trabajo brindado a quienes más lo necesitan. Visibilizar los hostigamientos que vienen sufriendo por parte del Gobierno de la Ciudad, a través de la Policía de la Ciudad y del Ministerio de Espacios Públicos, que les exigen permisos que no existen para una tarea que no está tipificada como contravención. Impiden u obstruyen el reparto de comida, intimidan y realizan detenciones arbitrarias de integrantes de ollas y organizaciones. Se reclama por el cese de la persecución y garantía de políticas públicas integrales para las personas en situación de calle. Contactos de prensa Paola 1167410819 Giselle 1169612094.

Por Andrés Manrique, ANRed. 


Persecución y hostigamiento a personas en situación de calle. Apremios ilegales y abuso de autoridad por parte de la Policía de Buenos Aires junto a grupos conformados por el Ministerio de Espacios Públicos con atribuciones que no les corresponden y supuestas prohibiciones sin respaldo legal fueron vaciando las calles de la Ciudad. Ese vacío es otra cara del neofascismo. Conversamos con Ailin, una participante de la olla de Boedo, que actualiza el presente de las ollas populares en la ciudad.


¿Desde hace cuánto participás en la olla?


La Olla Popular de Boedo surgió desde la Asamblea Autoconvocada de Boedo, que se encuentra en pausa, aunque la olla continúe. Y yo estoy desde que se fundo la olla, hace dos años.


¿Qué cambió entre el momento en que empezaste y hoy?


Al principio no eran tantas las personas que se acercaban a buscar un plato de comida. De hecho, hace dos años, cuando comenzamos teníamos que salir a buscar a las personas. Ahora cada día son más.


¿Cómo consiguen la mercadería?


Todo es autogestivo, no recibimos ningún tipo de ayuda del Estado ni ninguna ONG ni sectores religiosos. Los alimentos secos los suelen donar de eventos culturales, de articulaciones que tenemos con centros culturales, escuelas, ferias. Los alimentos frescos (carne y verduras) los solventamos con donaciones de dinero que nos hacen conocides, vecines, y la comunidad en general. A veces hacemos rifas también.


¿Qué platos ofrecen?


En invierno cocinamos guisos de fideos, de arroz, de distintas legumbres con una variedad amplia de verduras. Siempre le ponemos carne (de pollo o de cerdo, chorizos). Y en verano, ya que la olla no se toma vacaciones, cocinamos salpicón. La decisión de ponerle carne a la comida fue algo que consideramos necesario debido a que entendemos que para muchas personas es la única posibilidad que tienen de incorporar proteínas.


Foto: Daniel Ávalos


La comida que servimos es la misma que comemos nosotres, quienes organizamos la olla. La preparamos con mucho amor y dedicación y quienes cocinamos disfrutamos de esa tarea porque también en el cocinar encontramos un espacio para nosotras, un espacio de apoyo para conversar sobre nuestros problemas y buscar soluciones, para hablar de política y organizarnos. Hay espacios que suelen quedar invisibilizados de las formas tradicionales de hacer política, nosotres hacemos política desde lo cotidiano, desde la cocina. No solo cocinamos comida, también trabajamos para sostener la vida. Resaltamos que somos mayoría de mujeres que extendemos nuestra labor doméstica de cuidados hacia lo comunitario.


 


¿Cuántas personas acuden por su plato?


Realizamos la olla en la Plaza Mariano Boedo los domingos a las 12.30. Se acercan aproximadamente 120 personas. Muchas de ellas se encuentran en situación de calle, otras son jubiladas, y otras no llegan a cubrir las comidas diarias con sus ingresos o trabajo.


Foto: Andrés Manrique


¿Viste cambios en la composición de quienes van a retirar su plato?


Hay mucha descomposición social, la precariedad estructural genera violencias, consumos, padecimientos, enfermedades, y cada día la situación socioeconómica es más cruda. Esto tiene un impacto en nuestras vidas, tanto para quienes vienen a comer como para quienes participamos de la …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado y llamado Internacional del Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC
content:
Como Frente en Defensa del Guaíba y contra la CMPC hacemos un llamado de solidaridad para enfrentar a la ofensiva ecocida de la multinacional fascista $hilena Celulosa CMPC, comandada por los Matte, en el territorio ancestral Guaraní M’Byá y lafken Guaíba, Barra do Ribeiro, sur de Bra$il.

El pasado miércoles 11 de noviembre se realizó una manifestación y marcha en el centro de Porto Alegre, donde se reunieron más de 300 personas para exigir la retirada total de dicha empresa y su nefasto «Projeto Natureza».

El «Projeto Natureza» es una planta procesadora de celulosa que pretende instalarse a las orillas del Rio Guaíba, en el fundo Barba Negra y en la Ponta da Formiga, territorio sagrado Guaraní M’byá. Su objetivo es duplicar la capacidad de producción total de celulosa de la CMPC. Hoy, cuentan con 44 plantas de procesamiento de celulosa en el continente, 3 de ellas en territorio $hileno, sumado a la planta que ya está instalada a las orillas del Guaíba en el municipio del mismo nombre. CMPC tiene la capacidad de producir 4,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Con el Projeto Natureza, su capacidad de producción podría llegar a 7,5 millones de toneladas de celulosa al año. Las consecuencias a largo plazo son difíciles de dimensionar, pero es sabido que el proyecto incluye el dragado del Guaíba, deforestación del bosque nativo, cambios en las leyes de protección ambiental, contaminación del agua y, sin dudas, la expansión masiva de plantaciones de eucalipto en Brasil, Uruguay y Argentina.

Al finalizar la marcha se realizó una acción directa coordinada en contra de la FEPAM, órgano del gobierno que otorga los permisos ambientales y de instalación a la CMPC. Manifestantes hicieron okupación de la institución, rayaron las paredes exigiendo «FUERA CMPC» y denunciando el actuar corrupto de la FEPAM, quienes ignoran por completo decenas de informes y cuestionamientos técnicos de diversas áreas sobre el impacto real de este proyecto en el territorio. Marcaron las paredes pulcras de ese actual antro de mafiosos que solo sirve como pantalla, ya que sin escrúpulos aprueban cualquier proyecto extractivista que se les ponga en frente.

El río Guaíba es parte medular de la vida en la ciudad de Porto Alegre y la región metropolitana. Es el horizonte con el que nos relacionamos cada día y gran parte del agua potable proviene de las aguas tratadas de este rio. Cuando protestamos contra la CMPC necesitamos que se entienda que esta empresa pretende derramar más desechos en el rio que toda la ciudad en su conjunto. Es un proyecto que básicamente contaminará el agua de consumo público de la región.

El actual gobierno de Lula, que basó su propaganda en ser una “alternativa al fascismo”, apoya y fomenta abiertamente el proyecto de la Familia Matte y la CMPC, que además de usurpar sistemáticamente territorio mapuche, apoyaron la dictadura de Pinochet y promovieron la Masacre de Laja en la que 19 trabajadores de la CMPC fueron fusilados por militares chilenos. El presidente Lula concedió a la CMPC una terminal portuaria de exportación en el puerto de Río Grande, en este puerto la empresa está asociada a Ultramar, empresa de la família Von Appen con infame trayectoria nazi.

Esta concesión transforma al rio Guaíba y a la Laguna dos Patos en hidrobia de madera y celulosa, impactando drásticamente la naturaleza y la pesca artesanal. Todo esto sin respetar y seguir los protocolos Guaraní y menos la convención 169 de la OIT que se supone consulta de manera previa, libre e informada a las comunidades indígenas afectadas. Esta maliciosa colaboración entre el gobierno y la CMPC se logra a través de la entrega de millones de pesos a algunas autoridades ancestrales para otorgar el visto bueno al gobierno, dividiendo a las comunidades y generando rupturas entre ellas.

Sobre la familia Matte es importante hacer memoria de que no es solo dueña de la celulosa CMPC, sino que también es dueña de Colbún, responsable por secar el Lago Chapo en la Región de Los Lagos en $hile, y de la Forestal Mininco, vieja empresa forestal conocida robar tierra mapuche, devastar bosque nativo, secar la tierra y por el asesinato de Alex Lemún de 17 años y de Pablo Marchant de 25, ambos asesinados en contexto de recuperación territorial y defensa de la tierra.

También, en 2021 se hizo famoso Fernando Puga Matte, uno de los integrantes de dicha familia, dueño del condominio de lujo Riñimapu donde trabajaban los «jardineros» que asesinaron a Emilia Milen, la Bau …

author: Rizomatica
title: Juana Paillalef denuncia discriminación racial hacia su familia y la infancia Mapuche en Lavkenmapu
content:
Luego de que la machi Millaray Garrido Paillalef, del territorio Lawen Mapu, Lanalhue, realizara un video denunciando violencia institucional y discriminación en el hospital de Arauco, su madre, Juana Paillalef, quien fue directora del Museo Mapuche de Cañete durante 20 años, junto a Mario Cayupi hacen una reflexión sobre diversas situaciones de discriminación racial hacia su familia.


Juana Paillalef a través de su relato explica cómo han vivido vulneraciones, violencia institucional y discriminación, a través de todas las generaciones de su familia. Ella, su hija y ahora su nieta, ven como se vulneran los derechos de niños, no solo mapuches. Comenta cómo han sido vulnerados en su mogen, en su vida como Mapuche, luego de haber levantado a su hija Machi, quien desde estudiante vivió vulneraciones, en el liceo se le discriminó por el uso de sus chaway y su tukuluwün y en la universidad también existieron educadores que la discriminaron por ser Mapuche. En su primer embarazo también vivió vulneraciones en centros de salud, y ahora en la actualidad denuncian haber vivido discriminación y maltratos por un profesional de la salud del hospital de Arauco en contra de su nieta.


“

Se habla de interculturalidad, cambiando por el racismo, ¿pero qué hemos visto de interculturalida hasta este momento? Seguimos en lo mismo. La colonización ha triturado nuestro pensamiento, nuestras formas de vida, nuestras formas de comportamiento, nuestra forma de exigir nuestros derechos, nos han apagado en vez de abrirnos. Llamo a la población a no dormirse, estar atentos y no dejar de caminar al lado de nuestros niños. Hay muchos niños y jóvenes en colegios que se están levantando como machi, y no hay como atender esas situaciones.”

Radio Kurruf

author: CMI Argentina
title: Santa Fe: ante la crecida del Paraná y la falta de respuestas gubernamentales, las y los vecinos se organizan
content:
Ante la crecida del Río Paraná y frente al abandono total por parte de las autoridades estatales en todos sus niveles, la Asamblea Autoconvocada de Vecinos de Arroyo Leyes y de la costa santafesina convocaron este lunes 16 a una conferencia de prensa frente al Centro de Salud N°13 de Arroyo Leyes exigiendo que se atiendan de forma urgente las demandas de las y los vecinos de la zona. Entre las principales demandas al gobierno provincial, a cargo de Maximiliano Pullaro, y la gestión comunal de Eduardo Luis Lorinz, están que informen un protocolo oficial en caso de una posible catástrofe; la realización de la postergada obra de defensa en el margen Oeste de la Ruta Provincial N°1; la provisión urgente de agua segura, alimentos, medios para cocinar, productos de higiene, repelente, generadores y nafta para zonas afectadas; garantizar un subsidio económico mensual a las familias afectadas durante el período de emergencia; garantizar la estabilidad laboral y el cobro efectivo y total del salario del personal público y privado afectado por la emergencia hídrica; garantizar la salud Pública; accesibilidad a viviendas dignas para las familias afectadas; y la provisión de embarcaciones a vecinos afectados.


Foto: corresponsal.


Por corresponsal, para ANRed.


Desde la asamblea convocaron a una conferencia de prensa el pasado lunes 16 de noviembre frente al Centro de Salud N°13 de Arroyo Leyes, donde advirtieron sobre el estado de las defensas y cuestionaron que no haya partidas previstas para obras en el presupuesto provincial 2027.


Así están las defensas construidas por los propios vecinos de Arroyo Leyes para proteger sus viviendas ante el avance del agua. Foto: Gentileza.


Durante la conferencia de prensa, también adelantaron que continuarán reuniéndose para coordinar acciones con otras asambleas de la Costa, para mantener un espacio de organización y participación que permita visibilizar las dificultades que atraviesan las distintas localidades y avanzar en una agenda común de reclamos frente a la emergencia hídrica.


Foto: corresponsal.


Por la crecida del río en Arroyo Leyes ya hay al menos 150 familias, entre personas evacuadas, autoevacuadas y vecinos/as que todavía permanecen en sus viviendas, sin electricidad desde hace más de tres días y con el agua en el acceso a sus casas. Vecinos/as trasladan sus pertenencias a zonas altas y reclaman por la falta de luz, dado que el comité de emergencia decidió que los lugares que estén anegados van a tener cortes de energía preventivos.


En las inmediaciones funcionan unas seis guarderías náuticas, con aproximadamente 800 embarcaciones, según informó el medio local

Aire de Santa Fe

, y algunos propietarios comenzaron a retirarlas ante el avance del agua. En este marco, las y los residentes afirman que no recibieron respuestas de las autoridades comunales ni provinciales. Ante la falta de respuestas, realizaron un corte de la ruta provincial 1 durante la tarde del pasado domingo 15.


Este es el pliego de revindicaciones:


La exigencia de un protocolo oficial en caso de una posible catástrofe (asistencia, acciones específicas y destinos específicos), dados ya los pronósticos de Instituto Nacional del Agua (INA) y de la Empresa Binacional Yacyretá (EBY)


La exigencia al gobierno provincial de la realización de la postergada obra de defensa en el margen Oeste de la Ruta Porvincial N°1, desde el kilómetro 8 al 22, de manera consensuada con la comunidad. Sin desmedro de la urgencia de la obra, que debe comenzar cuanto antes, se exige su inclusión en el presupuesto 2027, además del refuerzo, alteo y mantenimiento de todos los anillos de defensa de la provincia.


La provisión urgente de alimentos, medios para cocinar, productos de higiene, repelente y agua segura para zonas afectadas.


La provisión de agua segura a toda la población de la costa que depende del suministro de las napas, hoy en riesgo de contaminación producto de la crecida.


Garantizar un subsidio económico mensual durante el período de emergencia que sea suficiente para garantizar la canasta básica de las familias afectadas, la mayoría de las cuales viven del trabajo en negro o por cuenta propia.


Garantizar la estabilidad laboral y el cobro efectivo y total del salario del personal público y privado afectado por la emergencia hídrica.

author: Unknown
title: Doğan: Individual armament is a problem for society as a whole
content:
Ikram Doğan, Istanbul Branch Chair of the Association of Social Workers (SHUDER), spoke to ANF about the impact of individual gun ownership and violence on public health. Doğan stressed that violence cannot be explained solely by individuals' anger management problems or aggressive tendencies, drawing attention to economic insecurity, inequality, the perception of impunity and easy access to firearms.


According to media reports, 110,470 unlicensed firearms were seized across Turkey in 2025. Between 1 January and 26 March 2026, another 25,580 unlicensed firearms were confiscated.


Doğan said that individual gun ownership cannot be addressed solely as a matter of security and public order, emphasising the need to strengthen public social services and develop social policies aimed at preventing violence.


'The structural causes of violence are being obscured'


Doğan said that explaining incidents of violence solely through individual characteristics conceals the social dimensions of the problem.


Doğan said: "In an environment where gun ownership is becoming increasingly widespread, inequalities are deepening and social problems are increasingly being resolved through power relations, explaining violence solely in terms of individuals' anger management, aggressive tendencies or personal pathologies makes the structural causes of the problem invisible.


Violence is a consequence. The social inequalities that produce it, economic insecurity, gender relations, exclusion, discrimination, polarisation, the perception of impunity and the resulting distrust of justice, easy access to firearms, the normalisation of violence in everyday life and problems with public security policies must all be considered together. It is impossible to explain violence without questioning the social, economic and political conditions that produce it."


'Access to firearms increases the risk of fatal consequences'


Doğan said that easier access to firearms contributes to the spread of individual gun ownership and encourages the use of force and the perception of violence as a means of resolving social problems.


Doğan continued: "Easier access to firearms, in particular, increases the likelihood that even ordinary disagreements arising in everyday life will have fatal consequences. While firearms are increasingly regarded by some individuals as instruments of power and security, they also increase the risk of conflict and violence in social relations. Therefore, individual gun ownership is not merely a problem of individual behaviour but also an issue that must be addressed in terms of public oversight and social security."


'The impact of violence extends beyond those killed or injured'


Doğan said that the most visible impact of individual gun ownership on public health is the threat it poses to the right to life, noting that armed attacks, murders, injuries and suicides place a serious burden on public health.


Doğan stressed that the problem is not limited to those who lose their lives or suffer physical injuries. Doğan said: "Those who witness armed violence, those who lose loved ones, those who live under the threat of violence and everyone who feels unsafe are also direct or indirect victims of this process."


Doğan outlined the effects of individual gun ownership: "The threat of armed violence and witnessing violence can cause fear, anxiety, trauma, depression and symptoms of post-traumatic stress. A constant sense of threat negatively affects individuals' daily lives and social relationships.


When violence and firearms become part of everyday life, they undermine children's sense of security, developmental processes and social relationships. They increase the risk of children learning to regard violence as a demonstration of power or a method of solving problems.


The presence of firearms in the home can increase the risk of domestic conflicts, particularly violence against women, resulting in fatal consequences. It can pose serious threats to the lives and safety of women and children.


When people do not feel safe in public spaces, this leads to greater social insecurity, withdrawal from social life and a weakening of mutual trust. Violence therefore damages not only individuals' health but also the quality of social relationships.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Trilateral Meeting Between Xi, Trump, and Putin Results In Little Substance, But Taiwan Should Remain Cautious
content:
THE TRILATERAL SUMMIT between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Chinese President Xi Jinping that was held earlier this week resulted in little of substance. Nevertheless, the summit should raise risks for Taiwan, seeing as Taiwan could stand to have its freedoms traded off through Trump’s unpredictable dealmaking.

Indeed, if the summit was intended to harken back to Yalta in the dealmaking that ended World War II, it did not have such significance. The three leaders came to an agreement about peace and nuclear disarmament, as well as boosting fuel production.

Ukraine came up indirectly, and even as Russian strikes on Ukraine continued during the meeting and its talk of peace, no agreement was made between the US and Russia on it. As reflected in the eventual readout, during the meeting, Trump lashed out at the International Criminal Court in what might be read as a conciliatory gesture to Putin, seeing as he is wanted by the court.

It may be fortunate for Taiwan, then–as with Ukraine–that it did not come up in the meeting. It is thought that the possibility of Trump taking some stance on Taiwan that would have signed away its freedoms to China was lessened by allegations against Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang that he was involved in an affair with a Chinese spy. It is probable that foreign policy hawks in the US leveraged on the scandal and framed the affair between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang as one involving Chinese spying in order to constrain Trump’s actions in the meeting.

It proves dangerous, however, for both Taiwan and Ukraine that Trump, Xi, and Putin would have a meeting without any Ukrainian or Taiwanese leaders present. And the presence of Xi is concerning for Taiwan, in that he apparently is seen by Trump as a stakeholder in what might otherwise be a bilateral meeting between Trump and Putin. Perhaps this goes to show how the Russian and Chinese governments have become increasingly intertwined in terms of joint interests, however.

Indeed, Xi and Putin are probably well aware of the Democratic wave that swept the US in recent midterm elections. Trump is now a lame duck, but he may still be intent on exercising power. Xi and Putin, then, could perhaps take advantage of an eagerness by Trump for quick wins in order to win concessions on Taiwan and Ukraine, much as Trump struck an oil deal with Putin to try and win a quick win in lowering oil prices in the US ahead of the vote. Consequently, it proves important for Taiwan, Ukraine, and other political actors to keep a close eye on moves by the three leaders to hold meetings–and to try and sink the possibility of deals that Trump may be willing to sign with Xi and Putin ahead of the actual meetings taking place, or in order to constrain his actions.

Domestically, however, one expects some of the usual suspects to actually take the rhetoric of peace by Trump, Xi, and Putin at face value. Insofar as the KMT has tried to sink closer ties between the US and Taiwan by claiming that this would lead Taiwan to suffer a fate like Ukraine, with a view of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine as caused by Ukraine getting too close to NATO, it is possible that the KMT would embrace the view that Taiwan, too, should seek a bargain with China, and that Trump could perhaps be convinced to back such a bargain. And it is also not impossible that Taiwan factors into the calculus of such leaders. Intrusions by Russian fighter jets into Taiwan’s Air Defense Identification Zone, in an apparent first, earlier this week were likely timed ahead of the meeting as a means of projecting power. As it has been twice this week that Russian intrusions have occurred, it is to be seen if this is a new feature of regional security.

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Filipino migrant healthcare workers denounce ICE detention, deportation threats
content:
Image of packaged sent to Balllesteros (photo from CLSU USSC)

Filipino migrant healthcare workers condemned the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown while raising concerns over medical neglect inside US detention facilities.

Speaking at a press conference organized by Tanggol Migrante Movement USA on November 13, two Filipino healthcare workers called for humane treatment and due process for migrants, regardless of their immigration status or profession.

Mariae “LC” Nacu was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in Phoenix, Arizona, on August 22.

The 22-year-old registered nurse had been working at St. Joseph’s Hospital in Phoenix and has a valid employment authorization.

She was held at the Eloy Detention Center for three weeks before her release on bond, according to Tanggol Migrante Movement USA.

The organization said that her bond was set at $17,000 (P1.08 million) on November 13.

Nacu also estimated that she spent around $300 weekly (P19,068) on commissary items and phone calls while detained.

More than two months after her detention, ICE continued to hold her identification documents, including her driver’s license, according to the organization.

“The difficult part was that I wasn’t there [in the detention center] as a nurse. I was another person in detention, locked in a cell, trying to get someone to listen,” Nacu said.

She recalled witnessing a medical emergency involving another detainee and struggling to get someone to listen to her concerns.

Nacu described the separation from loved ones, handcuffing, and transfers between detention facilities without knowing where she was going as “traumatizing and dehumanizing.”

Dr. Veronica Velasquez, a Filipino physical therapist and recipient of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), faces the threat of being deported.

Co-chair of the Los Angeles Kalusugan Collective, Velasquez regularly visits detainees at the Adelanto Detention Center where she witnessed brutality and medical neglect.

Velasquez said that she has organized with Tanggol Migrante Movement USA for two years and continues to support detained migrants despite facing immigration-related uncertainty herself. “I am a healthcare worker who has seen firsthand the brutality inside detention centers. I, myself, am threatened with deportation and have experienced over 23 years of this immigrant injustice system. Even so, I’m here still fighting for my community while the community fights for me.”

She said that nearly 100 community members attended her first court hearing.

Both healthcare workers raised concerns about the treatment of migrants inside US detention facilities, particularly their access to medical attention.

Velasquez said that her experience in visiting detainees exposed her to cases of alleged brutality and medical neglect. “As healthcare workers, we are in a special position to shed light on these issues of migrants in detention […] You cannot deny us from saying that there is medical violence happening in these detention centers.”

Nacu’s account of witnessing another detainee’s medical emergency also underscored the difficulties people in detention face when seeking help.

Her testimony, however, does not independently establish the circumstances or outcome of the medical emergency.

Bulatlat previously reported the case of a Filipino detainee, Kuya G, who underwent a toe amputation after months of alleged medical neglect at the Northwest Detention Center in Tacoma, Washington.

Migrant rights advocates said that detention facility personnel failed to properly diagnose and address his condition.

The case adds to concerns raised by migrant organizations about the treatment and medical care available to people held in immigration detention.

Read: Filipino migrants face inhumane treatment at ICE detention centers

Velasquez raised concerns over the slow response and lack of accountability of Philippine consulates who are supposed to be assisting detained migrants. She cited one case where a consulate called the police on mothers of detainees who were seeking assistance.

Her remarks echo concerns raised by Filipino migrant organizations about the Philippine government’s response to the detention of Filipino nationals in the United States.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Muntinlupa refuses to free 15 Indigenous children despite release order
content:
Fifteen minors arrested by the police last Sunday remain in custody even as 216 adults and five fellow children already walked free from detention on Wednesday.


The Office of the City Prosecutor of Muntinlupa City ordered the release of the Indigenous children from Mindoro Island’s Mangyan community at approximately 9:00 PM on Tuesday. Muntinlupa Mayor Ruffy Biazon also announced on Tuesday the processing of the children’s release.


The city’s Bahay Pag-asa, however, refuses to release the remaining children in their custody, earning condemnation from the group Salinlahi Alliance for Children’s Concerns.


“Bahay Pag-asa [of] Muntinlupa must stop delaying their release and immediately, unconditionally, turn the children over to their families or legal guardians,” Salinlahi said.


Salinlahi revealed that Muntinlupa City’s Social Welfare and Development Office have instructed the children’s parents “to mislead paralegals” by claiming that the children must undergo another week of quarantine.


“If true, this is a deliberate obstruction of the children’s release and an additional form of harassment against already traumatized children and their families,” the group said.


The children’s rights advocates group pointed out that the children’s continued detention constitutes arbitrary deprivation of liberty.


“Bahay Pag-asa is mandated to protect and rehabilitate children—not become an instrument for prolonging their detention and suppressing their rights,” Salinlahi added.


Aged 11 to 14 and arrested with more than 200 other participants of the Lakbayan ng Timog Katagalugan by the police on Sunday, the 15 have been under custody for more than 90 hours as of Thursday morning.


Nine more protesters arrested in Manila on Sunday also remain in custody.


Meanwhile, rights group Karapatan announced a grand welcome for the hundreds of released activists on Thursday at the University of the Philippines campus in Quezon City.


The arrested protesters were supposed to join this week’s massive protests against US President Donald Trump and the US-led Pax Silica microchip supply chain control project.


Trump left the country on Wednesday, failing to sign an agreement with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. Bagong Alyansang Makabayan hailed the postponement of the signing as a “temporary victory,” crediting the protests as one of the reasons for the failure. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

author: Dae-Oup Chang
title: International Labour Solidarity from Below: Reflections on Inter-Asian Solidarity Building of Asia Monitor Resource Centre
content:
Since its establishment in 1976, the Asia Monitor Resource Centre (AMRC) has served as a regional hub for labour solidarity in Asia. This article reflects on the AMRC’s half-century journey towards building inter-Asian labour solidarity. It discusses not only what AMRC has achieved, but also what it has failed to achieve, why it has failed, and what these experiences might tell us about the future of inter-Asian labour solidarity. This is a personal reflection, drawing on my 23 years of involvement with the AMRC in various capacities: as a full-time activist, a member of the Board of Directors, a member of the Regional Council, and Chair of the Board of Directors.


International labour solidarity has long occupied a prominent place in the political imagination of labour movements. Almost every major trade union has declared its commitment to internationalism. However, there is a considerable distance between internationalism as a declared principle and internationalism as an actual process of movement building. Affiliation to international trade unions, participation in international conferences, and occasional solidarity campaigns do not necessarily generate lasting solidarity among workers across national borders.


This distinction between international solidarity as a dead principle and as a living practice was central to an experiment in building bottom-up inter-Asian labour solidarity in which I participated during the 2000s as an AMRC activist coordinating the Asian Transnational Corporation Monitoring Network (ATNC Network). As  one of the regional labour networks AMRC initiated, the ATNC network sought to connect grassroots workers’ organisations across Asia. Its broader ambition was to build an alternative foundation for international labour solidarity in Asia. 


Building a Network from Below


When I joined AMRC in 2003, the ATNC Network already existed as a pilot initiative, with a substantial emphasis on

corporate codes of conduct

. Such an approach was becoming increasingly popular in international labour advocacy, particularly following the emergence of consumer campaigns targeting major international brands during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

1


We were sceptical of the political consequences of this prevailing model of north–south labour solidarity. Our scepticism concerned the underlying structure of solidarity that this approach

reproduced

. Northern organisations possessed the resources, connections, and influence required to pressure major brands, while workers and their organisations in Asian production sites were primarily positioned as

recipients of assistance

. The political focus often shifted from workers’ collective struggles to consumer organisations’strategies and their relationships with corporations.


Such campaigns sometimes achieved meaningful results. They can generate international attention, provide protection to workers, and force employers to negotiate. We did not deny their practical value. However, they had little to do with building the larger collective power of workers. For us, workers’ power was something to be built collectively by workers in and beyond workplaces rather than granted by individual employers’ moral behaviour. 


Therefore, we sought to reverse the direction of the network’s activities. Instead of beginning with corporations and their codes of conduct, we wanted to begin with workers’ struggles, their own organisations emerging from such struggles, and solidarity-based relationships built  between such organisations. 


These relationships developed through practical engagement. A group of workers or worker organisations might initiate a strike or an organising campaign. AMRC and its local partners could support the struggles on the ground. Over time, this process allowed us to include more organisations, whether unions or NGOs. Through such activities, new relationships emerged between organisations participating in the same struggles. 


Our criteria for partnership were therefore not primarily based on size, institutional recognition, or formal representativeness. We were interested in organisations with real connections to workers’ struggles. This frequently meant working with small but independent unions and grassroots NGOs rather than established national trade union centres.


While building a network of such organisations, the network operated through collaborative research, education, organising, and advocacy. Activities involved …

author: John David Parol
title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

author: rti_admin
title: Building Safe Spaces: Women’s Safety Must Mean More Than Protection
content:
A safe workplace is not defined only by the absence of harassment. It is also a place where women can speak, disagree, seek support, and participate in decisions without fear.

We often assume that organizations are safe places because they have rules, policies, and systems in place. But is that enough? A workplace may have a policy against sexual harassment and a committee to receive complaints, yet a woman may still hesitate to speak because she fears being judged, ignored, or facing consequences. This makes me ask a simple question: what does it really mean for a woman to feel safe at work?

Safety is usually understood as protection from harm, injury, or danger. In a workplace, that includes physical safety and freedom from sexual harassment. But it also includes something less visible: the freedom to express an opinion, raise concern, disagree with a colleague, or ask for help without fear of humiliation or retaliation. A woman may be physically safe in an office and still feel unsafe if she cannot speak openly. For me, women’s safety is connected to dignity. It is about being able to work without fear, but also about being treated as a human being whose experiences, feelings, and responsibilities matter.

Physical safety means being protected from violence, injury, threats and other forms of bodily harm. It also includes a safe working environment, appropriate security arrangements, transport where required and access to help in an emergency. Sexual safety means being free from unwanted sexual comments, gestures, messages, touching, harassment and violence. Everyone should be able to decide what happens to their body and should not have to tolerate unwanted behaviour as part of working life. Economic safety includes fair wages, equal opportunities and the ability to earn a livelihood without exploitation or threats. Social and organizational safety means being treated fairly and respectfully, without discrimination, bullying or harassment based on gender, caste, colour or social background.

Psychological safety is equally important. It means being able to express thoughts, ask questions, raise concerns, share ideas and admit mistakes without fear of humiliation or punishment. Amy Edmondson has described it as a shared belief that a team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. Earlier work by Edgar Schein and Warren Bennis in 1965 also discussed psychological safety in relation to organisational learning and change. The central idea is straightforward: people should be able to speak honestly, ask for help and participate without worrying that they will be mocked, ignored or penalised. Psychological safety does not mean avoiding disagreement or accountability. It means that people can engage in difficult conversations without being degraded or threatened.

Safety should be a basic right, not a privilege available only in certain places or under certain conditions. Article 21 of the Constitution of India protects the right to life and personal liberty, and the right to live with dignity has been recognised as part of this constitutional protection. Yet many women continue to experience harassment, discrimination and fear in daily life. When women do not feel safe, the effects go beyond the immediate risk of harm. They may limit their movements, avoid certain jobs, turn down opportunities involving travel or give up professional goals. Insecurity can affect confidence, mental well-being, economic independence and participation in society. It becomes a barrier to equality and empowerment.

For many women, fear begins long before they reach the office. Roads, bus stops, railway stations, public transport, markets and the route home are all part of the working day. Some think twice before travelling alone, returning late or visiting an unfamiliar place. Some ask a father, brother, male relative or friend to accompany them because they believe another person’s presence may protect them from unwanted attention. Instead of feeling free to move independently, they make arrangements simply to feel secure.

A baseline household survey conducted in Delhi in October and November 2012 offers a stark illustration of this fear. The study, carried out by the International Center for Research on Women (ICRW) as part of the Safe Cities programme with UN Women and local partners, found that only 5% of women and girls surveyed ranked public spaces in Delhi as safe from sexual violence. This is sometimes summarized as 95% feeling …

author: Jim McIlroy
title: Activist Stephen Langford released after week in Silverwater
content:
Stephen Langford, long-time solidarity activist and member of Socialist Alliance, was released from Silverwater Correctional Complex on November 19 following a week-long stint after being arrested at a regular protest outside the former office of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in Marrickville.

Rachel Evans, Socialist Alliance candidate for Heffron, told a rally outside Newtown Court on the day of his release that Langford was targeted because he is a committed activist.

“The police came straight up to him at the protest action he takes every week… They said ‘You are under arrest’ but did not clarify what he was charged with,” she said.

“Stephen did not resist arrest, and was taken to Surry Hills police station, and then to Silverwater. He was only offered one phone call … and we were told Stephen would be held for between one to three weeks, and that we could not visit or video link him. They said he could only call us and refused to allow us to leave messages.

“We condemn all levels of police and corrective services for treating him this way. Stephen is a non-violent, peace and anti-war activist, who worked tirelessly to free East Timor, and was later granted an Order of Timor.”

Langford has previously been arrested for breaching bail conditions after pasting an 1816 quote by former NSW Governor Lachlan Macquarie on his statue in Hyde Park. Macquarie said: “All Aborigines from Sydney onwards are to be made prisoners of war and if they resist they are to be shot and their bodies hung from trees in the most conspicuous places near where they fall so as to strike fear into the hearts of surviving natives.”

Macquarie said this before the infamous Appin Massacre on April 17, 1816, in which at least 14 Aboriginal men, women, and children were killed — shot or driven over cliffs — and several others captured, imprisoned and tortured by colonial troops.

Langford's peaceful protest is intended to be an act of truth-telling, revealing the brutality of the colonial government towards First Nations people.

NSW Police imposed strict bail conditions on Langford, including including restricting his movement in a section of Marrickville, where his recent protests have taken place.

“Stephen is kind and generous. He is a retired nurse and feels injustice to others deeply. He would not hurt a fly, and has spent 30 years fighting to win freedom for oppressed peoples all over the world,” Evans said.

“Political graffiti should not be a jailable offence. Stephen should be given an apology and compensation for the way he's been treated.”

Langford is due to appear in court on January 21.

author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.


On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 


When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 


Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 


This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 


In

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 


More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 


So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 


There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to …

author: Jack Munafo
title: City of Newcastle chooses business bottom line over the climate
content:
The Newcastle City Council has voted to ban Rising Tide, Australia’s largest climate activist group, from hosting events on council-owned land. The motion, put by right-wing independent mayor and former weather reporter Gavin Morris, has sought to rid Newcastle of climate protests.

For many years, Rising Tide has forced the Newcastle City Council to confront the reality of hosting the world’s largest coal port. One hundred and fifty million tonnes of coal left the port in 2025, over 95 percent of which was sold to various Southeast Asian countries. Emissions from its usage, which are approximately 1 percent of Earth’s total CO2 emissions each year, are not counted towards Australia’s CO2 emissions.

The council motion passed 7-6. Voting against were three Greens and three Labor councillors. One Labor councillor, failed mayoral candidate Declan Clausen, voted for the bill. He attended the council meeting over Zoom from the COP31 climate conference in Türkiye. 

The council’s ban is not restricted to Rising Tide. It also applies to “its associates, subsidiaries, affiliated Issue Motivated Groups; and individuals”. Who counts as an “issue motivated group or individual” is at the discretion of the council. When interviewed by ABC Radio the morning after the vote, Morris said he “would be comfortable with” the wide-reaching powers of prohibition granted to the council targeting other groups. He specifically mentioned Palestine-related groups as being potentially affected by this motion.

Morris’ principal bugbear is Rising Tide’s annual People’s Blockade, where protesters take to Newcastle Harbour to prevent coal ships from moving into the port. Morris couched his motion in terms of community safety, but Business Hunter CEO Bob Hawes, in his letter of support for the motion, was willing to say the quiet part out loud:

“[Rising Tide] continues to have adverse impacts on regional businesses and the local visitor economy ... Rising Tide supporters might not like what some of these operators do but they are undertaking legal business activities ... and they have a right to undertake them without disruption.”

The operation of the port alone generated about $107 million in 2025, let alone the profits that come from actually selling the goods that move through it. 

Morris also received letters of support from NSW Premier Chris Minns and police minister Yasmin Catley. Their support tells you everything you need to know about Labor’s stance on climate change. These letters came only weeks after Minns’ approval of the largest coal expansion in NSW history, and months after his announcement that the Great Koala National Park will be funded by pay-to-pollute carbon credits.

Morris was elected in February this year. He has taken his election as a mandate from “the community” to clamp down on Rising Tide. We must show him that the Newcastle community stands with Rising Tide and for real action on climate change, not the profits of the coal industry.

author: Brett Wilkins
title: Israel extends imprisonment of Gaza doctor Hussam Abu Safiya for 6 more months
content:
Israeli authorities on November 18 extended the detention without charge of Dr Hussam Abu Safiya, the former director of northern Gaza’s Kamal Adwan Hospital, for another six months, prompting outrage from human rights defenders and renewed calls for the release of the pediatrician and scores of other imprisoned Palestinian medical professionals.

According to Abu Safiya’s lawyer, Nasser Odeh, an Israeli court in Beersheba extended the 53-year-old’s indefinite imprisonment through May 2027.

“Why must I spend another six months away from my family?” Dr Abu Safiya reportedly asked the court, claiming he is being punished for doing his job.

According to Al Jazeera, the court justified the continued detention by declaring that Abu Safiya “poses a threat to the state of Israel.”

Israel claims Abu Safiya is a colonel in Hamas’ Military Medical Services and has shown a photo of the doctor wearing a uniform that Al Jazeera said belongs to the Palestinian Directorate of General Military Medical Services, an organization providing healthcare to Gaza security personnel and civilians. The Qatar-based news network said that wearing the agency’s uniform does not establish Hamas membership.

There is also a dispute over the word “colonel”. Critics of Israel’s allegation say this is a professional or honorary designation within the medical services, not proof of a Hamas military command position, much like the United States surgeon-general is not an actual general.

The court’s decision came despite mounting international concern over Abu Safiya’s health and treatment in Israeli custody.

“The information that we are receiving about the health conditions of my father and how he’s being treated is very concerning,” Elias Abu Safiya, the imprisoned doctor’s son, told Al Jazeera on November 12. “My father weighs only 53 kilograms now, and he’s been suffering from very harsh conditions, three floors underground. He is in a solitary room, deprived of food, water, and medicine.”

Elias Abu Safiya continued: “We know he’s been subject to torture and bad treatment. My father still has some shrapnel stuck in his body, and he’s not seen a surgeon. This is inhumane, very harsh conditions that not even animals should be living in inside Israeli prisons. To add to this, he’s not been charged with anything. I don’t know why he’s being tortured this way. He’s a doctor, not a criminal or a murderer. He doesn’t deserve to be treated this way. The court denied the appeal to release him and 14 other doctors.”

Last week, Israel’s Supreme Court rejected a petition seeking the release of Abu Safiya and those 14 doctors, who are also imprisoned without charge or trial.

In July, the United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Israel to release the doctor immediately, or charge him and hold a fair trial. OHCHR said there were indications that Abu Safiya had been tortured and subjected to other abuse, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in serious injuries, and denial of medical care.

Abu Safiya’s 15-year-old son, Ibrahim Abu Safiya, was killed in an Israeli drone strike at the entrance to Kamal Adwan Hospital, where he was sheltering with his family, in October 2024. The following month, Abu Safiya suffered severe shrapnel wounds during yet another Israeli drone strike on the facility.

Israeli troops detained Abu Safiya on December 28, 2024 amid a prolonged siege and assault of the hospital after the director defied a forced displacement order and refused to evacuate the facility as long as patients were still being treated.

Former detainees released from Sde Teiman, the notorious torture prison in southern Israel, said they saw and met Abu Safiya there. According to testimonies collected by the Geneva-based Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Monitor, Abu Safiya was tortured prior to his arrival at Sde Teiman, and also while imprisoned there.

A United Nations commission concluded in 2024 that “Israel has perpetrated a concerted policy to destroy Gaza’s healthcare system as part of a broader assault on Gaza” that has left more than 250,000 Palestinians dead, maimed, or missing. The commission — which separately found that Israel is committing genocide in Gaza — further accused Israeli forces of “committing war crimes and the crime against humanity of extermination with relentless and deliberate attacks on medical personnel and facilities.”

author: Shirley Killen
title: Building the socialist movement in regional Victoria
content:
Victorians from Mildura to Mallacoota will have the chance to vote socialist for the first time in generations at this month’s state election. In a campaign that’s been full of milestones for the Victorian Socialists, one of the biggest is that the party is standing candidates in all 88 lower house seats for the first time. 

Networks of socialist activists have sprung up across the state with the goal of getting these candidates elected, putting on meetings, organising local rallies, door knocking and letterboxing. In some places, like Bendigo and Ballarat, local branches already existed, while in others, coordinators are starting from scratch.

David Suter is one of the local coordinators starting from scratch. He describes turning up to a polling booth after moving to Garfield, in eastern Victoria and part of the electorate of Narracan, looking at his options and thinking “this is bullshit”. The dearth of organised radical politics in regional areas could easily make a person feel disheartened. But David was encouraged by the result the Victorian Socialists achieved in last year’s federal election, so he signed up to attend the party’s state conference later that year. He left with a list of phone numbers and a plan to activate socialists in his region, and established a crew of seven who began sketching out a state election campaign. Now, the party has candidates contesting all eleven lower house seats, and the beginnings of local branches in Narracan, Shepparton, Bairnsdale and the Mornington Peninsula—to name just a few. 

These are “baby steps”, according to David. It’s a big task to rebuild (or just build, sometimes) a socialist tradition in regional Victoria. But the Victorian Socialists’ state election campaign so far has proved it is not impossible, and that with a common goal and some organisational infrastructure, socialists who previously felt isolated in the regions can make a difference.

Renee Nayef, the Victorian Socialists candidate for Mildura in Victoria’s north-west, described a “meet the candidate” event she put on recently. Two men drove into Mildura separately from a nearby town of 97 people, both assuming they were the only socialists for kilometres. They met for the first time at Renee’s event. Without the scaffolding of a statewide socialist campaign, they might have gone on for years not knowing there was another radical a couple of streets over. 

Sometimes these connections are made in unorthodox ways. For socialist campaigners in metropolitan Melbourne, the movement is built by knocking on other people’s doors and starting up conversations about socialism. Socialists in the regions report the opposite experience—locals are instead knocking on 

their 

doors because they’ve seen a yard sign and are thrilled to know there’s another socialist in town. 

In some parts of the state, the campaign is reviving largely forgotten radical traditions. Bass candidate for Victorian Socialists Chris Jobe had to correct the record when the local paper announced his candidacy with the headline “Red flag planted in Bass for the first time”. In fact, the seat of Bass takes in the old mining town Wonthaggi, known for much of the twentieth century as “Red Wonthaggi” because of the militancy of the local communist-led miners’ union. A more accurate headline would have been “Red flag planted in Bass 

again

”. 

The picture in regional Victoria today is clearly very different from the days when the Wonthaggi miners fought bitter industrial battles with coal bosses and the state. With few exceptions, these seats are the preserve of the Liberals and Nationals, with One Nation now poised to make serious gains. Socialists campaigning outside Melbourne don’t sugarcoat the challenges they are facing.

But socialist politics haven’t been seriously tested outside the state’s biggest cities in decades. It’s not surprising that conservative politics dominate when there’s nothing much else on offer. 

And working-class people in rural Victoria face the same stresses as their counterparts in Melbourne. The rising cost of living, the health system stretched to breaking point, the failure of successive governments to invest in transport and education—these issues are coming up all across the state. 

For Hera Sheppard, Victorian Socialists candidate for the South-West Coast, it was growing up in Warrnambool’s public housing that made her a socialist. She witnessed the way Labor neglected its housing stock and failed to …

author: @ndy
title: The struggle is real with Jillian Segal.
content:
See also : Jillian Segal and husband funding far-right group “Advance”, Anthony Klan, The Klaxon, July 12, 2025.

Jillian Segal — the South African–born Australian lawyer, business executive, and Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism — recently dropped another Report, ASECA Priorities. According to the Special Envoy, a newly-hatched “modern progressive antisemitism” … is taking “the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes”.

My first reaction on reading this passage was to recall the unforgettable 2014 framing by the Australian Defence League of the alleged “evil anarcho-pinko-anarchist-islamic cabal of dirt”; the wicked coalition then allegedly intent on turning Penrith into a no-go zone for patriots.

In any case, inre the Report, Jeffrey Loewenstein doesn’t hold back in It’s time to sack Jillian Segal (Deepcut News, November 2, 2026), the Jewish Council of Australia (October 30, 2026) has slammed it, and Jeff Sparrow has characterised it, not unfairly, as a Trumpian plan to curtail free speech (Crikey, November 2, 2026). The Report is also subject to critical scrutiny by Robert Manne, who examines it in On the Rise of Antisemitism in Australia (November 8, 2026), along with the thoughts of Lord Andrew Roberts and Sir Simon Schama on the subject of ‘antisemitism’. Manne concludes that:

Schama believes he can help combat the rise of antisemitism in the Diaspora by defending the indefensible, the war crimes of the IDF under Benjamin Netanyahu. I believe a more likely remedy would be for leading Diaspora thinkers, like Schama, and influential publishers, like Morry Schwartz, and the leaders in Australia of the principal Israel and Jewish lobbies, like Jillian Segal, to speak the truth about what, under Netanyahu and the two Kahanist-fascist members of his Government, Israel has become, and the moral revolution that has to happen in Israel if Jews in the Diaspora are to be spared from the dreadful rise of antisemitism that is spreading around the Western world.

FWIW, for over 20 years I’ve been attempting, inter alia, to monitor and document organised, public expressions of antisemitism and other racisms in Australia — the better to disrupt it. I’m also an anarchist, and one of many people to hold the view that the Israeli state has engaged in a genocidal assault upon Palestine in the three years since October 7 (the latest chapter in a much longer history of deadly state violence). On that basis, I assume that Segal et. al. would categorise myself as an exponent of ‘far-left antisemitism’, the meaning of which is elaborated upon in this passage:

Far-left antisemitism or issue-motivated antisemitism

Far-left ideology and associated activism feature a worldview that casts the world in terms of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed’. Within this binary framework, Israel is portrayed as a colonial project that is inherently racist and Jews who support Israel’s existence are portrayed as representatives of ‘whiteness’ (regardless of their ethnicity), privilege (regardless of their means), imperialism (notwithstanding the absence of an empire), greedy capitalism and the projection of Western power.

This framing allows longstanding antisemitic motifs to be repackaged in the academic language of anti-racism, decolonisation, human rights, social justice and intersectionality, often in service of a traditional Marxist revolutionary agenda.

When a cause is believed – with ideological fervour – to be absolutely just, its ends can come to justify any means and its adherents can feel free to vilify, harass and seek to destroy those who associate with what is framed as evil.

Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes – apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc. – has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.

In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest.

The strange – but …
