author: Chris Lang
title: The Antalya AI pledge: Voluntary commitments to greenwash a destructive industry
content:
The COP31 Presidency and the International Telecommunication Union, the United Nations agency for digital technologies launched the Antalya AI Pledge at COP31 in Türkiye, on November 16.

The Pledge is yet another voluntary pledge produced over more than three decades of COP meetings that will do less than nothing to address the climate crisis. Worse, the governments endorsing the Pledge are actively supporting a massively polluting industry that is accelerating the climate crisis.

The Antalya AI Pledge was launched at a “High-level Green Digital Action Roundtable on AI”. The Roundtable discussion is available here.

Tomas Lamanauskas, the deputy secretary-general of the International Telecommunication Union told the meeting that, “AI is really the technology that’s transforming our lives and mostly for good, I should say. From our daily ability to write speeches ... to much more high level aspects from medicine to agriculture, to education, as well as industries.”

Obviously, Lamanauskas didn’t give any concrete examples of any of this. Neither did he mention that the AI bubble is threatening another global financial crisis. Or that the main use of AI is to extract ever more fossil fuels. And he made no mention of the military AI industry.

“It has a really transformative potential to make everyone’s lives much better,” Lamanauskas said. Presumably Lamanauskas is oblivious to the recent United States elections in which voters made their feelings crystal clear about the data centres that have devastated so many communities.

Lamanauskas talked about AI’s energy use as a “challenge that we need to rein in if we want AI to sustainable power the world and to make sure that AI is a solution not the problem”.

Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, told the meeting that, “AI and other frontier technologies are a double edged sword. The task ahead is to blunt their dangerous edges, sharpen their catalytic ones, and put these technologies responsibly to work.”

Stiell noted that communities are “pushing back against data centres, concerned about their water, their energy bills, and their environment. So public support is already sinking deeper under water.”

Companies should, according to Stiell, “power data centres with renewable energy”.

But the Pledge makes no mention of fossil fuels. Instead it consists of vague statements about powering and building AI “sustainably”, managing AI “responsibly”, reporting the environmental impacts, and strengthening “financial support and technical infrastructure for AI for climate action”.

There is no mechanism to hold any of the companies or governments that sign the Pledge to account if they breach the terms of the Pledge.

The reality is that the Antalya AI Pledge is greenwashing a massively destructive, extractive, unethical, thieving industry. “AI companies’ license to operate is already on thin ice, right across political spectrums in many countries. And under that thin ice lie some potentially very deep regulatory waters, as political landscapes shift,” Stiell said in his speech at the launch.

“Very deep regulatory waters” is exactly what the world needs to prevent the damage that AI is already causing — damage that is accelerating every day.

“CEOs and boards need to step-up, and align business and investment plans with the world’s agreed climate goals,” Stiell said. The voluntary Antalya AI Pledge exists to allow the AI industry to continue its destructive business as usual.

Justine Calma, writing in The Verge, describes the Pledge as a “cruel joke”.

She points out that the Pledge even states that, “these objectives of the pledge are voluntary and non-prescriptive, create no new obligations, and are to be implemented in accordance with national circumstances”.

“In other words,” Calma writes, “these are voluntary commitments that countries can choose to follow or not follow based on their whims”.

On the same day as the launch of the Antalya AI Pledge, an assessment of the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres was published in Nature Sustainability. This is the first peer-reviewed estimate of the climate impact of data centres in the US.

The study estimates that hyperscale data centres in the US emitted between 21-31 million metric tonnes of CO₂ from May 2024 to April 2025 and used about 2% of US electricity. As Emily Atkin writes in Heated, these are big numbers, but “they’re also …

author: Sarah Garnham
title: One Nation is waging war on progress. Why won't progressives fight back?
content:
In 2018, One Nation struggled to get registered as a political party in Victoria, and progressives across the state took pride in it. Labor won the state election that year with a whopping 43 percent primary vote. Twenty years earlier, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson had been prevented from organising in Melbourne by protests, blockades and community events.

Today, the snarling menace and enemy of workers and the left that is One Nation is a major force in Victoria; it enjoys mass support, is vying for lower house seats, and setting the agenda in the state election campaign. The party and its policies have been legitimised by the capitalist press, the Liberal Party and, to a lesser extent, Labor. One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, has been invited to appear at the leaders’ debate.  

Progressive Victoria should be in uproar. This is the state of Trades Hall, Treaty and Pride. But aside from a few important exceptions—most notably high school students—the response to One Nation’s rise has been decidedly muted. Progressive NGOs and organisations have mostly stayed silent or offered tepid statements focusing on the fears of their constituents rather than forthright denunciation of One Nation and all it represents. The mood is closer to stunned awe than anger, almost as if the capacity to generate the ever-more-elusive commodity of popularity makes a party worthy of respect, however the popularity might be gained. 

Worse still, a layer of trade union organisers, Greens members and other progressives is arguing that the left must sympathise with the concerns of One Nation voters, or at least avoid antagonising them through political argument. In practice, this means sidestepping the signature issues that One Nation is pushing and building a base around. 

GetUp and Victorian Trades Hall Council (VTHC) are 

directing

 campaigners not to “play the racism card” or explicitly attack Pauline Hanson. After its costly and high-profile intervention in the Farrer by-election, GetUp concluded that criticising Hanson, her wealthy backer Gina Rinehart, celebrity defector Barnaby Joyce or the party’s links to Trump is not electorally expedient. Campaigners should instead seek to establish common ground with potential One Nation voters based on economic grievances. 

Senior VTHC researcher Oscar Kaspi-Crutchett 

argues

 to ignore the politics: “Don’t listen to the lyrics, listen to the beat of what they are saying”. The beat, he says, is dissatisfaction with the status quo, so supporters should be helped to “tease out” what that looks like and how it makes them feel. 

Federal Greens leader David Shoebridge 

says

 he has “understood the anger” driving One Nation support. Former Queensland Greens MP Max Chandler-Mathers 

goes further

, arguing that One Nation voters, especially the workers among them, are expressing legitimate protest against the system. He says they are driven by an “almost political nihilism”, and a desire to “blow it up” that makes them open to left-wing arguments and solutions. 

The same basic approach is being taken by more establishment political forces. Teal consultant Sue Barret gives the 

same advice

in four steps: validate the feeling, not the target; ask a genuine question and then be quiet; acknowledge the ground you share; offer a different path, not a different diagnosis.

Labor’s federal treasurer likewise 

warns

 progressives not to “scold” One Nation supporters, and to approach them “from a place of genuine respect and understanding”. The same advice is given by the media, from the establishment right through to liberal outlets. And all of this helps to reinforce One Nation’s 

spin

 about itself: that it is the party of “everyday Australians” who are “sick and tired of being ignored”. 

This appeasement goes further than merely tempering criticisms of One Nation for fear of alienating the party’s voters; it leads to actively opposing efforts to build resistance. 

The Labor-controlled National Union of Students, for example, pulled out of supporting the second student walkout against One Nation, and attacked office bearers for promoting it. Some Greens MPs have endorsed and spoken at the rallies, but others refused to speak on the grounds that it is not strategic and would alienate bigots. When a socialist promoted an anti-One Nation rally in a union activist online forum, the Victorian secretary of the CPSU and long-time leftist Jiselle Hanna replied that it is “more …

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31 week one: A summit without discussion of fossil fuels
content:
If you followed the first week of COP31 from Australia, you probably heard about the $32,000 coffee cart at the Australian pavilion and the hot mic that caught Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and energy minister Chris Bowen joking about where to keep their phones.

Much less was said about what happened in Türkiye on the opening day.

On November 9, while the summit opened with a lavish ceremony in Antalya, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan came out of a cabinet meeting in Ankara with good news: 135 million barrels of new oil potential had been found at Gabar, in Türkiye’s south-east.

The same day, at the HABAŞ steel plant in Aliağa, near İzmir, an overhead crane fell and ruptured a gas line. The explosion that followed killed 19 workers.

This workplace disaster did not make the agenda of the climate summit. HABAŞ runs its arc furnace on electricity from coal and gas, and supplies steel to the construction and car industries.

But COP31 does not talk about fossil fuels as a material order made of steel, cement and workers. It talks about an abstract “emission” to be managed from a distance. A worker killed in a fossil plant falls, by definition, is outside the frame.

Three days later, union confederations met inside the COP31 venue to discuss “just transition”. Nineteen workers were killed and Türkiye is speeding up its transition to fossil fuels but neither was on their agenda.

Türkiye, which holds the COP31 presidency, prepared well for a climate-changing summit. Since it was named host, it has signed 19 fossil fuel supply and exploration agreements, plus six nuclear and mining deals. It kept signing during the summit.

Australia, which presides over the negotiations, is no different. Labor had already approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects. Weeks before the summit it made it 38, clearing the Boggabri coal mine to dig another 30 million tonnes.

In Antalya, Albanese put the Pacific Island nations at the centre of his speech and then spent more time on home batteries than on coal and gas.

Bowen told the ABC that coal and gas exports have not damaged Australia's standing in the talks, and that his job is to land “the most ambitious outcome that consensus will allow”.

Tuvalu’s Prime Minister Feleti Teo described new fossil fuel projects “a death sentence for us”.

The Pacific Resilience Facility, Australia’s showpiece, reached US$200 million in Antalya. By Albanese’s own account, 46% of the money, so far, has come from Pacific countries themselves.

Meanwhile, according to Climate Action Network, Australia has joined the European Union, Japan and Norway in opposing a commitment to triple adaptation finance, in the very text it is supposed to be steering.

This is what I call climate-changing policy. Once you know it, you can see the climate-changing summit behind the “climate summit” and the transition to fossil fuels behind the “just transition” slogan.

COP31 President Murat Kurum, Türkiye’s environment minister, did not say the word “fossil” once in his opening speech. Bowen said it twice. At the leaders’ summit, Erdoğan and Albanese barely touched it.

In the first week, 56 negotiating documents were published; draft texts, informal notes, draft conclusions and decisions. They run to 268 pages. Coal and oil do not appear in them. “Fossil” turns up, at most, in a heading.

The only text that plainly mentions transitioning away from fossil fuels is a non-binding summary of views from the presidency. It repeats the 2023 Dubai sentence, limited to “energy systems”, so asphalt, cement and plastics are out from the start.

Brazil’s road map is voluntary. Even so, the Arab Group reportedly objected from day one to any reference to the road map in decision texts.

The words are missing because of how COP31 works. Decisions are taken by consensus, so a single bloc can strike it. The hosts are sitting on their own fossil expansion and have no wish to force it. The silence suits everyone.

Instead, Türkiye and Australia are selling another target: Lifting electricity’s share of final energy use to 35% by 2035. Whether that electricity comes from renewables or from fossil fuels is not the question. Bowen says tying it to renewables would be too hard for many countries.

Türkiye generates much of its own electricity by burning coal and gas, and Australia is among its top five coal suppliers.

The other big topic is finance: Extra money for climate projects, while the public keeps paying for the fossil order. Free …

author: Nick Everett
title: Remembering the Santa Cruz massacre
content:
Thirty-five years ago, Indonesian elite Kopassus troops opened fire on a peaceful procession in Dili, the capital of then Indonesian-occupied East Timor (today known as Timor Leste), killing hundreds. The Indonesian generals responsible have never faced justice, protected by the Western governments who armed them and abetted their crimes. 

The procession, on the morning of 12 November 1991, followed a memorial mass at Motael Church for Sebastião Gomes Rangel, a young Timorese man killed by Indonesian security forces two weeks earlier. As the procession of 3,000 mourners made its way to Santa Cruz cemetery, pro-independence banners and flags were unfurled. Minutes after the crowd arrived at the cemetery, troops opened fire without warning.

Shooting continued as people tried to scale the cemetery’s high walls. Some were shot in the back while running away. Others while seeking shelter behind tombstones or in the cemetery’s chapel. More were stabbed and shot as they lay on the ground in pools of blood. According to survivor testimonies, dozens more were executed or disappeared after being taken to the Wira Husada Military Hospital. 

At least 271 East Timorese were killed that day, and an equal number disappeared, believed dead, according to the East Timor Action Network.

Australian foreign minister Gareth Evans was quick to defend Indonesia’s military, which had invaded East Timor in December 1975 and maintained a brutal occupation of the former Portuguese colony. A month after the massacre, Evans

told

 parliament that while the incident was “‘deplorable”, it “was not ... a calculated or deliberate act of the [Indonesian] government as such”. Rather, it was “the product of aberrant behaviour by a subgroup within the country”. 

Two years earlier, Evans had joined his Indonesian counterpart, Ali Alatas, to toast the signing of the Timor Gap Treaty in a plane above the Timor Sea. With a glass of champagne in his hand, Evans declared: “This is a uniquely historical moment that is truly, uniquely historical”.

The treaty, several years in the making, carved up the rich oil and gas resources beneath the Timor Sea and opened the way for their exploitation by Australian resource companies. 

The Santa Cruz massacre was not unique. Many had preceded it, including the Kraras massacres, in the southern municipality of Viqueque in 1983. Prabowo Subianto, a rising star in the army and the son-in-law of Indonesian dictator, General Suharto, commanded the Kopassus special forces unit responsible. 

The Kraras massacres have been

compared

 with the US army’s massacre of Vietnamese civilians in the village of Mai Lai in 1968. Much like the strategy pursued by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon, such attacks sought to isolate combatants via major military operations that killed and displaced large numbers of civilians.

In 2005, East Timor’s Truth and Reconciliation Commission (CAVR)

concluded

 that Indonesia’s 24-year-long occupation resulted in between 102,800 and 183,000 conflict-related deaths, alongside widespread systematic torture, unlawful killings, enforced disappearances, forced displacement, and sexual violence. Many human rights organisations, including

Genocide Watch

, argue that Indonesia committed a genocide in East Timor.

What made the 1991 Santa Cruz massacre different from those that preceded it was that it was caught on

film

. When British cameraman Max Stahl’s footage was subsequently broadcast, it shone a light on Indonesia’s crimes and revived a global solidarity movement.

In Australia in the 1990s, socialists led a campaign group called Action in Solidarity with Indonesia and East Timor (ASIET), which coordinated demonstrations in conjunction with other East Timor solidarity groups across the country to commemorate the Santa Cruz massacre on 12 November each year.

We argued that the overthrow of Indonesia’s military dictatorship would open the road to Timorese independence, and that we therefore needed to support not only the resistance to the occupation, but also the growing student and worker movements in Indonesia that were calling for an end to Suharto’s military rule. We demanded that our own government break military ties with Indonesia.

Military and diplomatic ties between the two countries were extensive and growing, and by 1996 included a military pact. At the time, Australia was training Kopassus forces at the Kokoda Barracks on the Gold Coast. The Keating government also shamefully (and …

title: Dünya Çocuk Hakları Gününde 5 çocuk işçi anlatıyor: Hakları yok, patronları var
content:
Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Bugün 20 Kasım Dünya Çocuk Hakları Günü. Başta bakanlık düzeyindeki yetkililer olmak üzere pek çok kişi açıklamalar yaparken bugün Türkiye’de çocukların karşı karşıya olduğu en büyük sorunlardan biri çocuk işçilik.

Adana’da sanayide çalışan çocukların anlattıkları, hem çocuk işçiliğin arkasındaki nedenleri ortaya koyuyor hem de yoksullukla artan çocuk işçiliğin nasıl kurumsallaştırıldığını gösteriyor. Kimi okulda başarısız olduğu düşüncesiyle eğitimden kopuyor, kimi ailesinin içinde olduğu yoksulluk nedeniyle çalışmaya başlıyor. 11 yaşında çalışmaya başlayan çocuklar, MESEM’e kayıt yaptırabilmek için 15 yaşını doldurmayı bekliyor.

Adana’da oto sanayi alanında görüştüğümüz çocukların hikayeleri; Dünya Çocuk Hakları Günü’nde çocukların içinde bulunduğu durumu gösteriyor.

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Sanayi sitesinde görüştüğümüz çocuklardan 14 yaşındaki Deniz, üç yıldır oto tamir işinde çalışıyor. Altıncı sınıfa geçtiği dönemde okulu bırakan Deniz, çalışmaya 11 yaşında başlamış. Nasıl başladığını anlatırken “Babamla konuştum. ‘Çalışmak istiyorum’ dedim. Sınavlarım kötüydü. Matematik de biraz zordu, yapamadım” diyor. Deniz, okulu bırakmayı derslerine bağlasa da kazandığı paranın büyük bölümünü ailesine veriyor: “Anneme veriyorum. Bana bir şey kalmıyor. 500 lira kendime alıyorum. Arkadaşlarımla pazar günleri AVM’ye gidiyorum. Yemek yiyorum.”

Deniz’in 15 yaşını doldurmasına bir ay kalmış. Yaşını doldurduğunda MESEM’e kaydolacak. 3 yıldır okulla eğitimi birlikte götürmeye çalışmış. Eğitimine devam etmek yerine mesleği sürdürmek istediğini söylüyor. Deniz’in ailesinde kendisinden başka çalışan çocuklar da var. Üç kardeş olduklarını, küçük kardeşinin dört yaşında olduğunu söyleyen Deniz, diğer kardeşinin de çalıştığını belirtiyor. Babası sanayide kaporta-boya işinde çalışıyor. Kendi kazancının eve katkısını ise “biraz” diye anlatıyor.

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

17 yaşına girmeye hazırlanan Utku da 14 yaşındaki kardeşinin MESEM’e başlayabilmek için 15 yaşına gelmesini beklediğini söylüyor. Kendisi beş yıldır aynı atölyede, öncesinde de iki yıl başka bir iş yerinde çalışmış. Utku, sanayiye yönelme kararını “Dedim, ‘Sokakta sürüneceğime gider sanayide sürünürüm daha iyi.’ En azından elimde bir altın bileziğim olsun, cebime para girsin” sözleriyle anlatıyor. Utku ayda 15 bin lira kazandığını, bunun yarısının MESEM tarafından karşılandığını söylüyor. Kazandığı paranın yarısını eve verdiğini, kalanını kendisi için kullandığını anlatıyor. Evde kendisi, kardeşi ve babası olmak üzere üç kişinin çalıştığını belirten Utku, 14 yaşındaki kardeşinin de 15 yaşına geldiğinde MESEM’e başlayacağını söylüyor.

15 yaşındaki Hasan da bir yıldır şanzıman tamiri işinde çalışıyor. Bu işe nasıl başladığı sorulduğunda “Ailem ‘şanzımancı ol’ dedi, biz de geldik, öğreniyoruz abi” diyor. Hasan da MESEM öğrencisi olduğunu, haftanın bir günü, perşembe günü okula gittiğini söylüyor. Haftanın beş günü iş yerinde çalışıyor, cumartesi yarım gün de atölyeye geliyor.

MESEM’deki eğitimini nasıl değerlendirdiği soruduğumuzda “İş. En çok iş abi. Pek okul gibi değil. İşe gidip geldiğimiz için ders çalışamıyoruz. Zaten hocalar da sınıfta bırakmıyor. MESEM’i de bitirdikten sonra çalışmaya devam edeceğim” diyor. Üniversite eğitimine ise “Lazım değil” diye cevap veriyor.

Hasan kazandığı paranın büyük bölümünü ailesine veriyor. 2 bin lira kadar kendisine ayırdığını, gerisini ailesine verdiğini anlatan Hasan’ın evde kendisi, 20 yaşındaki motor tamircisi ağabeyi ve çiftçilik yapan babası çalışıyor. Çocukların mutlu olup olmadığı sorusuna ise “mutsuz” yanıtını veriyor ve ekliyor, “Ülkenin durumu pek iyi değil.”

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Fotoğraf: Volkan Pekal/Evrensel

Aynı kaporta atölyesinde çalışan Berat ve kardeşi Bilal’in anlattıkları da çocukların çalışma hayatına yönelmesinde aile koşullarının ve okuldan kopuşun etkisini gösteriyor. 15 yaşındaki Berat, dokuzuncu sınıfta okuyor ve MESEM’e geçmek için başvuru hazırlığında. Yaşını yeni doldurduğunu, dayısının iş yeriyle ilgili evrakların tamamlanmasını beklediğini söylüyor. Berat, ailesinin ekonomik durumunu anlatırken “Bir tek babam çalışıyor. O da yetmiyor. Mecburen çalışıyoruz” diyor. MESEM’de hem çalışıp hem okula devam edebildiği ve para alabildiği için bu yolu tercih ettiğini belirtiyor. author: Katie Myers
title: Trump Admin Proposes Easing Protections for Coal Miners From Black Lung Disease
content:
Miners’ advocates said revisions to a Biden-era rule on silica exposure would weaken already insufficient protections.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

Coal mining is dangerous and takes a toll on the body, but a miner working underground can earn enough to buy a house, drive a nice car, and send the kids to college. There was a time when John Robinson thought the trade-off was worth it. No longer. He was diagnosed with black lung disease at age 47, a consequence of inhaling toxic silica dust in the mines of Virginia.

“These companies will bait you in with this big money,” said Robinson, who is now 60 and vice president of the National Black Lung Association. “When you get down and out, well, guess what? You’re like an old wore-out tire on the car or something. They’ll throw you to the side ’cause you ain’t worth nothing.”

For more than 50 years, coal miners, their families, and advocates have pressed the federal government for stricter limits on silica exposure, stronger enforcement of rules meant to protect miners, and improved health benefits for those disabled by the disease. In 2024, the Biden administration set the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica at 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air, matching the Occupational Safety and Health Administration threshold for workers in other industries. The rule was finalized in 2024, with coal companies required to comply beginning in April 2025.

That regulation was meant to update protections in coal mines and in what regulators call metal and nonmetal mines, which extract everything from copper and critical minerals to stone, sand, and gravel. All of them carry a risk of inhaling silica dust, whose fine particles can lodge deep in the lungs. But research over the past two decades has shown that Central Appalachian coal miners have experienced an acute increase in exposure and the most severe forms of lung disease associated with it, including progressive massive fibrosis.

Though the Biden-era revision wasn’t perfect, advocates like Robinson and his wife Vonda Robinson, who is president of the National Black Lung Association, were hopeful. It seemed as though decades of organizing for a stronger standard were finally coming to an end. But a federal appeals court put the rule on hold last year while it considered legal challenges filed by the mining industry. Now the Mine Safety and Health Administration wants to revise the rule.

Its proposal would retain the 50-microgram silica limit while changing several requirements governing how mines monitor exposure and protect workers. Brendan Muckian-Bates, a policy analyst with Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center, said those revisions could substantially weaken the protections behind the stricter limit.

Black lung is the common name for coal worker’s pneumoconiosis, an incurable, progressive, and fatal respiratory disease caused by inhaling coal dust and fine silica particles, which can cause severe inflammation in the lungs. Over time, that irritant scars and stiffens lung tissue, making respiration increasingly difficult until many of those afflicted with it cannot breathe at all.

In the 1960s and 1970s, according to the National Institutes of Health, as many as 1 in 3 miners with more than 25 years of work experience were testing positive for black lung. The United Mine Workers of America agitated for stricter protections again the disease, and in 1969, Congress passed the Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act, which required regular inspections. Disease rates plummeted to a historic low in the 2000s, only to begin climbing again. Rates of black lung are now at a 50-year high and still climbing. A study led by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, or NIOSH, found these increases across all age groups, including miners in their 20s and 30s, although rates remained highest among those who had spent decades underground. In routine health screenings by the agency during the past three years, more than 1 in 3 miners in Central Appalachia once again tested positive for the disease, making the epidemic into a U-shaped curve.

The new rule was published in the Federal Register on November 12 and will be open for public comment until January 11. Although the stricter limit of 50 micrograms remains, Muckian-Bates said the fine print matters: Other changes in the rule …

title: Tesla und Elon Musk in der brandenburgischen Provinz: Viel Aufregung um eine Mobilität für die gehobene Mittelschicht
content:
Dossier


„

Die Mitteilung des Tesla-Chefs Elon Musk, er wolle „in der Nähe von Berlin“ eine neue Tesla-Fabrik errichten und „Tausende neue Arbeitsplätze“ schaffen, wird von so gut wie allen Seiten des politischen Spektrums gelobt (…) Es gehe schließlich nicht nur um neue Jobs, sondern vor allem um einen Beitrag für eine „klimafreundliche Mobilität“. (…) Es handelt sich bei dem Vorhaben von Tesla erstens um eine Investition, mit der eher Luxusmobilität für eine gut betuchte, westliche Gruppe optimiert und gesteigert werden soll. Zweitens handelt es sich um eine Investition im Rahmen des allgemeinen Hypes um Elektro-Pkw-Mobilität, die ablenkt von den eigentlichen Aufgaben einer Mobilitäts- und Transportorganisation, die den Anforderungen des Klimawandels gerecht wird. Drittens sind die wenigen tausend neuen Jobs in der möglichen neuen Tesla-Fabrik ab dem Jahr 2022 in ein Verhältnis zu setzen (…) zu den mehreren Tausend Jobs im Bereich der erneuerbaren Energien, so der Windkraft-Industrie, die aktuell konkret abgebaut werden

… “

Artikel von Winfried Wolf vom 14. November 2019 bei den Nachdenkseiten

 

 – siehe die weitere Entwicklung sowohl hinsichtlich der Arbeitsbedingungen als auch ökologisch (bewusst durcheinander, da zusammenhängend):


‪

Strafbefehl gegen Tesla-Geschäftsführer wegen übler Nachrede mit dem Vorwurf der Aufzeichnung der Betriebsratssitzung durch einen IG Metall-Funktionär


Vorwürfe gegen IG-Metall-Mitarbeiter; Strafbefehl gegen Tesla-Werkschef wegen „übler Nachrede“


„

Das Amtsgericht Fürstenwalde hat einen Strafbefehl gegen den Werksleiter von Tesla in Grünheide (Oder-Spree), André Thierig, wegen übler Nachrede erlassen. Das hat Amtsgerichtsdirektorin Jasmin Wiriadidjaja dem rbb bestätigt. Thierig soll demnach eine Geldstrafe von 80 Tagessätzen zahlen. (…)

author: Unknown
title: How the Riots Spread to Italy : An Account from the October 17 Uprising in Milan
content:
Across Europe, young people are rising up in rebellion. From

Spain

 and

France

 to Albania and even

Germany

, demonstrators are breaking with complacency and obedience and breaking through the constraints intended to control them.


This is reminiscent of the previous wave of unrest. In November 2018, the

Yellow Vest

 movement broke out in France, precipitating

several months

 of street conflict throughout the country. By fall of 2019, a global wave of uprisings was underway from

Hong Kong

,

Ecuador

, and

Chile

 to

Sudan

,

Catalunya

, and

Lebanon

. All this set the stage for the

George Floyd Rebellion

 to spread

around the United States

 in 2020.


It remains to be seen whether the wave of protest emanating from France today is indicative of a new groundswell of worldwide momentum—and it remains uncertain what it would take for these movements to address the fundamental problems of our time. Everywhere around the world, the movements of 2019 and 2020 reached an

impasse

 when they exhausted the force they could bring to bear in the streets and shifted instead to doomed electoral and reformist campaigns. The heroic failure of those powerful movements suggests that nothing short of a revolutionary transformation of our society can address the catastrophes that

capitalism

 and the consolidation of political power in the hands of autocrats are creating.


Hopefully, these upheavals can serve as laboratories in which a new generation of revolutionaries can experiment with methods for making profound change. In the following account, anarchists in Italy describe the moment in October 2026 at which the movement in Italy exceeded control.


Cracks in the Façade


In Italy, despite soaring prices, stagnating wages, and deteriorating schools and public services, the right-wing regime of Giorgia Meloni continues to ignore widespread misery while increasing military spending. Did they think we would not resist as wealthy elites attempt to loot our future?


This fall, cracks began to appear in the façade of the ruling order. On September 22 and 23 in Modena, about fifty young people organized themselves to loot supermarkets. They all walked in together and recorded footage of themselves taking whatever they wanted. Since the beginning of October, truck drivers across southern Italy have been blocking the roads and striking in protest against the rising price of diesel. For weeks, supermarkets in the south lay nearly empty.


As the ferment slowly grew, a call from a newly formed initiative called “Italia in piazza” [“Italy in the Squares”] circulated on social media. Anonymous chats on Telegram channels began to promote a date to mobilize against the high cost of living: October 17. The call was picked up on TikTok and Instagram and circulated widely. In Milan, the group called for a convergence in a city park. This contributed to swelling the ranks of protesters.


The protests of October 17 took an array of different forms in cities across the country. In Turin, Bergamo, and Milan, widespread unrest and looting indicated a political dimension rarely seen in Italy.


The demonstrators who assembled in Milan’s Piazza del Duomo on October 17 only traveled a few streets before the police blocked them. This would usually stop a protest in its tracks, but that day was different. Within the blocked group of approximately five hundred demonstrators, the energy remained strong. They chanted and threw themselves against the assembled cops, applying pressure until they finally broke through the police line and poured into the side streets. This time, the repressive maneuvers of the police failed, enabling anyone who so desired to join in the protest.


The following week, the Meloni regime called in the army to repress the demonstrations, which only infuriated people further. On October 30, a nationwide strike brought tens of thousands into the streets in over 40 cities around Italy. Since then, protests have continued around the country. But the uprisings of October 17 marked the turning point when masses of young people shattered the consumer spectacle in an explosion of looting and street fighting.


The following testimony reaches us from some participants in the unrest of October 17 and 18 in Milan.


Under the Madonnina


Gleaming atop the dome of Milan Cathedral, the famous golden statue of the Virgin Mary known as the Madonnina looms over a city in revolt. Beneath her gilded gaze, cobblestones fly at …

author: CMI Argentina
title: Neuquén: piden la renuncia de Carlos Quintriqueo a la CTA por su alianza electoral con Sobisch
content:
La conformación de una lista electoral entre el ex gobernador Jorge Sobisch y el actual secretario general de la Central de Trabajadores de la Argentina (CTA) Neuquén, Carlos Quintriqueo, generó el rechazo de distintos sindicatos de la provincia. Las organizaciones cuestionan que Quintriqueo haya puesto el sello de su partido a disposición de Sobisch para competir por la gobernación.


Escuchar el reporte de Fm Pocahullo de San Martín de los Andes


El repudio se centra tanto en la reaparición política de Sobisch, quien fue gobernador de Neuquén en tres oportunidades y responsable político del operativo represivo en el que fue asesinado el docente Carlos Fuentealba, como en el acompañamiento de Quintriqueo a esa candidatura.


Ante esta decisión, sindicatos como el gremio judicial, ATEN y otras organizaciones docentes, junto con la CTERA y distintas entidades gremiales, reclamaron la renuncia de Quintriqueo a la conducción de la CTA.


Carolina de Benedetti, secretaria local del gremio docente, expresó el rechazo a la alianza y cuestionó el regreso de Sobisch a la política provincial. “Nosotros seguimos sosteniendo, a pesar de que la Justicia dice lo contrario, que Sobich es el asesino de nuestro compañero Carlos Fuentealba y seguimos exigiendo justicia en ese sentido”, manifestó.


De Benedetti sostuvo que quienes conducen la CTA deben representar los intereses de las organizaciones y de la clase trabajadora. Por eso, consideró urgente que Quintriqueo y quienes acompañen la alianza den un paso al costado.


“Hay un acto de traición con la clase trabajadora, con los otros sindicatos que acompañaron ese proceso de unidad para la conformación de la lista y la presentación de elecciones”, afirmó. También señaló que la decisión de llevar a Sobisch como candidato no representa los intereses de los sectores trabajadores.

author: CNT Valladolid
title: Vivienda y antifascismo en tiempos de Desokupa
content:
El miércoles 21 de octubre, como parte de las jornadas de inauguración del nuestro nuevo local en Valladolid, se celebró un debate sobre el tema de la vivienda desde tres perspectivas complementarias: la del

Sindicato de Vivienda de Valladolid

, la del Sindicato de Inquilinas (por parte de

Javier Gil

, autor del libro

Generación Inquilina

, que se vendió durante el acto) y la de

Sistema 161

, grupo de investigación de entramados reaccionarios.


Gracias a los ponentes se perfiló una detallada imagen del problema de la vivienda mostrando que éste es consustancial a un capitalismo que año tras año ha ido deviniendo en un capitalismo rentista en lugar de productivo, especialmente en el Estado español. Lo que la clase trabajadora arañamos a los empresaurios como sueldo, se lo devolvemos teniendo que pagar precios de vivienda inflados por la especulación.


La inversión en vivienda está siendo la tabla de salvación de un capitalismo en crisis, sin tener en cuenta costes humanos de los aumentos de rentabilidad, y eso ha convertido a la vivienda en una palanca estratégica para el cambio social.


Apoyando y sosteniendo este sistema encontramos desde empresas de desokupación encargadas de llevar a cabo brutalmente los desalojos de la nueva clase rentista, hasta todos los gobiernos del Estado españoi, que no han contribuido a dar salida a esta situación e incluso la han empeorado con medidas legislativas que favorecen los desahucios.


La impunidad de las empresas de Desokupa -cuyo sórdido árbol genealógico pudo consultarse en una exposición simultánea a la mesa redonda- es un nuevo ejemplo de que “los ricos siempre han llevado mal que los pobres tengan derechos”; estas empresas son un nuevo nicho de negocio que facilita a la clase rentista saltarse la ley, y que opera gracias a la tolerancia policial y a las campañas favorecedoras de determinados medios.


Quedó claro que el silenciamiento no sólo del historial delictivo de los componentes de estas empresas, sino de sus vínculos tangibles con el negocio inmobiliario -adquiriendo los pisos que desahucian- es algo que los medios de comunicación masiva ocultan por, en el mejor de los casos, negligencia.


Pero el rechazo generalizado a los desahucios que se va extendiendo en la población está restando espacio a esta propaganda, y convocatorias como la de huelga general por la vivienda están desmantelando un espacio público en el que los debates fomentados por la ultraderecha ocupaban el lugar de la discusión de problemas reales.


Es significativo que una semana de acampadas por la vivienda hayan provocado un adelanto de elecciones que no han producido dos años de manifestaciones ultras frente a las sedes del PSOE pidiendo lo mismo, pero también está claro que hay que ir más allá de las elecciones.


Dada la ausencia de una representatividad de la clase obrera en los sistemas parlamentarios habituales en la que ésta vea sus intereses de clase expresados y llevados a cabo, se impone la necesidad de reconstruir una acción política al margen de estos cauces habituales.


Necesidad que se percibe también en todas las movilizaciones por la vivienda, que han abandonado la posición anti-organización que tuvo peso en algunas acampadas del 15M. Las acampadas y movilizaciones por la vivienda no están siendo una repetición del 15M, sino un paso hacia una articulación de una nueva forma de política desde la base.


Una nueva forma de acción política que pasa por hacer nuevas formas de sindicalismo – más combativo y autogestionado- y por fortalecer un nuevo sentido común compartido, y que sean un dique contra las soluciones autoritarias a la pérdida de rentabilidad de los negocios capitalistas.

.

author: Michael_1973
title: South Africa’s ANC Is Collapsing. The Far Right Is Rising.
content:
The African National Congress is losing its working-class base. The beneficiaries: parties of the Right. South Africa’s local elections expose the fallout of three decades of economic failure — and the need to rebuild working-class power.

In this article, Zwelinzima Vavi, the General Secretary of the South Africa Federation of Trade Unions, reflects on the rout of the ANC in the local government elections on 4 November 2026.

While the global left celebrates the recent successes of the Workers’ Party in Brazil and the Democratic Socialists of America in the United States, the African National Congress (ANC) has suffered a historic collapse in South Africa’s November 4 local government elections. After three decades of mass unemployment, deepening inequality, corruption, and economic policies that have failed the working class, the former liberation movement is losing its political authority. The principal beneficiaries of the ANC’s electoral rout are parties of the Right, including an increasingly powerful far right that has built its project around aggressive and often violent xenophobia.

With more than 70 percent of votes counted, the ANC’s national share of the vote fell to around 32 percent. The ANC is not expected to retain an outright majority in any major city, and the center-right Democratic Alliance (DA), historically the principal party of the white liberal establishment, is making substantial gains and is projected to become the largest party in most of South Africa’s big cities. Former President Jacob Zuma’s Zulu nationalist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (MKP) is on track to be the largest party in Durban. The far-right ActionSA has made a strong showing in Johannesburg and Pretoria and is likely to be the second-largest party in Pretoria, with the ANC in third place.

The central question is not only why the ANC has lost so much support. It is why the suffering and anger of the working class have failed to produce a powerful democratic socialist alternative, and why the Right has been so successful in presenting itself as the answer to a crisis created by the existing economic and political order.

The defeat of apartheid was an extraordinary achievement. We won universal suffrage, democratic institutions, constitutional rights, and legal protections for workers. Those victories were won through generations of sacrifice and collective struggle, and they must be defended. But political apartheid was defeated while the economic structures inherited from apartheid remained largely intact.

The liberation movement historically brought together different classes and social groups united against racial oppression. That unity was indispensable to apartheid’s defeat. But national identity does not abolish class contradictions. Instead of using democracy to transform the ownership and control of the economy in the interests of the majority, the ANC increasingly became an instrument through which a new elite could enter and benefit from the existing economic order.

The ownership and control of the commanding heights of the economy were never fundamentally transformed. Land ownership remained extraordinarily unequal. The former Bantustans, created as reservoirs of cheap African labor, were never provided with the productive economic foundations needed to overcome their inherited poverty.

Over time, the ANC came to treat the advancement of an emerging black capitalist class as evidence of economic transformation. A narrow layer of businesspeople accumulated wealth, in some cases extraordinary wealth, through access to political power, state contracts, and opportunities created by the Black Economic Empowerment policy, while the overwhelming majority remained excluded from meaningful economic power.

The ANC’s adoption of neoliberal economic policies in the 1990s deepened this problem. The language of economic liberation gave way to investor confidence, competitiveness, and market reform. Brutal austerity, liberalization, and dependence on private investment displaced the redistributive ambitions of the liberation struggle.

We were repeatedly told that economic growth would eventually deliver employment and redistribution. We were also told that redistribution must wait for economic growth and the development of the productive forces. But if redistribution had to wait while productive capacity developed, why did South Africa simultaneously deindustrialize?

We have become what I have described as a “warehouse economy …

author: Jenny Brown
title: Labor Mobilized for ‘Many vs. Mighty’ Midterms
content:
Something different was in the air as the labor movement mobilized for the midterms.


More than usual, unions were willing to support insurgent candidates who refused corporate donations and bucked the Democratic Party establishment. They championed a Bernie Sanders-style list of working-class issues: Medicare for All, a higher minimum wage, union rights, immigrant rights, stopping war, and taxing the rich. Many are union members themselves. And they won.


United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain called the election “the many versus the mighty.”


In Michigan, the UAW was a key backer of the victorious Abdul El-Sayed, who earlier defeated the party’s depressing primary choice for U.S. Senate.  “You had a lot of rich people who tried to… buy a seat, to buy these races,” Fain told

Michigan Advance

. “Michiganders… are telling these people they’re not for sale.”


Logger and union member Troy Jackson won a Senate seat against 30-year incumbent Republican Susan Collins in Maine after the UAW and the Maine AFL-CIO helped defeat the establishment choice in the primary there. In Ohio, labor stalwart Sherrod Brown faced a river of crypto lobby cash but recovered the Senate seat he lost in 2024.


In Texas, the Communications Workers (CWA) mobilized for union-member candidates up and down the ticket, asking candidates to commit to a

“Contract with Working Texans.”

 Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa signed on—she’s a labor lawyer, member of Texas State Employees Union/CWA, and the first Democrat elected Texas governor since 1990.


Various union members and leaders are headed for Congress. Ironworker Brian Poindexter won in Ohio. Pennsylvanians elected firefighter and union president Bob Brooks. Forest Service smokejumper and local union vice president Sam Forstag won in Montana. VA nurse and union member Mitchell Berman beat a Republican incumbent in Wisconsin.


In New York, UAW members and Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) congressional candidates Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier defeated establishment Democrats in the primary, then romped November 3.


Richard Ojeda, a champion of the West Virginia teachers’ strike of 2018, won a Congressional seat in North Carolina, beating the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. "We were elected to elevate the lives of working people across this country,”

said Ojeda

. “We're coming in LASER FOCUSED on the mission. Help people. Hold anyone who has hurt people accountable. Tax the billionaires. The end.”


Others lost, but came way closer than expected. In Nebraska, Kellogg’s strike leader and independent Dan Osborn came up short (44-50) for U.S. Senate. He faced ferocious attack ads, with $24 million in ‘independent’ spending. In Florida, former SEIU organizer and DSA member Angie Nixon defeated the establishment Democrat in the primary and almost won (48-50) a Senate race the pundits had written off. She got zero support from the national Democratic Party.


CORPORATE DEMS UNDER FIRE


Now some unions have come out swinging, demanding more from the party. The Machinists (IAM) sent a letter

urging Senator Chuck Schumer to resign as party leader

. OPEIU

did the same

.


The IAM “is through with any member of leadership, in any political party, who stops one iota short of being a ferocious, unyielding and unbending champion of working people,” said President Brian Bryant. “This means… sweeping economic policy changes that will recalibrate the vast, immoral, economic injustice in this country.”


The United Electrical Workers concurred: “The credit for these wins belongs not to the Democratic Party—whose leadership has offered at best tepid resistance to the Republican agenda over the past two years—but to the working people across the country who have spent the last two years organizing and fighting back in their communities and workplaces.”


UE set out an ambitious agenda

: a $25 minimum wage, Medicare for All, dismantling ICE, taxing the rich, protecting Social Security, and passing labor law reform including the PRO Act and card-check recognition for speedier union recognition. National Nurses United said voters expect a stop to health care cuts, stat.


President Trump can veto most bills Congress passes, but Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders

insisted

 on November 9 that Congress needs to do its job and pass a bold working-class agenda. If Trump vetoes the bills, that’ll raise the stakes in 2028 to elect a president who will sign them …

author: Mehran Khalili
title: What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests?
content:
This article

What’s next for Europe’s autumn of protests? 

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


It was a Wednesday afternoon in late October, and several marches were converging on Syntagma Square in Athens, the epicenter of Greek protest. There were teachers on strike, university students who’d camped in the square overnight, and high schoolers holding painted banners that read “From Greece to France, we’re fighting for modern schools.” Parents pushed strollers through the growing crowd, their toddlers looking on in wonder.


But not everyone was there for the same reason. Groups of black-clad young men ducking in and out of the march, faces covered, were play-fighting each other in a way that looked like a rehearsal. Riot police were lining the side streets, watching over it all with the bored expression of men waiting for their shift to end. And photojournalists were circling, hoping for the youths and the police to meet in a burst of violence that would pay for their day.


The violence didn’t happen this time. According to the

police count

, 10,000 people marched peacefully through central Athens. Afterwards, people hung around, arguing about politics and passing water bottles in the autumn sun. 


I keep thinking about those bored riot police, though, because they seemed to understand what organizers sometimes don’t: A government that has seen a lot of marches knows how to wait one out. The question for the teachers and students in Athens — and in Paris, Milan, Brussels, Lisbon, Madrid, Berlin, Vienna, Tirana and every other city caught up in Europe’s autumn of protest — is how to make saying no cost their governments more than saying yes.


An autumn of anger


The energy in Europe’s streets is bigger than many realize.  Young people have been protesting in at least nine European countries this autumn, most of them since mid-September. 


In France, a walkout over the lack of teachers at one high school in Créteil in September

spread to hundreds of schools

 within weeks. By mid-October, about 550,000 people (by the

government’s own count

) were marching in cities and towns across the country. In Spain and Portugal, the anger is about housing. Protesters set up camps in

Madrid’s Puerta del Sol

 and

Lisbon’s Rossio,

 and on Nov. 11, Spain’s tenants’ unions, backed by the big trade unions, held the country’s

first general strike in 14 years.

 It came after Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old widow in fragile health, was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for most of her life. She

died in hospital

 two weeks later.


Demonstrators march for the right to housing  after the eviction of  an 87-year-old woman from the home where she had lived for around seventy years in Madrid, Spain. (Wikimedia Commons)


The grievances overlap without being the same. It’s about schools in France and Greece, university tuition in

Belgium

 and

Albania

, university budgets in

Austria

, military conscription in

Germany

, and rent in Portugal and Spain, where the average rent is now

98.7 percent

 of what a young person earns in a month. But running beneath most of them is a familiar story: governments that say there’s no money for schools, or for people who are struggling, always, somehow, manage to find it for something else, often weapons.


In France, Germany and

Italy

, protesters have made that link. France’s

2027 budget

 adds $7 billion for defense and just $1.2 billion for schools, while

cutting 1,588 teaching posts

. In Germany, young people marched in more than 30 cities on Oct. 31, angry, as

Al Jazeera reported

, that military spending is rising while education funding is cut. 


The protests have achieved some modest wins. On Oct. 26, France’s government promised to

replace Parcoursup

, the hated university admissions system, cap first-year high school classes at 28, and add 500 teaching posts. And in Serbia, a student movement that began after a railway station canopy

collapsed in Novi Sad two years ago

 turned itself into an electoral list and, on Oct. 25,

beat Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s strongman of 14 years

. 


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Facts like these are why, in my organizing circles, there’s a lot of talk of a “European wave.” I think we should be careful with that phrase, though, because it suggests a level of coordination and a plan that doesn’t — yet — exist. The reporting I …

author: By L. Cam Anderson, Contributor
title: James O’Keefe and Cam Higby Evade Press and Protesters After Hearing, Cancel Presser
content:
Minneapolis, MN – Far-right content creators James O’Keefe and Cam Higby appeared at the Hennepin County Public Safety Facility to be arraigned in court for charges stemming from a video the duo filmed in August fraudulently identifying themselves as Minneapolis-area voters while attempting to poke holes in the state’s election laws.


The two men, surrounded by a security detail led by former Minneapolis Policeman Bob Kroll, rushed into the building without speaking a word while press and protesters surrounded them.


Cam Higby (left) and James O’Keefe (To the right of Higby) waving at press, supporters and protesters, following their arraignment on Nov. 16.


“Due to the mob outside the courthouse sheriffs had to escort us through the skyway with my defense lawyer [Chris Madel] and First Amendment litigator [Benjamin Barr],” O’Keefe posted later on X. “This is retaliation for journalism, plain and simple.”


The “mob” was ultimately the excuse for not conducting a press conference outside of the building, for which cameras and microphones had been set up well in advance. Instead, the two slinked out the back while other high-profile supporters took the opportunity to leave.


On Oct. 28, Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced felony charges

 of identity theft and unlawful voting against the two men for a video filmed during Minnesota’s primary election in August. In the video, the men dress up as Muslims and enter Minneapolis polling locations, where they give the workers the names of real people who are registered to vote in their respective precincts.


“Minnesota law states clearly that no individual shall intentionally misrepresent their identity in applying for a ballot,” Moriarty said “The charges filed today are appropriate to address the conduct of Mr. O’Keefe and Mr. Higby.”


Protesters on both sides of the political aisle began gathering outside the building roughly half an hour before the arraignment was slated to begin, although those supporting the charges against Higby and O’Keefe never reached more than 10.


On the other side, O’Keefe’s calls for other journalists and “patriots” was heeded by a number of right-wing personalities, including Republican state senators Walter Hudson and Michael Holmstrom, Jr.


Both Hudson and Holmstrom are part of the far-right Minnesota Freedom Caucus, which was formed earlier this year in February. During Operation Metro Surge,

Hudson was a vocal advocate

 of Trump

using the Insurrection Act of 1807 to deal with resistance

 to federal immigration enforcement.


Also among O’Keefe and Higby’s supporters were far-right social media influencers Savanah Hernandez of Turning Point USA and Frank Scale of Surge Media, as well as David Hoch, the man who accompanied Nick Shirley in December to uncover supposed fraud in the Somali community.


Former Police Officers Federation of Minneapolis President Bob Kroll arrived in a convoy of two white SUVs, accompanied by several suited men. Kroll, who led the Minneapolis Police Department’s union during the unrest of 2020,

is barred from policing in three counties for 10 years

 over his treatment of demonstrators during the George Floyd protests.


Bob Kroll, pictured center left.


Kroll, along with a security detail, later escorted O’Keefe and Higby through the protesters and press and into the building.


Kroll’s wife Liz Collins, a former anchor for the local CBS affiliate and now with right-wing publication Alpha News, later snagged an exclusive interview with the two men and their attorneys.


Far-right provocateur Zak X, who is currently facing assault charges after attacking protesters at Whipple during Operation Metro Surge, made an early appearance, heckling protesters while streaming and brandishing pepper spray on multiple occasions.


At one point, Scale told Zak he didn’t like the latter’s provocative “style.”


“He’s a fucking wannabe Charlie Kirk,” Zak said to Scale, confronting him on his livestream. “Charlie Kirk fucking went out because he’s a beta male like you!”


Zak later retracted the statement about Kirk, posting to his social media that he loves Kirk, and that he and Iryna Zarutska inspired him to “stand up.” Zarutska was a Ukrainian refugee who was murdered on a light rail train in Charlotte, North Carolina, who has since become a racist dog-whistle among the far-right.


In a more subdued role, MAGA activist Blake Marnell – known as “Brick Suit” for his brick-patterned suit – was present …

author: Unknown
title: I nipotini del fascismo usano l’antisemitismo per mettere il bavaglio sulla Palestina
content:
Gli eredi politici di chi promulgò le leggi razziali del 1938 approvano una legge che confonde antisemitismo e critica a Israele. Un’operazione di potere che protegge il governo responsabile del genocidio a Gaza e punta a reprimere la solidarietà con il popolo palestinese.


da

OsservatorioRepressione


C’è qualcosa di politicamente osceno nel vedere gli eredi del fascismo italiano ergersi a difensori della lotta contro l’antisemitismo. Sono gli eredi di una tradizione politica che nel 1938 trasformò il razzismo antiebraico in legge dello Stato, espulse gli ebrei dalle scuole, dalle università, dagli impieghi pubblici e contribuì, con la Repubblica sociale italiana, alla loro persecuzione e deportazione nei campi di sterminio. Oggi quella stessa tradizione politica, attraverso i suoi discendenti, pretende di stabilire quali critiche allo Stato di Israele siano ammissibili e quali debbano essere considerate manifestazioni di antisemitismo. Non è una contraddizione accidentale. È un’operazione politica che utilizza la memoria della persecuzione antiebraica per legittimare nuove forme di repressione del dissenso.


Con 147 voti favorevoli, 93 contrari e 5 astenuti,

 la Camera ha approvato definitivamente il disegno di legge sull’antisemitismo, già passato al Senato. Il provvedimento recepisce la controversa definizione 

dell’International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA)

, che attraverso i suoi esempi applicativi rischia di 

sovrapporre l’odio antiebraico alla critica politica dello Stato di Israele e del sionismo. 

Non introduce un divieto penale generale di criticare Israele, ma costruisce un dispositivo istituzionale che può essere utilizzato per colpire la libertà di espressione, la ricerca universitaria e le mobilitazioni politiche. Il problema non è dunque soltanto ciò che la legge vieta espressamente, ma ciò che rende possibile attraverso interpretazioni estensive, provvedimenti disciplinari, pressioni amministrative e forme di censura preventiva.


La maggioranza ha respinto tutti gli emendamenti delle opposizioni, compreso quello che chiedeva di impedire l’intitolazione di strade, monumenti ed edifici pubblici a persone che avessero sostenuto o propagandato l’antisemitismo e l’odio razziale. Un passaggio che rivela molto della natura politica dell’operazione. Chi pretende di combattere l’antisemitismo attraverso una legge che rischia di criminalizzare l’antisionismo non ha voluto accogliere neppure una disposizione diretta a contrastare la celebrazione pubblica dei propagandisti dell’odio razziale. E mentre si votava una legge presentata come necessaria per difendere la memoria della persecuzione antiebraica, nell’aula di Montecitorio alcuni deputati della destra riabilitavano Giovanni Gentile e insultavano i partigiani comunisti che lo uccisero. Rossano Sasso li ha definiti «vigliacchi», mentre Alessandro Amorese di Fratelli d’Italia ha parlato di un «commando di assassini». La risposta di Gianni Cuperlo, «State zitti, fascisti!», ha restituito almeno per un momento il significato storico di quella discussione.


Ma sarebbe un errore fermarsi all’ipocrisia dei postfascisti. Il rapporto tra le destre europee e il governo israeliano ha assunto negli ultimi anni una precisa funzione politica. L’adesione alla definizione IHRA permette a formazioni provenienti da tradizioni nazionaliste, razziste e antisemite di presentarsi come difensori delle comunità ebraiche, senza mettere realmente in discussione la propria concezione etnica della nazione. In cambio, il governo Netanyahu trova alleati disponibili a sostenere le sue politiche e a delegittimare chi denuncia l’occupazione, l’apartheid e il genocidio in Palestina. La conferenza internazionale sull’antisemitismo promossa nel 2025 dal ministro israeliano Amichai Chikli, con la partecipazione di esponenti dell’estrema destra, ha reso evidente questa convergenza. Il punto di incontro non è l’universalismo dei diritti, ma un nazionalismo fondato sull’esclusione, sull’individuazione di nemici interni e sulla criminalizzazione di chi contesta il potere.


La nuova legge italiana si inserisce perfettamente in questo disegno. Dopo due anni di mobilitazioni contro il genocidio a Gaza, il governo Meloni ha dovuto fare i conti con manifestazioni di massa, occupazioni universitarie, scioperi, campagne di boicottaggio e iniziative di solidarietà che hanno denunciato anche le responsabilità politiche e materiali dell’Italia nel sostegno a Israele. author: Bulatlat Staff
title: ‘No red carpet’ for Trump’s arrival in the Philippines
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates hold an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

By Aaron Ernest Cruz and Anne Marxze Umil

“The Filipino people will never welcome a warmonger, racist, fascist, misogynist, sexual offender, and corrupt leader like Trump.”

Despite attempts to derail their protest, progressive groups continued with their action as US President Donald Trump arrived in the country on November 17.

“The Filipino people will never welcome a warmonger, racist, fascist, misogynist, sexual offender, and corrupt leader like Trump,” Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan) said in a statement.

“His war on Iran, support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, military interventions in Venezuela, Cuba, and the Carribean, tariff wars and brutal trade sanctions, and racist immigration policies have hurt people all over the world, destroyed the global economy, and undermined world peace,” Bayan added.

An estimated 6,000 individuals trooped at Liwasang Bonifacio to express their condemnation of the government’s red carpet welcome for Trump and the Pax Silica deal.

According to Bayan, the police blocked the truck to be used in their program and attempted to get their sound system. But the group managed to bring the sound system to Liwasang Bonifacio. During the early morning, the group reported that there were many police deployed in the area.

“Manila is just like a garrison as police were scattered around the city’s entry point,” Bayan Secretary-General Mong Palatino said in an interview.

Bayan President Renato Reyes Jr. also condemned the police for attempting to tow their vehicle, stressing that police violated the Batas Pambansa Blg. 880 which protects the right to hold protests in designated freedom parks without permits. “We don’t need your [police] here and we won’t allow you to tow our vehicle just like what happened last Sunday [November 15].”

Funa-ay Claver, secretary-general of Indigenous group Katribu described the Marcos Jr. administration as a lapdog of the US government, giving up the country’s land for Pax Silica.

“They say it is for development, but we should always ask: Who will benefit from it? It is clear that Pax Silica serves foreign interests rather than the interests of its own people,” Claver said.

Karapatan said that it is not surprising that Marcos Jr. had an extravagant welcome for Trump. “Trump is a fascist, a warmonger and enabler of brutal, genocidal regimes, making the extravagant welcome prepared for him by his fellow fascist and tyrant Ferdinand Marcos Jr. come as no surprise,” the group said in a statement.

Karapata said that it was under Trump that the Marcos Jr. regime began to transform the Philippines into a manufacturing hub for US armaments.

They said that the country became a cog in the US global supply chain, making parts for weapons now being used in US wars of aggression against countries that have stood up against US hegemony. “Only a fellow fascist and tyrant like Ferdinand Marcos Jr. could be motivated to welcome the likes of Donald Trump to our shores.”

The groups tried to march to the ASEAN Summit venue but were blocked by the police. There are also Special Weapon and Tactics (SWAT) personnel holding rifles at the flyover. Under Batas Pambasa Bldg. 880, law enforcers are prohibited to bring guns in a peaceful protest.

“These guards of Trump are arrogant because they have shields and weapons. But the weapons of the Filipino people are truth, democracy, and militant struggle,” Bayan Chairperson Teddy Casiño said in front of the police. He added that even though they were not able to march through PICC where Trump is, he said, their protest is resonating around the world. (DAA)
