author: Igor de Paula
title: Primeira geração de cotistas formados torna-se referência para familiares, diz professor
content:
A Lei de Cotas que regulamentou a reserva de vagas em instituições de ensino superior no Brasil completou 14 anos em 2026. Sancionada em 29 de agosto de 2012 pela então presidente Dilma Rousseff, a Lei nº 12.711/2012 iniciou o processo de democratização ao estabelecer políticas afirmativas para o ingresso de estudantes negros, indígenas e de baixa renda, e seus resultados já são mensurados. 


Em 2012, estudantes negros representavam 20,3% das matrículas nas instituições de ensino superior. Em 2024, o percentual de universitários pretos e pardos já estava em 48,3% do total de matriculados.

 Os dados são do último Censo de Educação Superior, realizado pelo Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep). Também segundo o Inep, entre 2013 e 2024, cerca de 1,4 milhão de cotistas ingressaram em um curso superior no Brasil. 


Para o professor Rodrigo Ednilson de Jesus, coordenador de Políticas de Ações Afirmativas e Inclusão Social da Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais (UFMG) e membro da Associação Brasileira de Pesquisadores/as Negros/as (ABPN), a política de cotas raciais foi positiva tanto para os estudantes que ingressaram na universidade, como para a própria Academia que foi instada a criar novas linhas de pesquisas e absorver outros referenciais para atender as demandas dos alunos que traziam uma outra bagagem cultural.   


Professor Rodrigo Ednilson de Jesus coordenou uma pesquisa sobre os primeiros alunos negros cotistas nas universidades


Por um lado, o acesso às universidades ampliou as oportunidades dos alunos cotistas e levou às suas famílias e comunidades o que o coordenador chama de “consciência do direito” à educação superior. 


Essa é uma das conclusões de Jesus, que é pós-doutor em Ações Afirmativas, Heteroidentificação racial e identidade nacional no Brasil, após produzir o documentário “

Trajetórias de cotistas: por onde anda a primeira geração?

”,  lançado neste mês, em que 12 profissionais que fizeram parte da primeira geração de formandos cotistas das universidades brasileiras são entrevistados. Direção, roteiro, produção e edição de textos do vídeo documentário são da jornalista mineira Queila Ariadne. 


“O ‘Trajetória de Cotistas’ vai mostrar não apenas que a universidade aumentou a renda dessas pessoas, a qualidade de vida, a qualidade de vida das suas famílias, mas também aumentou o sentimento de direito em relação à educação.

Essas pessoas se tornaram referências para as suas famílias, para os filhos, para os sobrinhos. E isso produziu o que a gente chama de consciência do direito. O direito de estar na universidade, o direito de sonhar com uma vida melhor”

, declara.


A produção é um desdobramento de uma pesquisa coordenada por Jesus em 2016, que avaliava os impactos na vida dos primeiros cotistas negros que estavam se formando. Na época, os relatos dos estudantes foram compilados em um livro: “Reafirmando Direitos: Trajetórias de Estudantes Cotistas Negros no Ensino Superior Brasileiro”. Dez anos depois, Jesus reuniu novamente 12 deles para abordar o legado da educação em suas trajetórias.  


Já as universidades, na visão de Jesus, foram favorecidas pelas cotas porque tiveram suas dinâmicas alteradas. Para ele,

estudantes trazidos pelas cotas “obrigaram as universidades a pensar sobre os seus próprios currículos, sobre os referenciais teóricos e a ampliação de linhas de pesquisa. Então, isso também foi muito positivo para as próprias universidades, não só para os estudantes”

, acrescenta. 


Em entrevista à

Agência Pública

, Ednilson de Jesus também aborda os desafios que foram enfrentados para que os cotistas entrevistados conseguissem se formar. Para ele, que chega a citar o racismo vindo dos prórios professores, estudantes negros e negras enfrentaram desafios de fundo “material e simbólico”.  


Os obstáculos de caráter material estão relacionados ao fato de muitos cotistas serem de famílias de baixa renda e, portanto, programas de assistência estudantil facilitam a mitigar a situação.


Já no campo simbólico, Jesus salienta que as experiências são mais duras.

“A permanência simbólica significava também o enfrentamento de situações de discriminação, de racismo explícito, de não ver tantas outras pessoas como eles mesmos; situações, às vezes, de desconsideração e racismo por parte dos professores, que foi mais recorrente de observar”

, afirma.


As dificuldades, no entanto, não impediram que o sucesso acadêmico de estudantes cotistas fosse …

author: James Hamill
title: A Disaster Waiting to Happen?  Brent Bozell and the US-South Africa Relationship
content:
President Donald Trump’s appointment of Leo Brent Bozell as the United States ambassador to South Africa in 2025 was a deliberately provocative act on his part. The appointment always seemed purposely designed to further damage a US-South Africa bilateral relationship which was already fraught due to differences over South Africa’s domestic and foreign policy choices. Put bluntly, for decades Bozell has been a conservative activist not a diplomat and he lacks the basic skills set to hold such an important and sensitive position Trump appoints Leo Brent Bozell III, a defender of apartheid in the 1980s, as ambassador to South Africa | U.S. | EL PAÍS English. As his behaviour in South Africa is demonstrating, that is an environment likely to produce partisan ideologues rather than people with the tact, nuance, patience, and knowledge required for high level inter-state diplomacy. Since taking up the role of US ambassador in February 2026, he has consistently abused his position through hostile posturing and ‘megaphone diplomacy.’ He has disrespected South Africa’s independent judiciary, publicly berated the host government, and has persistently interfered in South African domestic politics – in clear violation of Article 41.1 of the 1961 Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, 1961– by aligning himself with Afrikaner nationalist groupings, Afriforum and Solidarity, and amplifying their grievances Between candour and coercion — why SA won’t bend to Washington’s dictates. He has issued a series of ‘asks’ – US demands in effect – on issues such as farm murders and rural crime, Black Economic Empowerment, land expropriation without compensation in exceptional circumstances US to make SA to pay the price of doing nothing. Consequently, he has now been démarched – summoned to receive a diplomatic reprimand – by the South African Department of International Relations and Co-operation on no less than three separate occasions in 2026: in March (after less than one month in position), June and September Dirco summons US ambassador Bozell again over ‘undiplomatic conduct’.

Bozell’s ‘extraordinary experience’ All of this was very predictable. Bozell’s appointment has captured in microcosm the broader failings of the Trump administration’s approach to diplomacy and international relations: it was incendiary and was designed primarily to appease white nationalist opinion within Trump’s MAGA base rather than to help mend US-South African relations. In a reversal of standard diplomatic practice, Bozell was sent to South Africa to exacerbate rather than ease tensions and to promote discord. Although Trump stated that Bozell brought ‘extraordinary experience’ to his role Trump appoints Leo Brent Bozell III, a defender of apartheid in the 1980s, as ambassador to South Africa | U.S. | EL PAÍS English, it is actually his South African ‘experience’ which is the main problem. Bozell has a long history of opposition to the African National Congress (ANC) whom he labelled ‘terrorists’ during the 1980s liberation struggle era. He enlisted his National Conservative Political Action Committee in a so-called ‘Coalition Against ANC Terrorism’, a collection of American conservative groupings supportive of the apartheid regime. He strongly opposed the US’s opening of formal diplomatic contacts with the ANC, initiated by then Secretary of State George Shultz in January 1987, in which the Reagan administration effectively acknowledged that there could be no long term South African settlement without its involvement Trump’s Pick For Ambassador To South Africa Actively Opposed Fight To End Apartheid. Bozell was also hostile to the liberation struggle per se as was demonstrated by his support in the 1980s for the regime of President P W Botha, his opposition to the global anti-apartheid movement, and his opposition to the US sanctions contained in the Comprehensive Anti-Apartheid Act (CAAA) of October 1986. The CAAA proved to be of crucial importance in intensifying pressure on the regime and helping to move South Africa beyond apartheid. Anyone doubting its impact need only look at the striking similarity between the US demands, as set out in the CAAA, and the changes announced by President F W De Klerk in his historic speech of 2nd February 1990, over three years later. Bozell was profoundly wrong on everything South Africa-related in the 1980s: wrong to attempt to shore up a failing Botha regime which was …

author: dev
title: Lorenzaccio de David Bobée ou l'insuffisance politique
content:
Acclamée par la critique, l'adaptation de

Lorrenzaccio

 de Musset par le metteur en scène David Bobée nous plonge dans l'impuissance politique de l'Italie du XVI

e

 siècle pour mieux nous renvoyer à notre impuissance contemporaine, c'est ce que raconte France Inter. Adèle Aldokas, y a surtout vu une complaisance narcissique, de l'art institutionnel qui ne critique pas grand chose et un public qui « à la fin, se lève, incapable de se soulever. »


Après le couronnement du bouffon, la lumière tombe et le public se lève pour applaudir généreusement. C'est la preuve que le spectacle a plu et que le public est d'accord : nous n'arrivons pas à nous libérer de la tyrannie, les roitelets se succèdent et la République démocratique reste un idéal.


Mais est-ce vraiment pour cela que le public se lève ?


Une chose est sûre, la performance des acteurs est remarquable. Félix Back est stupéfiant et sa prestation unanimement saluée. Sa présence est délicate, toute en contrastes et de nuances, d'une virtuosité assurée. Et pourtant le début de la pièce est dominé par Mexianu Medenou, dont le charisme et la puissance corporelle fascinent, effraient, révulsent. Les deux acteurs portent la pièce, avec aisance, et on s'émerveille encore de la justesse de Greg Germain (Philippe Strozzi), de Catherine Dewitt (Maria ; Le Cardinal), de Djamil Mohamed (Tebaldeo) ou encore, parmi les autres, d'Yassim Aït Adbelmalek (Maffio ; Capponi). Et c'est sans doute le plus important : ce jeu des acteurs qui fait de la pièce de David Bobée un grand moment de théâtre.


Les fans de Bobée, par ailleurs, ne seront pas déçu-es. Nous retrouvons sa patte et son esprit : une esthétique néo-baroque, par le mélange des techniques, et une approche

woke

 assumée, qui fait la part belle aux acteur-ices noir-es et racisé-es. Un rôle muet est même proposé à Jules Turlet (Pierre Strozzi), et l'homosexualité (auquel invite ce joli mot Valois de Musset : « mignon ») est au rendez-vous.


On aura entendu dire qu'il y avait peut-être un peu trop de son et de lumière, de vidéos, que ça pouvait occulter parfois le jeu virtuose de Félix Back, que ce théâtre regardait un peu trop du côté du cinéma, ou que les beaux chants de Nicolas Moumbounou tranchaient avec son personnage grossier de sire Maurice. On aura entendu dire, au contraire, que cette musique, ces lumières, ces vidéos, ces fumigènes (malgré les crises de toux), rendaient dynamiques et accessibles une pièce que le texte de Musset pouvait parfois alourdir (c'est, on s'en souvient, un « théâtre pour un fauteuil »). L'hémoglobine qui dégouline allégrement plaît ou déplaît, question de goût. La scène de la mort de Louise et même celle de l'assassinat d'Alexandre (adaptée de Sand) ont suscité quelques rires, mais on pourrait invoquer le mélange des genres, en plus du mélange des techniques, un grotesque plus ou moins voulu ou bienvenu. Le tout reste réussi : on ne s'ennuie pas, le public en redemande.


Il faut bien sûr saluer cette présence forte, sans concession, décisive d'acteurices racisé-es et d'un muet. Du reste, on sait, par les quelques portraits d'époque d'Alexandre, qu'il n'était pas blanc. Il est toujours bon de rappeler le métissage profond de l'Italie d'hier et d'aujourd'hui, entre Normands, Lombards, Arabes, Espagnols plus ou moins maures, qui ont envahi violemment Sicile, Calabre, Campanie, loin des migrations du désespoir et des exils pacifiques actuels pourtant stigmatisés. La pièce le clame : le problème n'est pas là, il réside dans la fascisme. C'est le péril d'aujourd'hui.


Pourtant, on peut aussi (et on doit le faire) interroger les limites de ces présences. On aura entendu demander, non sans raison : « cette inclusivité est-elle réelle ? », « Pourquoi n'avoir pas surtitré toute la pièce, si on veut inclure les sourd-es ? » On se flatte de pouvoir mettre en scène des « minorités », mais c'est dans l'écrin d'un théâtre bourgeois. On se flatte d'applaudir à cette « intégration », mais pour qui vote-t-on quand on va voter ? Pour qui travaille-t-on ? Que produit-on et que consomme-t-on ? Que fait-on concrètement, sinon bavarder, comme les Républicains de la pièce ? On est content-e de voir que les Noirs et les Arabes peuvent se produire sur une grande scène, tout comme les Blancs, qu'ils peuvent être homosexuels, qu'ils peuvent bien assimiler les codes de la République, et on oublie finalement que cette République n'en a que le nom, et que ses valeurs, par nature, excluent la vraie diversité …

author: Yasmine Johnson
title: Jillian Segal’s war on the left
content:
Antisemitism Special Envoy Jillian Segal’s “Plan to combat antisemitism” is nothing of the sort. Her latest report, published 30 October, is a stunning piece of Trumpist propaganda. It is riddled with conspiracy theories about malign radical-left and Islamist influence in Australian institutions. It calls for sweeping crackdowns on free speech, political activism and migration, all in the name of protecting Israel’s reputation. It is an indictment of the Labor government that commissioned it.

Labor named Segal “special envoy to combat antisemitism” knowing her record as a right-wing warrior and campaigner for Israel’s murderous wars. Her appointment was part of a multi-faceted offensive against the Palestine solidarity movement. She has consistently used this platform to shield the Israeli government from criticism and attack opponents of the war.

Segal’s new report pays little attention to the growing antisemitic far right. Since her appointment, Nazis have addressed thousands at anti-migrant marches. One Nation, a party

riddled with Hitler fanatics

, has shot up in the polls. But far-right antisemitism is minimised because it isn’t the “primary source of concern or anxiety to members of the Jewish community”.

The real danger is “modern, progressive antisemitism”, which Segal labels “the most pervasive manifestation of antisemitism facing Australia”. 

Segal claims that anti-Israel progressives have simply repackaged an age-old hatred: 

“The language of human rights and its greatest crimes—apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc.—has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.” 

Segal doesn’t bother disputing the many well-evidenced allegations of apartheid, ethnic cleansing and genocide levelled at Israel. Nor does she consider that comparisons to the Nazis might diminish if Israel dismantled its concentration camps and Israeli politicians stopped quoting Hitler. Her report is remarkably devoid of any facts or engagement with arguments and counter-arguments. It reads like a News Corp opinion piece.

That’s because her primary objective is to dismiss criticism of Israel out of hand on the basis that it inevitably leads to anti-Jewish racism. While she concedes that criticism of Israel is not

inherently

antisemitic, she argues it is “utilised to create an environment where that sentiment can so easily morph into hostility towards Jewish people”. She terms this “ambient antisemitism”, which increases the danger of “conflation”, where “Jews in Australia are treated as collectively responsible for the actions of Israel”. 

There

is

 a danger that people disgusted by Israel’s actions misdirect their anger toward Jewish people as a whole. The Palestine solidarity movement has made every effort to combat this by distinguishing between Jewish people as a politically diverse religious and ethnic group on the one hand, and the state of Israel on the other. 

Segal, for her part, reinforces this conflation. It is laid out explicitly in her report: “Jewish identity is inherently linked to the land of Israel; it is central to the existence of Jewish people, the Jewish religion and culture”. This is echoed by Israeli politicians who cynically claim to represent the

entire Jewish community

 while committing unspeakable crimes. 

So far, these are the predictable arguments of the pro-Israel right. But as you dig deeper into the report, things get weirder. Segal thinks progressive antisemitism is dangerous not only because it legitimises criticism of Israel, but because it can act as a Trojan horse for more sinister ideologies.

Mainstream progressives are guilty, in her eyes, of “effectively laundering far-left antisemitism and Islamic extremism through a progressive lens … giving fundamentally extremist ideologies an apparently acceptable face”. 

Segal’s report makes repeated reference to this supposed intersection of radical-left politics and Islamic extremism, sanitised and promoted by respectable liberals. It is a wild conspiracy theory, one that sounds remarkably similar to Trump’s recent rants blaming rioting in France on an alliance of “migrants, jihadists, and communists”.

The language in her report mirrors that of right-wing intellectuals and government ministers overseas who rail against “Islamo-leftism”. This is the new iteration of the old myth of “Judeo-Bolshevism”, a …

author: Admin
title: Calendar of Racism and Resistance ( 16 – 30 April 2025)
content:
As anti-migrant, anti-equalities, anti-abortion, misogynistic and anti-LGBTQI rhetoric in electoral campaigning are increasingly interlinked, we reflect this in the coverage below which also includes information on the influence of the Christian Right as well as the religious Right generally.

17 April: Centre-left parties in Italy file a complaint with the communications watchdog against the far-right League, led by Matteo Salvini, for using AI-generated racist, Islamophobic and xenophobic images in its campaigning. (Guardian, 18 April 2025)

17 April: Polish president Andrzej Duda fails to sign off on legislation, approved by parliament, expanding hate crime laws to include sexual orientation, sex/gender, age and disability, referring it instead to the Constitutional Tribunal on grounds that it violates free speech. (Notes from Poland, 17 April 2025)

21 April: After shadow justice secretary Robert Jenrick calls for the legal team representing Hamas in its application for removal from the list of proscribed groups to be struck off, the International Association for the Defence of Democratic Lawyers calls for better safeguards for UK lawyers. Fahad Ansari has since been subjected to racist abuse and Riverway Law lawyers fear for their safety. (X [IADL Law], 21 April 2025)

22 April: Migrant charities accuse Yvette Cooper of pandering to racism in the run-up to local elections as she orders officials to publish data on crimes committed by foreign nationals. (Guardian, 22 April 2025)

24 April: In a campaign speech on the Kent coast ahead of May local elections, Reform leader Nigel Farage demands the government creates a ‘minister for deportations’. (Mail Online, 24 April 2025)

25 April: Following a knife attack at a private school in France which left one student dead and several injured, the mayor of Nantes criticises national politicians for exploiting the attack on social media, adding that the issue is the ‘mental health of adolescents’. The interior minister denounces the ‘savagery’ of school attacks, blaming society for encouraging ‘laxity’, deconstructing order and hierarchy, giving ‘birth to all this violence’. (Libération, 24 April 2025)

26 April: As thousands join an anti-immigration rally in Dublin, Ireland, carrying ‘Irish Lives Matter’ signs, chanting ‘get them out’ and wearing ‘Make Ireland Great Again’ caps, Dublin city councillor Gavin Pepper calls for mass deportations and Conor McGregor shares a video supporting the protest and criticising the government. United Against Racism leads a counter-demonstration. (Irish Times, 26 April 2025)

28 April: Yvette Cooper announces an amendment to the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Bill which will ban all foreign nationals on the sex offenders’ register, whatever their sentence, from claiming asylum. (Guardian, 28 April 2025)

16 April: Following far-right attacks in France on students in Albi, Nancy and Nanterre, the Solidaire Étudiants union office in Montpellier, and provocations from La Bastide at Bordeaux Montaigne University, students and left-wing organisations form student anti-fascist committees. (Left Voice, 16 April 2025)

24 April: School student Justin P is taken to a psychiatric unit after stabbing four fellow students, killing 15-year-old Lorène, at the Notre-Dame de Toutes-Aides private school in Nantes, France. Students at the school say that the teenager had previously expressed support for Adolf Hitler and Nazism and that he had tried to form a romantic attachment with Lorène, who had refused his advances. (Le Monde, 24 April 2025; Yahoo News, 25 April 2025; La Dépêche, 25 April 2025)

25 April: Jean Messiha, a French far-right polemicist and supporter of Eric Zemmour, tweets in relation to Justin P that ‘the young bastard who stabbed several people in Nantes’ was a ‘radicalised young far-leftist’, adding ‘far-left and Islamised scum, same fight against France’. (Contre Attaque, 25 April 2025)

25 April: In France, it is revealed that Justin P placed a 13-page document entitled ‘Immune Action’ on the school’s digital workspace prior to the attack. An analysis by Contre Attaque says that the document, which calls for a ‘biological revolt’ against globalisation so that ‘the natural balance, however cruel’ can ‘regain its place’ against a ‘globalised ecocide’, is redolent of eco-fascism. (Le Monde, 24 April 2025; Yahoo News, 25 April 2025)

author: Coral Wynter
title: Standing with the women and girls of Afghanistan
content:
About 110 people from Australia and Britain joined Amnesty International (AI) in an on-line forum, on September 23, to hear about the human rights group's strategy to support women in Afghanistan. Kathy Allan from AI introduced the forum by saying that when Kabul fell on August 15, 2021, the United States handed over power to the Taliban, after the US Coalition, including Australian forces, had carried out a military intervention into Afghanistan for two decades.

The Taliban has 164 decrees targeting women and girls. Women have been barred from most jobs, and from working with non-government organisations (NGOs). Girls are banned from secondary school and university, parks, gyms and beauty salons. Women cannot speak publicly. LGBTIQ+ Afghans have been forced into hiding.

The Taliban is also attacking ethnic and religious minorities, as well as journalists and human rights defenders.

This institutionalised pattern of systemic domination and oppression based on gender has been labelled “gender apartheid”. Afghanistan is the only country in the world to impose this extreme form of gender discrimination.

Right now, international law has no statute that fully captures this situation. AI is calling for gender apartheid to be recognised as a crime under international law.

Muslima, an Afghan educator and writer, told the forum, “Almost overnight, the door to our classroom was closed. Just because you were a girl, you lost your classroom.

“I never imagined that my future would just mean I stay home ... simply because I was born a girl. Being at home every day felt like a prison, like being in jail. Where do I go? My human rights were wiped out.

“But now I have a computer, my classroom to the outside world. All that I have is a small screen in my room. If they find out, I can face charges.

“Thousands of girls have no access to a computer and internet, but I am lucky. Afghan women can’t talk about their stories, nor can they speak about these issues. Girls of 12 years of age are denied the simple right to education, to learn, to develop their skills, to make friends.

“The Taliban can’t build a strong future by excluding half of the population. Afghanistan is losing enormous [human] potential.

“I want the world to see something beyond our suffering. Women are still writing, working, advocating, creating, contributing and building. If you want to support Afghan women, you must listen to them.

“When the headlines disappear, Afghan women do not disappear.

“So my message is clear: make a space for us to speak. Share our voices.

“Sometimes solidarity begins with something as simple as a refusal to forget. Listen to the voices of Afghan women, who are denied their human rights,” Muslima concluded.

The next speaker was Shaharzad Akbar, a human rights activist from Afghanistan, currently living in exile. She talked about the Peoples Tribunal on Women of Afghanistan, which was held in Madrid, Spain, in October last year and hosted by four Afghan women’s organisations.

They are worried that the actions of the Taliban, as the de facto regime, are being normalised in the region. The Taliban currently have consulates in Germany, China, India and Turkiye, although only Russia officially recognises the Taliban government. Europe is now holding conversations with the Taliban regarding potentially deporting Afghan men and women.

Akbar said, “Women are not able to train as midwives or doctors ... Women will die from preventable diseases because there are not enough female health-care providers.”

Women are suffering from domestic abuse, but it is not considered a crime inside Afghanistan. Emotional, economic and physical abuses are not criminalised. Husbands are allowed by law to punish their wives for any offence.

Women can only go to a judge to make a complaint if they have obvious bruises or broken bones — and face many hurdles to do so. They are not allowed to leave the house alone and a male family member has to accompany them to the court. So a brother or father has to be convinced to support them.

The woman has to relay her message to the judge through a man. If she is believed and she has broken bones caused by her husband, he will be imprisoned for 15 days. He usually returns home only to repeat the abuse.

“We have had increased killing of women, increased suicides of women and a mental health crisis for women and girls in Afghanistan. They don’t see a future for themselves. They are imprisoned in their homes …

author: CNT Valladolid
title: Fuego al orden colonial: racismos, cuidados, trabajo y derechos
content:
Tengo mu poco dinero

pero no me quita el sueño.

Con dos duros me mantengo,

de mi libertad soy dueño.


El día 22 de octubre, dentro de las jornadas de inauguración del nuevo local de CNT en Valladolid, tuvimos una mesa redonda sobre ‘¿Qué sociedad queremos construir? Racismos, cuidados, trabajo y derechos’. En ella compartieron desde mesa sus conocimientos y experiencias sobre estos temas las siguientes personas, a las que agradecemos su generosidad:


Pastora Filigrana, investigadora y autora de

El pueblo gitano contra el Sistema-Mundo

 (Akal, 2020)


Gabriela Poblet, investigadora y autora de

Criadas de la globalización

 (Icaria, 2024)


Mónica Gortyare, activista de Articulación Antirracista de Madrid y  de Asamblea Regularización Ya de Madrid


Como en otras de estas jornadas, la mesa fue ocasión de abrir unos cuantos melones, que afectan no sólo a qué sociedad queremos, sino a qué movimientos sociales queremos pertenecer y qué mejorar dentro (y fuera) de nuestro sindicato. Pues como sindicato actuamos dentro de unas fronteras que causan desde hace años la muerte de miles de personas que quieren cruzarlas, donde se niegan o regatean derechos a quienes las cruzan, y dentro de una sociedad incapaz de superar la histórica persecución y exclusión del pueblo gitano, pero no siempre parece que nos afecte.


Muertes y discriminaciones ocurren bajo una indiferencia social a la que quizás somos menos ajenos de lo que pensamos, por sesgos, inercias y privilegios que tendríamos que revisar. Porque aunque como sindicato queramos ser de toda la clase trabajadora, es evidente que hay una buena parte de ella, la gitana, la migrada y la racializada, que no forma parte aún del mismo. No se trata de preguntarnos cómo conseguir más afiliades, sino de cómo apoyar y respaldar la lucha de los colectivos racializados que ya existen, que ya militan y que ya tienen fuertes redes de apoyo tejidas. Porque si no estamos todes, no hacemos nada.


Pastora Filigrana, desde su experiencia personal, su trabajo profesional y activista como abogada de trabajadoras migrantes del campo, puso sobre la mesa que el racismo no es una actitud o un prejuicio, sino un criterio estructural de distribución de la riqueza en el sistema-mundo, que despoja a unes y les hace instrumentos del bienestar y el enriquecimiento de otres -igual que lo es el patriarcado-. En este contexto, el antirracismo desde un sindicato no es una concesión solidaria, sino un elemento fundamental para ser inclusivo e interseccional.


Todas las intervenciones subrayaron que no es cosa de recursos o de puertas abiertas, sino de ser conscientes de que bajo el chantaje de la ley de extranjería hay miles de personas excluidas que arriesgan por manifestarse o movilizarse contra los convenios que se les aplican, fraudulentos cuando existen. También se trazó un paralelismo con las antiguas leyes antigitanas, que muestran cómo la legislación ha sido históricamente una herramienta de racismo institucional para limitar derechos, restringir el acceso al trabajo y mantener al pueblo gitano en una situación de exclusión.


Gabriela Poblet empezó su intervención recordando que la colonización no es una cosa de hace siglos, sino que sigue activa en fenómenos como los corralitos de los países de la llamada “América latina”, que evaporan los ingresos de todas las clases populares de un país por el ataque contra los bancos locales de los oligopolios financieros. Un método de esclavización a escala masiva no tan visible como las galeras de siglos pasados, pero igual de abusivo, pues somete a miles y miles al chantaje de la precariedad.


Son estos fenómenos los que incentivan que poblaciones migrantes acaben ocupando trabajos precarizados que no hace tanto eran cubiertos por las poblaciones rurales de los propios países del norte global, también sometidos a un proceso de vaciamiento no hace tantos años.


Es preciso referirse sin eufemismo ni coartadas paternales a estos trabajos de criada u otros a los que se ven empujadas muchas mujeres sin derechos laborales para mantener los privilegios de la población blanca adinerada que puede pagarse ese tráfico, y que no forma una patronal propiamente dicha -incluso amparando la explotación en el derecho a la intimidad de un hogar-.


Las medidas parciales que pueden atenuar esa explotación son ambivalentes -la mediación de los gobiernos para la contratación de esos servicios sería en el fondo una subvención a las clases contratantes-. La perspectiva …

author: Kevin Foster
title: CA Legislators Passed a Bill Targeting ICE Contractors. Newsom Vetoed It.
content:
The California governor singlehandedly shut down a bill that could have punished companies for working with ICE.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

California Assembly Bill 2465 passed out of both the California Senate and Assembly with near unanimous Democratic support, setting the stage for a first-of-its-kind bill to punish companies for working with immigration enforcement agencies — then Gov. Gavin Newsom killed it.

AB 2465 would have prohibited businesses from receiving any state-provided grant, loan, or tax credit if they directly invest in, own, operate, or manage a private detention facility, or contract with the federal government for immigration enforcement purposes. It also would have established the “Due Process for All Fund,” transferring money from the general fund toward immigration-related services and programs based on the total taxes collected from businesses made ineligible for tax credits by the bill.

Governor Newsom vetoed the bill on September 30, the final day for him to do so. When asked for comment, Diana Crofts-Pelayo, Newsom’s chief deputy director of communications, pointed to his veto message.

“I agree with the author that more must be done to hold the Trump administration accountable for the indiscriminate raids that have rounded up American citizens, people with legal status, and hardworking parents,” Newsom wrote. “While I appreciate the author’s goal of ensuring that state dollars do not support these egregious federal actions, this bill’s requirements are unclear and expand beyond the stated intent.”

Newsom’s concerns with the bill revolve around impacts on businesses “providing legitimate goods and services to a range of agencies with responsibilities beyond the type of immigration enforcement that inspired this bill.”

The bill would affect major private-prison contractors like CoreCivic and The GEO Group, but it contains a carveout for health care providers that contract with detention facilities or immigration enforcement to ensure they are not punished for tending to injured or ill people in detention.

California Assemblymember Liz Ortega, the author of the bill, took issue with Newsom’s veto justification.

“It is not a legitimate business practice to provide services to an agency that guns down citizens in the streets and violates people’s civil rights,” Ortega wrote in a statement for Truthout. “I was disappointed that AB 2465 was not signed. I still don’t think our tax dollars should be going to companies that are illegally locking up parents and separating families.”

The bill gathered 25 institutional opponents versus 144 supporters, per tracking from CalMatters. Some of those opponents included CalBroadband, the California Chamber of Commerce, and a range of construction, electrical, and manufacturing associations.

Immigrant Defenders Law Center was one of the many supporters. Luis Guerra, the law center’s director of advocacy and external relations, indicated the organization was not pleased with Newsom’s veto.

“Governor Newsom’s decision to veto AB 2465 was a missed opportunity to draw a clear line between California’s values and the corporations profiting from the detention, deportation, and separation of immigrant families,” Guerra told Truthout. “Every day, our attorneys see the devastating consequences of a system designed to detain and deport people while denying them a meaningful opportunity to defend their rights. California should be investing in due process and protecting immigrant communities, not preserving financial benefits for corporations that profit from their suffering.”

At the time of Newsom’s veto, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) had reported 24 deaths in custody in 2026. As of October 29, 2026, this number rose to 32, according to the National Immigration Project, their count including people confirmed dead within 30 days of release — ICE reportedly stopped counting these deaths in June, which immigrant rights groups opposed. This follows a record-high of 33 deaths in ICE custody in 2025, exhibiting a uniform pattern of medical neglect.

It’s unclear which specific businesses Newsom is concerned about — Crofts-Pelayo did not respond to a request for comment on this matter.

author: David Swanson
title: U.S. Voters Rejected Washington’s Foreign Policy; Congress Must Listen
content:
By David Vine, Christine Ahn, and Samer Araabi,

Common Dreams

, November 19, 2026


Members of Congress can create change by following a simple template provided by the People-First Foreign Policy Pledge: End the Iran War and all endless wars, cut the Pentagon budget and abolish ICE, and end support for governments like Israel’s that violate humans rights.


“The idea that US voters don’t care about foreign policy is over.” This is what we wrote in

Common Dreams

 in early October, almost a month before the midterms buried the notion that voters don’t care about foreign policy.


Now, the new Democratic majority has the public mandate and the tools to begin acting on voters’ demands by ending the Iran War, shrinking the

Pentagon


budget

, and stopping the arming of governments abusing

human rights

.


Democrats flipped over 40 House seats and nine in the Senate, providing sizable majorities in both chambers. Analysts across the political spectrum widely

agree

 on what

drove

 the

wave

: President Donald Trump’s unauthorized war on Iran and its role in pushing up the price of gas, groceries, and other basics.


Even Vice President

JD Vance

 conceded the point. “The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone,” Vance

wrote

 in a November 4

social media

 post that made headlines worldwide. “The reason we lost is the war.”


Other aspects of foreign policy also mattered: Voters backed candidates who opposed US support for Israel, Trump’s

tariffs

, and Trump’s

Immigration

 and Customs Enforcement (ICE) violent mass deportation campaign.


The new Democratic majorities, which include 109 incoming lawmakers—the largest class of newcomers since 1933—must seize this moment. With help from

Republicans

 who have read the results, they should use Congress’ power to deliver the change voters want in how the country engages with the world.


Members of Congress can create this change by following a simple template provided by the

People-First Foreign Policy Pledge

, a tool we helped launch before the election with the endorsement of dozens of foreign policy experts and national organizations.


The Pledge urges support for three commonsense foreign policy positions that the elections showed are broadly popular across the country and across significant parts of the political spectrum. The three positions are


Ending the Iran War and other endless wars;


Cutting the Pentagon budget and abolishing ICE; and


Ending support for Israel and other governments that abuse human rights.


To deliver the change that voters are demanding and we desperately need, Congress should follow the Pledge to embrace a foreign policy that prioritizes the safety, security, and well-being of the people of our country and the world over those profiting off war.


End the Iran War and All Endless Wars


Conventional wisdom once said that voters don’t care about foreign policy because it’s too far removed from their lives. This was likely never true, and it certainly isn’t now.


NBC News exit polls

show

 that 74% of voters surveyed said the Iran War was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their vote. Anti-war messages were central to winning Senate campaigns in swing states as diverse as

Texas

,

 Georgia

, and

Ohio

, as well as in

dozens

 of

house

 races

. This is unsurprising for a war that quickly has become the most

unpopular

 in US history, according to Stephen Semler of the Center for International Policy.


The public clearly understands how waging an illegal, offensive war of choice has made their lives less affordable by driving up gas, grocery, and other prices. They likewise know the war is wasting tens of billions of taxpayer dollars that could meet people’s urgent needs at home, while killing and injuring tens of thousands, starting on its first day, when a strike on a school in Minab, Iran killed 168

children

 and other civilians.

Benjamin Netanyahu

 and other Israeli leaders, and

Washington

, DC foreign policy elites who long pushed for the war.

author: Andrea DiP
title: Países europeus adotam “modelo Trump” e criam centro de deportação em Ruanda
content:
Na última segunda-feira (16/11), cinco países europeus anunciaram que irão criar um centro de deportação em Ruanda, que deve funcionar a partir de 2027. Áustria, Dinamarca, Alemanha, Grécia e Holanda querem intensificar as remoções de imigrantes que tiveram os vistos negados na Europa ou não tiveram seus pedidos de refúgio aceitos e não podem voltar aos seus países de origem. Ruanda, em troca, deve receber verbas dos governos europeus para construir e gerir os centros, que ficarão na capital, Kigali.


O acordo vem na sequência de uma recente reforma da União Europeia que permitiu a criação de centros fora do bloco. Em uma coletiva de imprensa conjunta realizada em Viena na segunda-feira, o chanceler austríaco Christian Stocker afirmou que os cinco países desejavam “aliviar a pressão” sobre os sistemas europeus de asilo e impedir que traficantes organizassem viagens mortais pelo Mediterrâneo. Em comunicado escrito, o governo holandês afirmou que os cinco países vão repatriar, na primeira fase do acordo, apenas homens solteiros.


O anúncio foi recebido como um escândalo por organizações de direitos humanos, que publicaram um comunicado dizendo que os planos permitem que pessoas sem direito de permanecer na UE sejam enviadas para países com os quais não têm nenhuma ligação. “Essas políticas transferem as pessoas, e a responsabilidade por sua segurança e direitos, para fora da vista do público e além do escrutínio”, diz a carta, assinada por 45 ONGs de quize países. 


A escolha de Ruanda também preocupa. A Human Rights Watch (HRW) apontou para o “histórico de repressão à dissidência, detenção arbitrária, maus-tratos em centros de detenção” do país e o apoio de Ruanda a um grupo armado antigovernamental na República Democrática do Congo. “Centros de deportação fora do território europeu são a mais recente expressão cínica do esforço da União Europeia para transferir suas responsabilidades para outros países”, afirmou, em um comunicado, Clementine de Montjoye, pesquisadora sênior sobre a África e especialista em Ruanda na organização HRW. 


“Pagar a Kigali para sediar um programa de deportação não só causaria sofrimento e danos aos deportados, como também financiaria e proporcionaria influência política a um governo responsável por graves violações dos direitos humanos no próprio país e no exterior”, disse o pesquisador em entrevista ao jornal Le Monde Diplomatique. 


O anúncio marca a conclusão de uma iniciativa da UE para aumentar as deportações, lançada em 2024, à medida que a migração se torna um tema cada vez mais explorado por partidos de extrema-direita em vários países.


Com eleições se aproximando em vários países da Europa, os partidos de direita e centro direita tentam abocanhar parte desse eleitorado da extrema-direita que comprou a ideia (nada nova) de que as crises políticas, econômicas e o aumento da criminalidade são culpa dos imigrantes e que tudo estaria resolvido com deportações em massa. 


Eu conheço bem essa retórica e a sua eficácia. Em uma recente conferência de centro-direita que acompanhei em Berlin, um pesquisador apresentava divergências e convergências dentro do Parlamento Europeu sobre diversos temas; o único que unia da extrema-direita ao centro era o combate à imigração. 


Na Alemanha, por exemplo, já há algumas eleições o partido de extrema-direita AfD tem baseado suas campanhas em planos de deportação em massa, colocando nas caixas de correio de bairros com alto índice de imigrantes papéis que imitam “passaportes só de volta”. Nas eleições de 2024 para chanceler, ficaram famosos vídeos em que jovens da AfD cantavam músicas sobre “deportar aos milhões”. Em 2025, eu também me infiltrei em um congresso da AfD cujo tema principal eram os 10 anos de abertura das fronteiras do país pela ex-chanceler Angela Merkel e, diziam, o “fato” que a experiência multicultural havia falhado e enchido a Alemanha de “criminosos”, “terroristas” e pessoas que não se integram à cultura local e apenas se aproveitam dos benefícios sociais. Tudo baseado em dados falsos, vídeos sensacionalistas e até um ranking de crimes cometidos por cada nacionalidade. 


O plano europeu segue a mesma lógica de deportação para países terceiros – aqueles com os quais o imigrante não tem qualquer relação – que o

governo Trump

 tem aplicado desde 2025.  Os Estados Unidos têm acordos com mais de uma dúzia de países africanos (alguns sigilosos inclusive), como Ruanda, Uganda, Camarões, Gana, além de outros na América Latina …

author: Stelinsky
title: Επιστολή «προς τον αδελφό ελληνικό λαό»
content:
Στα τέλη Αυγούστου του 2026 δημοσιεύτηκε μία επιστολή 300 μεταναστών που βρίσκονταν εκείνη την περίοδο έγκλειστοι στο καμπ της Σιντικής. Παραθέτουμε εδώ κάποια αποσπάσματα, θέλοντας ο λόγος των ίδιων των ανθρώπων να ακουστεί:

«Εσείς ακούσατε για εξέγερση στη Σιντική. Τι συνέβη και γιατί; Είμαστε στον καταυλισμό της Σιντικής. Είμαστε εδώ 14 μήνες.

Θέλουμε να βγούμε έξω και να κερδίσουμε τα προς το ζην. Είμαστε κουρασμένοι. Είμαστε παγιδευμένοι εδώ και 14 μήνες […].

Πού είναι οι οργανώσεις ανθρωπίνων δικαιωμάτων; Πού είναι οι οργανώσεις για τη δικαιοσύνη; Ζούμε εδώ με φαγητό που μόλις και μετά βίας επαρκεί για τη μέρα. Λάβαμε ένα πιάτο ρύζι, δύο μπιφτέκια και τρία αυγά για ολόκληρη την ημέρα.

Είμαστε εξαντλημένοι και πολλοί από εμάς σκέφτονται την αυτοκτονία. Αυτοί οι άνθρωποι έχουν δει τον θάνατο στη θάλασσα και έχουν υποστεί ταπεινώσεις και εξευτελισμό στα στρατόπεδα εδώ […].

Ναι, θέλουν να μας απελάσουν. Δεν μπορούμε να επιστρέψουμε στην πατρίδα μας. Υποφέρουμε, παρακαλούμε βοηθήστε μας, παρακαλούμε σώστε μας […].

Οι άνθρωποι εδώ είναι σαν ωρολογιακές βόμβες, αλλά κανείς δεν μας προσέχει. Είμαστε συντετριμμένοι σωματικά, ψυχολογικά και ηθικά. Έχουμε χάσει τόσα πολλά και κανείς δεν νιώθει τον πόνο μας […].

Ζούμε υπό καθεστώς καταπίεσης για πάνω από έναν χρόνο. Είδαμε τον πόνο στη Λιβύη, είδαμε τον θάνατο στη θάλασσα και είδαμε τον εξευτελισμό και την καταπίεση στο κλειστό κέντρο της Σιντικής. Χωρίς ρούχα και φαγητό, χωρίς μια αξιοπρεπή ζωή. Το μόνο που κάναμε ήταν να ονειρευόμαστε και να αγαπάμε την Ευρώπη […]».

Τα «κέντρα φιλοξενίας», δεν είναι παρά οι σύγχρονες φυλακές του πλεονάζοντος προλεταριάτου. Από τα σύνορα και τα αστυνομικά τμήματα μέχρι τα δικαστήρια, τα κέντρα κράτησης και τις φυλακές, οι μετανάστ(ρι)ες έρχονται αντιμέτωποι και αντιμέτωπες με ένα πλέγμα νομικών, διοικητικών και κατασταλτικών μηχανισμών, απειλητικών προς την ίδια τους την ύπαρξη.

Η αλληλεγγύη είναι όπλο ταξικό και διεθνιστικό. Ο αγώνας για την καταστροφή των στρατοπέδων συγκέντρωσης και το γκρέμισμα των συνόρων είναι κομμάτι του ευρύτερου αγώνα για την κοινωνική απελευθέρωση, ενάντια σε κράτος και κεφάλαιο. Στους αγώνες αυτούς, ο φασισμός αποτελεί την πιο πιστή εφεδρεία του συστήματος και το μακρύ χέρι της κρατικής καταστολής, σπέρνοντας μίσος σε μια προσπάθεια να διαιρέσει τις καταπιεσμένες.

Στεκόμαστε πάντα απέναντι στη θανατοπολιτική των κλειστών συνόρων, των δολοφονικών επαναπροωθήσεων και του συστημικού ρατσισμού και αντιλαμβανόμαστε τις εξεγέρσεις των μεταναστών μέσα στα camps ως ρωγμές στο μονοπώλιο της κρατικής βίας, ως φάρους αξιοπρέπειας. Δεν αντιμετωπίζουμε τους μετανάστες ως παθητικά θύματα που χρήζουν φιλανθρωπίας, αλλά ως ταξικά μας αδέλφια και υποκείμενα των κοινών μας αγώνων. Στεκόμαστε δίπλα στους μετανάστες της Σιντικής που διεκδικούν τα αυτονόητα αναδεικνύοντας τα βασανιστήρια και την εξαθλίωση που τους επιβάλλει το κράτος και ο φασισμός.

Ντόπιες και μετανάστριες να ενώσουμε τις οργές μας και να τσακίσουμε τη ρητορική μίσους σε κάθε γειτονιά, σχολείο και χώρο εργασίας. Οι εξεγερμένοι μέσα στα κολαστήρια είναι η δική μας φωνή πίσω από τα συρματοπλέγματα, και η δική μας δράση στους δρόμους οφείλει να είναι η δική τους ανάσα.

Μέχρι το ξήλωμα του τελευταίου συρματοπλέγματος.

author: Fabrizio Floris
title: The Sahara was never a border
content:
In July, Algeria and Mali reinstated their ambassadors and reopened their airspace to each other, more than a year after Algerian forces shot down a Malian drone near the border town of Tin Zaouatine.

Al Jazeera reported the thaw

; Agence France-Presse (AFP)

added

 that rebel advances in northern Mali had accelerated it, and that restoring cross-border security cooperation was a priority. In September, Algeria’s prime minister was

received in Bamako with military honors

. 

The reconciliation is about a border that both governments say they cannot control.

Farther east, on the Algeria–Niger frontier, the same logic works differently. The Niger-based NGO, Alarme Phone Sahara, counted more than 34,000 people

expelled from Algeria to Niger in 2025

, a record, up from 31,404 in 2024 and 26,031 in 2023. Migrants who are not Nigerien are left at a desert spot known as Point Zéro and they walk about 15km to Assamaka.

Both stories treat the Sahara as a line to be secured: a front to be held, a space to be cleared of the wrong people. Judith Scheele’s

Shifting Sands: A Human History of the Sahara

 (2025) is a sustained argument that this is the wrong picture. An anthropologist at the

École des hautes études en sciences sociales

, Scheele

combines historical archives, including many Arabic-language accounts, with decades of fieldwork

 and interviews with Saharans themselves. Edward Said taught us that places are imagined before they are governed; Fernand Braudel, that seas link as much as they divide. Scheele applies both lessons to a desert.

Scheele’s Sahara is a human world. The book moves from a city-building civilization in Libya’s Fezzan, contemporary with the Roman Empire, through the caravan trades that carried gold, salt, textiles, and enslaved people to the borderlands of Algeria, Mali, Niger, Chad, and Libya that she knows from her own travels.

The caravan of gold and spice is the image that outsiders inherited, and Scheele asks readers to separate Saharan from trans-Saharan trade: the second is the part that crosses the region and so leaves traces in archaeological sites and in sources written beyond it. Most Saharan trade, she suggests, was in staples, the cereals, dates, salt, cloth, dried meat and skins that groups such as the Arba’a and the Tubu carried. The fabled gold was something the explorer René Caillié never saw in Timbuktu.

The trade in staples survives, and it remains, in Scheele’s phrase, “relatively democratic”: anyone with a four-by-four, some capital and enough cousins along the road can become a carrier or trade on their own account, and negotiate with Malian customs officials. She also notes that the advance of trade routes, and the political rivalries that followed in the Maghreb, pushed North Africans deeper into the desert until they had little choice but to become trans-Saharan traders. Mobility, here, was as much pressure as opportunity. In northern Mali, she visits al-Khalil in 2009 and finds its trade booming. The oldest permanent house there dates from 1993 and began as a store for arms for the separatist rebellion of the early 1990s. Commerce, rebellion and settlement, in the Sahara, are often built with the same walls. What these cases share is a desert that is never empty. It is inhabited not by permanent settlements alone but by routes, encounters, negotiations, and obligations.

Scheele applies the same method to the subjects that dominate the headlines. Slavery, racism, religious militancy, terrorism and desertification each get their own treatment, and in each case, as a

reviewer for


Foreign Affairs


notes

, she shows how familiar narratives often grow out of outsiders’ fantasies of the desert as an inhospitable, impermeable barrier. She does not romanticize that circulation. The same routes carried enslaved people, reproduced racial hierarchies and concentrated wealth in few hands. Nor did colonial rule invent every division: Saharan societies had their own rivalries and territorial distinctions. But colonial administrations hardened them into borders drawn around distant capitals, and began to treat older routes as marginal, illicit, or dangerous. Independent states inherited that architecture, and with it a contradiction: communities keep depending on cross-border movement, while official policy reads that movement as a failure of control.

This is why emptiness is never an innocent description. Calling an inhabited space empty lets existing relationships …

author: Karen Gullo
title: European Commission Plan to Give Frontex Trusted Flagger Status Is A Threat to Free Speech
content:
EFF and 27 other human rights organizations

called

 on the European Commission today to retract a dangerous proposal granting its border agency Frontex to request that national authorities issue takedown orders for social media content and giving it “trusted flagger” status under the Digital Services Act (DSA), the EU regulation governing online platforms and content moderation in the region.

The extraordinarily improper proposal not only disregards the provisions of the DSA but also places a mechanism of enforcement overreach in the hands of a law enforcement agency that has

failed to safeguard people

 against serious human rights violations at EU borders.

Under the

proposal

, Frontex has the power to “monitor publicly accessible social media content, detect developments relevant to external border management, and support action against illegal online content linked to border-security risks.” Granting Frontex trusted flagger privileges on top of its existing mandate risks creating a powerful mechanism for over-enforcement, stifling the free expression of migrants, asylum seekers, and other marginalized groups. We warned the Commission of these risks in a

letter

.

The DSA is supposed to make online platforms more accountable and protect users’ fundamental rights, not give the EU power to sic its border police on people for exercising their right to free expression.

EFF and other rights organizations have for years

sounded alarms

about potential abuse under the DSA’s trusted flagger provision, which gives “Digital Services Coordinators” the ability to award entities—including law enforcement agencies—a privileged channel to alert online platforms about illegal content. We’ve taken the firm position that law enforcement cannot be trusted to properly flag illegal content. In July, we

told

 the Commission that giving law enforcement trusted flagger status could undermine fundamental rights and said that police agencies like Frontex should not be made trusted flaggers. 

The EU proposal gives Frontex decision-making power over free expression that is not envisaged under the DSA. First, content removal orders can only be issued by relevant national authorities. The DSA does not foresee a role for entities like Frontex to request such orders. Second,

trusted flaggers

 notify platforms of suspected illegal content—platforms must prioritize these notices and they have sole responsibility to decide to remove content. It’s not flaggers’ role to request removal orders from national authorities. Combining these powers blur enforcement and flagging functions, which the Commission’s own

draft guidelines

 on trusted flaggers explicitly caution against. 

“The risk of Frontex utilizing its power as both a Trusted Flagger and authority that can demand removal orders, to surveil user-generated speech, and over-flag content under the guise of  ‘border security risk’ is clear. This will likely result in platforms over-censoring content and chilling the speech of already marginalized groups, particularly those from migrant and asylum-seeking communities,” the letter says. 

We urge the Commission to rescind the proposal. It undermines the DSA, threatens fundamental rights of citizens and non-citizens, and is enforcement overreach that does not align with international human rights standards.

author: Unknown
title: Iranian border guards kill a Kurdish kolbar
content:
Iranian border guards shot and killed a Kurdish border kolbar on 14 November in the border area of Baneh, Kurdistan Province.


The Kurdistan Human Rights Network (KHRN) has reported that in the early hours of Saturday, Iranian border guards opened fire on a group of kolbars from close range and without prior warning in the Surkew border area, killing 34-year-old Tayeb Rostami.


The authorities transferred Rostami’s body to the forensic medicine department in Baneh before handing it over to his family, who buried him later that evening.


Rostami was the father of one child, and his wife is reportedly pregnant.


Since the beginning of this year, Iranian border guards have shot and killed at least eight kolbars in various border areas of Kurdistan. Another kolbar died this year from injuries he sustained when border guards shot him last year.

author: Mag
title: Ein Flüchtlingsbekämpfungs-Deal nach dem anderen: Deutschland und die EU und ihre »Migrationspartnerschaften«
content:
Dossier


„

Das Treffen des Europäischen Rats am 20./21.10. wird zum Abschottungsgipfel: Unter dem Label »Migrationspartnerschaft« werden Abkommen mit einer Reihe von Staaten in Afrika und Asien vorbereitet. Dahinter steckt eine Auslagerungs- und Abschiebepolitik in neokolonialer Manier. Menschenrechtlich begründete Tabus scheinen sich für die EU erledigt zu haben. In einem PRO ASYL vorliegenden Beschlussentwurf des Europäischen Rates wird gefordert, nach der Schließung der Fluchtroute über die Ägäis nunmehr auch die zentrale Mittelmeerroute dicht zu machen. Auch die Abschiebungen von Griechenland in die Türkei sollen erhöht werden…

“

Beitrag von und bei Pro Asyl vom 20. Oktober 2016

. Siehe ganz unten die Hintergründe im LabourNet und hier dazu:


Abschiebezentrum: Offenbar Einigung mit Ruanda – Befürworter hoffen auf abschreckende Wirkung, Kritiker sehen „Flucht vor jeglicher Kontrolle“


„

Österreich und vier weitere EU-Staaten wollen abgelehnte Asylwerber und Asylwerberinnen künftig in ein Abschiebezentrum in Ruanda bringen. Entsprechende Pläne dürften Innenminister Gerhard Karner (ÖVP) und drei Amtskollegen und eine Amtskollegin aus Deutschland, Griechenland, Dänemark und den Niederlanden laut Diplomaten am Montag in Wien vorstellen. Zuvor hatten bereits der „Standard“ und Reuters über die Einigung berichtet. (…)


Die Teilnahme der Innenminister Österreichs, Deutschlands, Dänemarks, der Niederlande und Griechenlands an der jährlichen Wiener Migrationskonferenz hatte seit Tagen Spekulationen über eine Einigung genährt. Immerhin wurde zur „Vienna Migration Conference“ des in Wien ansässigen Internationalen Zentrums für Migrationspolitik (ICMPD) auch der ruandische Innenminister Vincent Biruta erwartet. Ruanda wird seit Monaten als möglicher Standort für ein Abschiebezentrum kolportiert.


Außerdem kommt am Montag die dänische Premierministerin Mette Frederiksen zu einem Arbeitsbesuch nach Wien. Die Innenminister der selbst ernannten „Gruppe der Umsetzer“ hatten wiederholt betont, dass bis Ende des Jahres ein Vertrag mit einem Land außerhalb der EU stehen soll. Erste Abschiebungen dorthin solle es 2027 geben, wie es bisher außerdem hieß.


Befürworter hoffen auf abschreckende Wirkung


Nach Ruanda dürften abgelehnte Asylwerber gebracht werden, die nicht in ihre Herkunftsländer abgeschoben werden können. Die Pläne sind Teil der Bemühungen in Europa, die Zahl der Abschiebungen zu erhöhen und die irreguläre Migration einzudämmen. (…)


Die EU-Kommission begrüßte die Initiative. Die Vorbereitungsarbeiten der fünf Mitgliedsstaaten seien aufmerksam verfolgt worden, sagte der zuständige Sprecher am Montag in Brüssel. Die Finanzierung von „Rückführungszentren“ sei prinzipiell Sache der Mitgliedsstaaten, aber die EU könnte begleitende Maßnahmen unterstützen, so der Sprecher weiter. Das müsse „von Fall zu Fall und auf der Grundlage konkreter Anträge der betreffenden Mitgliedsstaaten“ geprüft werden.


„Beschämend“: NGOs kritisieren Pläne scharf


An den Plänen gibt es scharfe Kritik. Ärzte ohne Grenzen Österreich bezeichnete diese am Montag als „beschämend“. Abschiebezentren in Drittstaaten fügten „der Serie unmenschlicher Behandlung von Geflüchteten ein weiteres Kapitel hinzu“. Petar Rosandic von der NGO SOS Balkanroute bezeichnete die kolportierte Einigung als eine „Bankrotterklärung gegenüber den Menschenrechten und eine Flucht vor jeglicher Kontrolle“

…“

ORF-Meldung vom 16.11.2026

 


Siehe aktuell:

Das ist euer GEAS 2026: Maskierte kroatische Polizisten prügeln an der kroatisch-bosnischen Grenze 53 Menschen zurück, fünf Schwerverletzte


Siehe zum Hintergrund das Dossier:

Migrationspakt und GEAS: Neuer Anlauf in der EU-Flüchtlingspolitik (???)


Dämpfer für „Return Hubs“: Albanien lehnt weitere Abschiebezentren für Geflüchtete ab


„

Mehrere EU-Staaten wollen bis Jahresende zu einer Vereinbarung mit Drittstaaten über Rückkehrzentren für abgelehnte Asylbewerber kommen. Jetzt winkt Albanien ab. Pläne für Afrika stehen massiv in der Kritik – hier wie da. (…) Einer vor 2024 mit Italien geschlossenen Vereinbarung für Flüchtlingszentren habe er nur zugestimmt, weil beide Länder besonders enge Partner seien, erklärte Rama in dem Interview. Italien sei „unser europäisches Alter Ego“, fügte er hinzu. „Aber anderen sagen wir Nein, denn Zentren in Drittstaaten allein sind nicht die Lösung“, erklärte der albanische Regierungschef auf die Frage, ober er etwa einer Anfrage aus Deutschland zustimmen würde

…“

author: anred
title: Embarcación: cuando la destrucción del monte prepara el terreno para la catástrofe
content:
El violento temporal que azotó a Embarcación, en la provincia de Salta, el jueves 12 de noviembre dejó alrededor de 150 personas que necesitaron atención médica, viviendas dañadas, escuelas afectadas y árboles, postes y tendidos eléctricos derribados. Pero detrás de la devastación provocada por las lluvias y los fuertes vientos hay una historia que no comenzó con la tormenta: décadas de desmontes, avance de la frontera agropecuaria y explotación de los bienes comunes que transformaron profundamente el territorio.

Por Adrián Flores, para Red Eco Alternativo.


Salta – La localidad de Embarcación, en el departamento General José de San Martín, fue el epicentro de un fenómeno meteorológico de enorme intensidad. Las precipitaciones, las ráfagas de viento y la actividad eléctrica provocaron voladuras de techos, caída de árboles y postes de media tensión, cortes de electricidad y daños en establecimientos educativos. La magnitud del temporal obligó a desplegar operativos de emergencia y suspender las clases en las escuelas afectadas.


La violencia de esta tormenta también debe leerse en el contexto de los fenómenos climáticos extremos asociados a El Niño, cuya intensidad puede incrementar las precipitaciones y elevar el riesgo de inundaciones en distintas regiones. El escenario del Súper Niño vuelve todavía más preocupante esta situación. Pero estos fenómenos no actúan sobre territorios intactos: encuentran ecosistemas profundamente degradados por décadas de explotación.


Aquí se cruzan dos dimensiones de una misma crisis. Por un lado, un modelo de producción y consumo capitalista basado en la explotación intensiva de la naturaleza, que contribuye al calentamiento global. Por otro, la expansión de la frontera agropecuaria, los desmontes y la destrucción de los bosques nativos, que reducen la capacidad de los territorios para absorber y regular las lluvias.


En Embarcación, ambas dimensiones convergen dramáticamente. La misma matriz extractivista que impulsa la destrucción del monte profundiza las condiciones para que los fenómenos meteorológicos extremos se conviertan en catástrofes sociales. Las tormentas tienen causas meteorológicas, pero sus consecuencias están profundamente condicionadas por las decisiones económicas y políticas que transforman los territorios en mercancías.


Topadoras sobre territorios ancestralesMientras Embarcación enfrenta las consecuencias del temporal, las comunidades originarias del departamento San Martín continúan resistiendo el avance de los desmontes y el despojo territorial.


A principios de enero de 2026, en Misión Chaqueña, una comunidad wichí de más de 2.000 habitantes ubicada a 48 kilómetros de Embarcación, sus integrantes detectaron nuevamente a personas que derribaban árboles y quemaban sectores del bosque nativo. La respuesta fue inmediata: decenas de mujeres se organizaron y cortaron el camino para impedir el avance sobre su territorio ancestral.


El conflicto involucra al empresario agrícola salteño Claudio Ferrari, quien desde 2023 pretende apropiarse de una franja de monte que rodea a la comunidad. Aquel año, trabajadores vinculados al empresario comenzaron a abrir picadas, talar árboles y colocar postes para alambrar la zona. Ferrari sostuvo que había comprado esas tierras, aunque, según el abogado que acompaña a la comunidad, no presentó documentación que respalde sus pretensiones.


La defensa del territorio también tuvo consecuencias represivas. El miércoles 7 de enero de 2026 fueron detenidos Leonardo Pantoja y Marta Herrera cuando se presentaron en un destacamento policial para denunciar la tala del monte y las amenazas atribuidas al empresario. Marta fue liberada, mientras Greenpeace reclamó la inmediata libertad de Pantoja.


La comunidad cuenta con carpeta técnica, relevamiento georreferenciado y registro de Asuntos Indígenas. Sin embargo, sus integrantes denuncian obstáculos para acceder a la Justicia y señalan que el empresario pretende avanzar sobre tierras ocupadas ancestralmente por el pueblo wichí.


No se trata solamente de una disputa por la propiedad de la tierra. Es la defensa de un territorio que sostiene la identidad, la cultura y las condiciones materiales de vida de generaciones.


3.300 hectáreas arrasadas en territorio wichíLa dimensión de la destrucción quedó nuevamente expuesta en octubre de 2026, cuando Greenpeace difundió una denuncia realizada junto con comunidades wichí por el desmonte de más de 3.300 hectáreas de bosques nativos en el área …

author: Steven Methven
title: Cuts to Benefits Are Not the ‘End to Neoliberalism’ We Were Promised
content:
Tomorrow, the government will publish the Milburn report. That’s a long-awaited review into Britain’s one million young people not in employment, education or training – the so-called NEETs. Its contents, though, won’t come as a huge surprise, with its author, Tony Blair-era health secretary Alan Milburn, taking to the Sunday morning news rounds to pitch his plans while others briefed its contents to the press.


They’re trying to get ahead of what could be

a significant rebellion

 amongst backbench Labour MPs. And who can blame the rebels? After all, with swingeing cuts incoming, they’re the ones who’ll have to explain to young voters with disabilities and other health issues – as well as angry parents – why their lives are apparently worth less than those just a few years older than them.


In politics, life comes at you fast. But not so fast that we can’t remember what prime minister Andy Burnham pledged just four months ago – an

end to neoliberalism in this country

. That’s a tricky term to define, and while Burnham mentioned deregulation, privatisation and the fantasy of trickle-down economics as its major symptoms, there’s a simpler understanding near at hand. Neoliberalism is when a state decides that corporations, rather than citizens, are its clients.


Far from killing neoliberalism off, there’s more than an element of it in Milburn’s NEET plans. 


The shape of his proposals are familiar, the usual carrot-and-stick approach to welfare aimed at the bottom line, rather than the underlying conditions that put people in need of it. First, the cuts. Milburn will recommend that under-25s will

no longer be able to claim sickness and disability benefits

. Instead, there’ll be a one-stop “youth allowance”, capped at the standard rate of universal credit. So that will be a sharp cut to those who might expect to receive the additional universal credit health element. 


Personal independence payments will also be restricted: under 25s will no longer be able to access PIP. Instead, they’ll be able to

apply to “local funds” for help

 with specific “short-term expenses,” though those with the most severe needs will have their existing entitlements protected. 


Who knew that disability or debilitating illness take on a special reality when a person turns 25? Obviously, they don’t. But that ever-present national thought is at the heart of these proposed cuts: the problems – even the health problems – of the young are always a little bit unserious. They won’t be helped by empathy or care, that thought goes on, but only discipline and downplaying.


In his

government report released last month

, professor Peter Fonagy lists in detail the material conditions driving the mental health crisis in the country’s youth. Increased poverty, insecurity and crippling housing costs. Atomisation, loneliness and lack of opportunity. Growing existential dread around the climate, technology and the political future. An education system impoverished by alienation, comparison and intense scrutiny. 


Burnham has called the number of young people on existing benefits

“a moral failure”

. And it’s a profound one for sure. But it’s not their moral failure. It’s ours.


So will our collective failure be addressed in this review?


Unlikely. Instead, what’s been briefed is that the new, pared-back youth allowance will likely be contingent on recipients engaging with programmes aimed at getting them back into work. And while the scope of the cuts are crystal clear, that positive package remains vague. The papers have been told there’ll be investment for employment advisers, mental health support and internships, backed up by – potentially –

a new legal duty on the government

 to furnish every young person with a route into work. 


Great – but maybe let’s get that in place before the cuts? 


No, no. Young people must always get the stick first. And business? It’s the carrot for them.


“I think we should subsidise wages,”

Milburn told Laura Kuenssberg

 on Sunday, “Because young people today are walking into the workplace often with a mental health problem, ADHD or anxiety, and if you’re a small business, that’s a cost that you’ve got to absorb. The state has a responsibility to help them with that.”


The state has a responsibility to help

businesses

 to solve the social problems caused by the state relying on businesses to solve the social problems caused by the state relying on…


Stop the merry-go-round, it’s making us sick.

author: Unknown
title: “Gen Z Regulates” : A New Wave of Unrest in Germany?
content:
For months, unrest has been spreading across Europe. In

Spain

, a movement against evictions and gentrification culminated on November 11 in a countrywide general strike. In

France

, student revolt set off the most intense street confrontations since the

Yellow Vest movement

. Albania has seen wave upon wave of clashes since last February. On Halloween, the European youth protests finally reached Germany.


Under the motto

“Gen Z regelt”

 (“Gen Z regulates”), tens of thousands took to the streets of nearly 40 German cities on October 31. While a large-scale uprising like the

one

 in France remains unlikely, the first cracks in the pacification of society are starting to show. In this report, two anarchists describe their experiences in two different demonstrations and discuss the potential of the events.


More demonstrations on the same theme are scheduled for

November 20

.


A stylish banner in front of the “Gen Z Regelt” protest in Göttingen. What would Goethe have said?


Germany in Crisis


The demonstration on October 31 took place in a general context of crisis. In Germany, as elsewhere around the globe, inflation has run rampant over the last six years, driven by the pandemic, Putin’s invasion of Ukraine and the consequent loss of cheap natural gas from Russia, and, most recently, the US-Iran war.


Another growing influence on the economy is the climate catastrophe. It is

estimated

 that Germany will lose around 30 billion euros a year as a consequence of its impact. In one week, a heatwave at the end of June

killed

 close to 10,000 people. Unlike countries that have long-term experience with temperatures above 40 degrees Celsius, only 10% of homes in Germany have air conditioning; with the exception of intensive care units and operating rooms, most hospitals and nursing homes don’t have it, so people who experienced heat stroke were treated in overheated rooms. Senior citizens and those with preexisting health problems were especially hard hit: in at least one nursing home, temperatures

reached

 up to 50 degrees Celsius.


A protester in the German city of Essen asks to stop some of the impacts of climate change.


Who dies as a consequence of climate change is determined mostly by class. Germany also faces a housing crisis—

something like 53% of people live in rented homes

—and the cheapest flats are generally located right beneath the roofs of buildings several stories high. These buildings were built to keep heat in, so during heat waves, temperatures in the flats at night often stayed above the outside temperatures at same time.


On top of this, the government comprised of the neoliberal left (SPD) and Christian conservative (CDU/CSU) parties has introduced an unpopular austerity program in order to push through a massive increase in military spending, which started after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. It would take another article to list all the financial cuts involved. Workers and middle-class people will have many billions less in “social benefits”—in other words, they get less back from the work and resources that the state and capitalists take from them.


Some 12% of all jobs in Germany are

directly in state institutions

, in addition to fully state-owned companies and other organizations connected to the state, like the public health insurance agencies and public media companies. Many of these have stop hiring because of the financial situation. At the same time, German economic growth is stagnating. Consequently, “Gen Z” career entrants confront a context in which companies are trying to figure out how to use artificial intelligence to replace them amid an employment market that is already much worse than previous generations faced. This is undermining the last vestiges of a social contract between companies and the state on one side and segments of the youth on the other.


Study, get degree, and you can have a middle-class life? Not anymore.


Finally, some international fashions trends like ski glasses are reaching German youth.


Unemployment is rising among university and college graduates. The social situation isn’t as catastrophic as it has become in other countries, but by contrast with many other countries, people in Germany do not have much experience helping each other directly. German society has focused on the state as the only thinkable source of support when people lose their jobs or experience other setbacks.


As a result, anger has spread …
