author: Isaac Nellist
title: Community picket shuts down Bisalloy Steel for 36-hours over ties to Israel’s genocide
content:
A community picket has shut down operations the Bisalloy Steel factor in Unanderra, in Tharawal/Wollongong, for the 11th time, over November 15–17, for its role in arming Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Bisalloy Steel supplies armoured steel to Israel that is used for armoured vehicles, tanks and other military technology used in its genocide of Palestinian’s in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank.

The picket was organised by Wollongong Friends of Palestine (WFoP) and supported by many Palestine solidarity and anti-militarism groups.

“We had amazing community support,” Safaa Rayan, social worker and WFoP spokesperson, told Green Left. “It was cold and rainy but we still managed to have hundreds of people not just turn up, but camp out. The street was lined with tents, each full with people.

“Parents turned up with their children, we had three DJ performances each day … we even had people join in who have never been to a protest or picket before.”

At the previous picket in June, NSW Police attempted to break up the picket, arresting at least one person and pushing others to the ground. One woman was concussed after police allegedly pushed her head into the pavement.

“The police violence at the last picket really shows how Bisalloy and the cops are working together to protect the genocide supply chain,” Rayan said. “It's clear the NSW government values business as usual for genocide suppliers far more than the rights of citizens, let alone the lives of Palestinians.”

Rayan said the police presence was minimal this time. “They sent out a car every three hours, would drive past and leave.

“Our pickets are extraordinarily peaceful, and people are very respectful of the area and the environment.”

Local campaigner and Jewish woman Kim Sattler said the deepening militarisation of Wollongong and the appointment of Bisalloy into the AUKUS supply chain was concerning. “This endangers our local community and leads us into war.”

Rayan said “AUKUS is a threat to not only Australia's sovereignty, but also to our environment bringing nuclear submarines at our shores, particularly as they want to build a base here at Port Kembla”.

Climate organiser and youth worker Jayne Hoschke said Bisalloy should make things that the community needs to address the climate crisis. “Instead, they’re determined to help make things that make the world worse … our community won’t let that happen.”

“It's all interconnected,” Rayyan told GL. “We will continue to picket at Bisalloy until they divest from the military industrial complex.”

She also called on the federal and state government to take action. “It is their obligation under the United Nations statue to not supply weapons or weapons parts to a country committing a genocide.

“Because of their inaction, we as the citizens are having to do the work.”

Wollongong Friends of Palestine

author: Cas Smith
title: Hazelmere locals reject plans for mega AI data centre
content:
About 200 people rallied outside Midland Town Hall on November 11 to oppose plans for a hyperscale artificial intelligence data centre in Hazelmere, in Perth’s eastern suburbs.

Gwenaël (Gwen) Velge, a Research Associate at Murdoch University’s Mineral Policy Institute; Kate Herron from Trillion Trees; and former Labor MLA Matthew Hughes addressed the rally and highlighted the disruptive nature of CDC Data Centres’ planned project, which is expected to cause significant noise pollution and energy usage.

At a consultation meeting last month, a CDC technician said the data centre would have an energy allotment of 192 megawatts (MW) with 96 generators.

This would make it significantly larger than the 120 MW, 88 generator data centre previously proposed by Greensquare, which was rejected earlier this year by the City of Swan, following community backlash and concerns about noise pollution.

Velge noted the significance of this decision in the Mining Monitor on October 29. “Earlier this year, the City recommended refusing the GreenSquare proposal over the potential noise of its 88 generators.

“CDC proposes 96 generators, [which] come within 1dB (decibels) of the limit modelled at 75% load, and approach ‘the limits of compliance’; whereas Greensquare was asked to model at 100% load.”

He said the “sheer scale” of the energy demand of hyperscale data centres makes it harder to achieve a renewable energy transition.

“Renewable energy capacity meant to replace coal and gas is directly absorbed by this new demand. In the best-case scenario, this added demand slows down the transition, in the worst-case scenario the narrative and promises of ‘transition’ justifies and legitimates actual energy addition.

“Of course, some grid growth is to be expected as we electrify. But data centres are a clear case of addition: that demand did not exist before and it competes directly with the electrification part of the transition.”

The Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) expects consumption on the region’s electrical grid to increase by 57% in the next decade, from 20.4 to 32.1 terrawatt-hours (TWh).

However, this excludes the energy demands from data centre projects already in the pipeline, which are expected to be excessive, based on the ‘cooling’ requirement for servers.

Two planned projects in WA, the Hazelmere data centre and a project in Maddington — both proposed by CDC — are expected to consume 4.3TWh a year in total (or on a single hot day, up to 550–590MW).

Velge said this would be “more than five times AEMO’s forecast for the entire sector, and nearly 40% of the total projected growth for the next decade”.

“With huge amounts of heat comes huge amounts of emissions, and heat which must be displaced with either water or with fans.

“So, the choice is between huge water usage or noise. Adding this much extra demand on the grid is bound to push the price of electricity much higher than it already is.”

Another concern is the lack of transparency around the Hazelmere project, with many questions remaining about how it might develop. CDC’s application, for example, refers to the planned building as “HA1”, which raises the question: should people be expecting a HA2?

Local residents have discovered that CDC has acquired the adjoining lots at 170 Bushmead Road and 40 and 50 Hazelmere Crescent, making a larger project down the track a real possibility, even if the acquisitions had not been included in the current application.

This meant that CDC could be using a “salami-slicing” approach, splitting the project into smaller units, so that its cumulative impacts can’t be assessed as a whole.

In any case, Gwen argued that data centre projects should be approached like mining ones.

“Treating data centres like mining projects means applying our Mining Policy Principles: the right of affected communities to veto, assessment of cumulative impacts not just project by project assessments and a meaningful test of whether the project serves communities and the transition or if it serves private profits....

“We shouldn’t let ourselves be priced out of our own public utilities to release more carbon emissions and more heat into our globally warming atmosphere.

“As we know from the US, data centres are also an opportunity to rally people from all walks of life and all political stripes around something everyone opposes — a genuinely positive sight in the polarising times we live in.

“The numbers don’t add up. People and ecosystems …

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: No red carpet for empire: State repression and the fight against Pax Silica
content:
Kampuhan Kontra Pax Silica, a UP Diliman-based formation, together with progressive groups, students, faculty members, and rights advocates hold an indignation protest along Katipunan Avenue in Quezon City on November 15, 2026. Photo by Carlo Manalansan/Bulatlat

At the center of this escalation is Pax Silica, Washington’s emerging high-tech, resource-intensive war infrastructure. If NATO is the military apparatus built to fight U.S.-led wars, Pax Silica is the pre-war supply chain alliance designed to sustain them.

6,000-strong at Liwasang Bonifacio alone—and the numbers continue to surge as protesters march toward the PICC as U.S. President Donald Trump sets foot on Philippine soil. For over a century, U.S. imperialism has plundered this territory and oppressed its people, dating back to how it usurped the Katipunan’s hard-won 1896 triumph over Spanish colonialism. This is not the first time the Filipino people have fiercely rejected a Trump visit; they rose in protest during the ASEAN Summit in November 2017, and they are rising again.

The Filipino public’s refusal to welcome Trump—standing in sharp contrast to the Marcos Jr. administration’s eagerness to accommodate Washington—cannot justify the sweeping crackdown on activists exercising their fundamental rights to assembly, expression, and association. International observers have been alarmed by the scale and intensity of police brutality under Marcos Jr., which echoes the state terror unleashed over half a century ago under the U.S.-backed Martial Law dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos Sr.—a regime only toppled in 1986 after a protracted, heroic struggle against U.S. imperialism and its client-dictator.

Yet this violence is not merely a nostalgic return to his father’s Martial Law era; it is the continuation of an unbroken war against the poor. In the Philippine countryside, landless peasants live in a state of perpetual siege, battered by recurring tiempo muerto (dead seasons), massacres, and state-backed counterinsurgency campaigns that target cooperative leaders and their families. In the cities, whenever public anger boils over—such as during last year’s mass anti-corruption demonstrations—state repression falls hardest on patriotic youth—students and urban poor—the very demographics with the greatest stake in systemic change.

At the center of this escalation is Pax Silica, Washington’s emerging high-tech, resource-intensive war infrastructure. If NATO is the military apparatus built to fight U.S.-led wars, Pax Silica is the pre-war supply chain alliance designed to sustain them. Before a single bomb is dropped, it secures the physical pillars of modern warfare and artificial intelligence—water, energy grids, land, and semiconductor supply chains—within allied borders. Designated as the United States’ key strategic ally in Asia, the Philippines is being positioned as a primary resource frontline.

The lethal purpose of Pax Silica’s weaponry and intelligence apparatus is already on full display in Palestine—one of its primary targets, and the sharpest expression of a settler colonialism that never stops settling. As this colonial project expands, so too does the global infrastructure required to endlessly reproduce the war machine. That relentless reproduction of war stands in stark, irreconcilable opposition to the social reproduction of human life and labor. This is precisely why the Filipino working poor and youth are determined to junk Pax Silica and reject the presence of a war criminal like Trump. For us Filipinos, defiance against this weaponized interdependence is an imperative of national self-defense.

In oppressed nations like the Philippines, where the people are actively working to resolve their primary contradiction against U.S. imperialism, defending the social reproduction of life and labor inevitably requires taking to the streets. When protesters march despite knowing they will face state violence and police brutality, it is not because they invite harm or court repression; rather, it is how the peoples of oppressed nations shed the illusions of safety and docility under U.S. imperialist diktat. Only by confronting that violence do we reclaim our dignity—a dignity rooted in land, national patrimony, solidarity, and the camaraderie in struggle that Filipinos have always been proud of and known for.

This collective resolve has deep historical roots. From the basic masses and Indigenous Peoples to professionals, students, cultural …

author: Pip Hinman
title: NSW Labor goes full tilt to support coal
content:
As Yasmin Catley, police minister and NSW Labor MP for Swansea, in the Hunter, continues to rail about a climate protest she had wanted to ban, NSW Labor is rushing through a pro-coal bill which critics say undermines a recent federal High Court ruling.

The Paddle for the Planet, organised by Rising Tide, drew around 1000 people to Horseshoe Beach in Muloobinba/Newcastle on November 14. The protest was designed to highlight Australia’s lack of leadership at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye.

Its attendance was boosted by NSW Labor’s last-ditch undemocratic attempts to prevent it from going ahead. This included Premier Chris Minns’ direct intervention into Newcastle City Council, demanding it ban Rising Tide and, shockingly, “associates, subsidiaries, other groups and individuals” from holding events or protests on council land.

The motion only passed with the casting vote of independent Mayor Gavin Morris, after Labor councillor Declan Clausen crossed the floor to support the ban.

But the NSW Supreme Court’s decision to favour individuals’ right to peacefully express themselves knocked NSW Police’s efforts to ban the protest on its head.

At least 800 people took to the water in canoes and kayaks on a calm and sunny day. There was not one NSW Police officer in sight — nor any coal ships.

Climate activists occupied the channel for an hour to make their views known about Labor’s pretense over its commitment to the climate while approving new coal and gas projects.

Even after the peaceful event, Catley continued to rail against the climate activists for being “reckless” and “dangerous for everybody”.

Meanwhile, Cately and Minns are pushing a new pro-coal bill, favouring MACH Energy, which aims to circumvent a High Court decision on that company’s mine in the Hunter Valley.

The Environmental Defenders’ Office (EDO) described the Mount Pleasant Mine Bill 2026 bill, which went to parliament on November 10, as “eroding the rule of law, the separation of powers and public trust in independent decision-making”.

The bill, which Labor wants to push through this week, authorises MACH Energy to continue mining thermal coal at Mount Pleasant until 2032 (up to 16.5 million tonnes).

The EDO said not only does it override the pending process and decision of the Land and Environment Court of NSW, following the High Court decision, it contains a dangerously broad clause which allows the Planning Minister to be the consent authority for the approval, not the Independent Planning Commission. It would circumvent parliamentary scrutiny.

Jacqui Mumford, Nature Conservation Council NSW (NCC) CEO, said this “would give the Resources Minister unfettered power to override all other laws in relation to the Mount Pleasant coal mine” adding, “this kind of power is a major corruption risk”. She said such a law “would take NSW back to the days of [disgraced Labor MP] Eddie Obeid by bypassing independent assessments and public consultation”.

Labor’s talking points about “protecting jobs” at the Mount Pleasant mine are also being challenged.

While the bill contains a “jobs guarantee”, to which mining corporations must agree, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG) pointed out that Labor has not shown a commitment to coal workers at Mount Pleasant, as most are on insecure labour hire contracts.

Labor signed off on a transition authority and investment fund which are supposed to support workers wanting to leave the fossil fuel industry. But with no dedicated funding figure in the Future Jobs and Investment Fund, it remains abstract.

Retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy and barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson have publicly criticised NSW Labor over its new coal bill. “I think it’s disgraceful,” Watson, a director at the Centre for Public Integrity and former senior counsel assisting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption, told The Guardian on October 21.

“This is, in effect, to overturn a decision of the high court of Australia after a fair hearing. In my book it’s contrary to the separation of powers which acknowledges that each branch of government has its own area or domain.”

Whealy told the ABC on October 20 that the government’s bill is “reprehensible” because it “obliterates” the legal process.

“With an election early in 2027, such matters do not seem to phase NSW Labor, which seems more singularly concerned about winning votes back from One Nation in coal …

title: Μαζικές διαδηλώσεις για την επέτειο του Πολυτεχνείου σε Αθήνα και Θεσσαλονίκη (φωτορεπορτάζ & video)
content:
Μαζικές διαδηλώσεις για την επέτειο του Πολυτεχνείου σε Αθήνα και Θεσσαλονίκη (φωτορεπορτάζ & video).


Αθήνα


Δεκάδες χιλιάδες άνθρωποι έδωσαν και φέτος το παρόν στους δρόμους της πρωτεύουσας τιμώντας τη μνήμη της εξέγερσης του Πολυτεχνείου. 53 χρόνια μετά από εκείνον τον Νοέμβρη του 1973, η εξέγερση συνεχίζει να εμπνέει και να αποτελεί σημείο αναφοράς στους σημερινούς αγώνες. Ο λαός της Αθήνας κατέκλυσε το κέντρο της Αθήνας στην καθιερωμένη πορεία προς την αμερικάνικη πρεσβεία. Τις προηγούμενες μέρες είχε σπάσει ντε φάκτο η απαγόρευση του πρύτανη του ΕΜΠ με την

κατάληψη του κτηρίου Γκίνη και το άνοιγμα της πύλης στη Στουρνάρη

.


Πιστή στο ραντεβού της κι η ΕΛ.ΑΣ. Για ακόμη μια φορά έδωσε ρεσιτάλ αποκτήνωσης και χυδαιότητας. Στο τέλος της πορείας τα κορδόνια των ΜΑΤ απαγόρευσαν στον κόσμο που συμμετείχε στα αναρχικά/αντιεξουσιαστικά μπλοκ να διαλυθεί προς την πλατεία Μαβίλη και τον ωθούσαν προς τη λεωφόρο Αλεξάνδρας. Εκεί τα ΜΑΤ επιτέθηκαν αναίτια, τραυματίζοντας σοβαρά 4 γυναίκες στο κεφάλι. Τουλάχιστον μια κοπέλα χτυπήθηκε με γκλοπ στο πίσω μέρος του κεφαλιού της.


https://www.alerta.gr/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/v-e-l-o-c-i-t-y-antireport-17-11-2026-Tonight：-the-moment-a-riot-cop—from-the-larges.mp4


Τα ΜΑΤ επιτέθηκαν επίσης μέσα στον σταθμό μετρό Αμπελοκήπων και έκαναν προσαγωγές στον σωρό μαζεύοντας κυρίως ανήλικους που φορούσαν μαύρα ρούχα.


Συνολικά έγιναν 15 προσαγωγές εκ των οποίων 2 μετατράπηκαν σε συλλήψεις. Αργά το βράδυ εκδόθηκε

κάλεσμα αλληλεγγύης στη ΓΑΔΑ

 για τους προσαχθέντες και συλληφθέντες της πορείας.


Θεσσαλονίκη


Πάνω από 10 χιλιάδες άτομα ανταποκρίθηκαν στα

καλέσματα

 φοιτητικών συλλόγων και σχημάτων, εργατικών σωματείων, κομμάτων και οργανώσεων της Αριστεράς και οργανώσεων και συλλογικοτήτων του αναρχικού/αντιεξουσιαστικού χώρου. Η πορεία, ξεκινώντας από την Πολυτεχνική Σχολή ΑΠΘ, διέσχισε όλο το κέντρο της Θεσσαλονίκης μέσω των οδών Εθνικής Αμύνης, Τσιμισκή, Βενιζέλου και Εγνατία ενώ κατέληξε στο άγαλμα Βενιζέλου. Καθ’ όλη τη διάρκεια τα αναρχικά/αντιεξουσιαστικά μπλοκ ήταν περικυκλωμένα από ισχυρές δυνάμεις των ΜΑΤ αλλά και από δεκάδες μαυροφορεμένους και κουκουλοφόρους ασφαλίτες που έφεραν σακίδια. Ένα φαινόμενο που επαναλαμβάνεται σε κάθε μεγάλη πορεία. Μετά το τέλος της πορείας μικροεπεισόδια ξέσπασαν στη Ρωμαϊκή Αγορά με δυνάμεις της ΕΛ.ΑΣ. να περικυκλώνουν και να αποκλείουν την περιοχή για παραπάνω από μια ώρα.

author: Sharon Zhang
title: As Congress Debates Ending Iran War, Trump Sends a Third Aircraft Carrier
content:
CENTCOM announced on Tuesday that it had carried out more strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

A third U.S. aircraft carrier with thousands of U.S. troops has arrived in the Middle East to support the Iran war, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced on Monday, adding to the U.S.’s arsenal in the area as President Donald Trump keeps his options open for escalating the war.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the area on Sunday, joining two other aircraft carriers, each with roughly 5,000 soldiers and dozens of fighter jets aboard, and about 20 other warships.

The carrier’s arrival comes as the U.S. continues its war on Iran with a naval blockade of Iranian ports, a sanctions campaign, and strikes. Reuters reported that the U.S. carried out a new round of airstrikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island on Tuesday. Iran began firing back on U.S. assets in the region in recent days after reports found earlier this month that the U.S. has been secretly attacking Qeshm for weeks, despite President Donald Trump saying at the time that “we haven’t been doing any fighting for months.”

Since then, Trump has said that the war is “militarily effectively over” and that he’s aiming to maintain “the status quo.” The status quo does still include U.S. military activity, and analysts have warned that inaction by Congress to force a withdrawal is stretching the conflict into a forever war.

Further, the arrival of the new aircraft carrier, which left its base in San Diego in September, gives Trump access to a massive amount of military might in the region that he could use at any time.

Reuters reported on Sunday that Trump has been telling allies that he may hold off on attacks if the U.S. doesn’t face new attacks from Iran or Houthi, or Ansar Allah, militants in Yemen. In public comments, he has indeed preferred to say that the war is winding down or is over.

However, Reuters, citing current and former U.S. officials, also noted that “Trump has alternated between threats of escalating the war with new strikes and winding down hostilities, and current and former officials say he does not appear ‌to have made up his mind about how to resolve the unpopular conflict.”

Trump has reportedly been calling around to regional allies, like Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Turkish President Tayyip ​Erdogan, apparently telling bin Salman in October that he was planning to resume intense attacks after the midterm elections. Both allies apparently asked him not to intensify strikes again.

Though the temperamental commander-in-chief may conduct a devastating campaign in Iran any time, Democrats in Congress who have pledged to end the war are dragging their feet on actually doing so. Though some progressives and Democrats have said that they plan to try to force a defunding of the war through the next government spending package, which is due December 11, others have said that they don’t want to risk a shutdown in order to end the war that killed roughly 3,500 Iranians as of July.

At the same time, lengthy deployments for U.S. soldiers on the aircraft carriers in the Middle East are overstretching the Navy, as reports have found that sailors have faced extreme hardship while on board, including a lack of food and a spike in suicidal ideation and attempts.

However, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao downplayed these concerns during his Senate confirmation hearing on Tuesday. Cao said that sailors who reported losing weight while deployed were just picky, “like my kids.” He said that the reported eight suicide attempts from the USS Abraham Lincoln earlier this year were not suicide attempts, but “eight suicide mitigations.”

Cao also displayed a complete disregard for basic facts about the costs of the war. Cao said he doesn’t know what the U.S.’s naval blockade on Iranian ports is costing daily in another line of questioning, and that Pentagon inspectors have still yet to fully assess damage to naval bases in the Middle East that were struck by Iran earlier in the war.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s …

author: Unknown
title: Peoples’ Climate Summit addresses energy trade and war in Gaza
content:
At the Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya, international environmental and solidarity organizations focused their discussions on the economic links between the fossil fuel industry and military violence. On the third day of the gathering, organized as an alternative to the UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), discussions centered on the destruction of livelihoods in Gaza, the role of international energy supplies and demands for a comprehensive embargo against Israel. Participants examined the extent to which climate justice also required overcoming war, occupation and military expansion.


Representatives of Energy Embargo for Palestine, the Global Sumud Flotilla, the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement and various international solidarity networks were among those taking part in the event.


Destruction in Gaza as an ecological crisis


Asad Rehman of Friends of the Earth highlighted the long-term environmental consequences of the war in Gaza. He stated that the destruction of water supply and sewage systems, damage to essential infrastructure and soil contamination caused by munitions, debris and untreated wastewater had devastated livelihoods that could take decades to restore.


Rehman argued that this destruction should also be examined from the perspective of ecocide. He also raised the question of political and economic control over natural resources: “Who extracts which resources, from whom, for whose benefit and under whose authority? That is the fundamental question.”


Ana Sanchez drew a connection between Israeli military policy, international arms trade relationships and the rise of far-right movements. In her assessment, Israel benefited from diplomatic support while supplying military and security technologies to right-wing governments. She argued that an effective arms embargo must go beyond halting individual arms deals and encompass entire supply chains, including the disruption of fuel shipments.


“Solidarity means disrupting supply chains. That means a two-way embargo: neither buying nor selling. It means stopping fuel deliveries,” Sanchez explained.


She emphasized that the liberation of Palestine was not an issue separate from the climate movement. Rather, she said, the fossil fuel-based economic system, patriarchal power structures and military violence were closely interconnected. “There can be no climate justice without freedom for Palestine,” she stressed.


Criticism of oil shipments through Turkey


Celine Isimbi of Energy Embargo for Palestine addressed specific economic ties, highlighting the importance of international oil trade to Israel’s energy supply, particularly shipments from Azerbaijan. According to Isimbi, Israel obtains more than 40 percent of its crude oil requirements from Azerbaijan. The oil is transported through the Baku–Tbilisi–Ceyhan pipeline to Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, from where it is shipped to Israel by tanker.


Isimbi stated that her organization had documented a total of 77 oil shipments along this route to Israeli ports between May 2024 and June 2026. She alleged that vessels had temporarily switched off their automatic tracking signals to conceal their actual destination ports.


Isimbi also said that Turkey’s Ministry of Transport and Infrastructure had confirmed that ships had provided false information to port authorities and that legal proceedings had been initiated in connection with these incidents.


The activist called for fossil fuel supplies to no longer be considered separately from their military and political uses. She argued that an energy embargo must also cover transportation routes and the companies involved.


Calls for reparations rather than development aid


Abeer Al Butmeh of the Palestinian environmental network PENGON called for reparations and the restoration of destroyed livelihoods. She argued that international development aid alone could not adequately address the political and material consequences of the destruction. She pointed out that the Palestinian population must be able to make its own decisions regarding energy supplies, water resources, land and reconstruction. “Palestinians must determine their own future and have the right to remain on their land, return to it and rebuild it,” Al Butmeh stated.


Şenol Karakaş of the Freedom for Palestine Platform also placed the war in Gaza within the context of global economic and political power structures. He criticized the support Israel receives from …

author: Unknown
title: Six lawyers detained in raids in Izmir
content:
Six lawyers were detained during a police operation in the western Turkish city of Izmir on Tuesday morning. Five of them are members of the Contemporary Lawyers’ Association (ÇHD). According to the organization, the lawyers were taken into custody during searches of their homes in the early morning hours.


Those detained include Veysi Çetin, secretary of the ÇHD’s Izmir branch, as well as association members Yemen Cankan, Emrah Kanbay, Göksel Akbaba and Erdoğan Akdoğdu. Lawyer Bahattin Özdemir was also detained.


According to the ÇHD, police seized electronic devices and data storage media during the house searches. Access to the investigation file has also been restricted. The detained lawyers have reportedly been unable to exercise their right to consult with legal counsel.


The ÇHD views the detentions as part of a systematic policy of repression against social opposition movements. The authorities are attempting to criminalize the practice of law and intimidate independent defense lawyers, the association’s Izmir branch stated. “This attack on the right to legal defense is nothing more than an attempt by the government to cover up the violations of the law, arbitrary practices and human rights abuses it perpetrates through the judiciary,” the statement said.


The ÇHD announced that it would provide legal support throughout the proceedings against the six detainees and continue to resist restrictions on the right to legal defense.

author: Gladys Stagno
title: Donde hay un trabajador precarizado, nace un moroso
content:
Un relevamiento provincia por provincia muestra la superposición entre precariedad laboral y endeudamiento familiar. Seis millones de personas acumulan atrasos en sus pagos y casi cuatro de cada diez jóvenes menores de 25 años están en situación de mora.


Ilustración: Marcelo Spotti


Por Gladys Stagno


En un escenario de alto endeudamiento familiar y morosidad récord, un estudio aporta un dato nuevo que surge de analizar las condiciones laborales de los endeudados.


En su último informe, el Mirador de la Actualidad del Trabajo y la Economía (MATE) realizó un mapeo de la caída del empleo formal y del aumento de la precariedad, provincia por provincia, en base a datos de la Secretaría de Trabajo, Empleo y Seguridad Social.


De igual manera, y sobre cifras del Banco Central (BCRA), el centro de investigación construyó un “mapa de la mora”, donde se evidencia en qué provincias el fenómeno se ha vuelto más grave.


Tucumán y San Juan son las dos que se encuentran al tope de ambas categorías: más del 50% de trabajadores en la informalidad, y más del 34% de personas en situación de mora. En situaciones similares se encuentran Catamarca, Corrientes, Chaco, Formosa, La Rioja, Mendoza, Misiones, Salta, San Luis y Santiago del Estero.


Una situación atípica ocurre en Santa Cruz, provincia con la menor tasa de informalidad (-30%) –junto con Neuquén– pero alta tasa de morosidad (entre el 30 y el 34%). La Pampa es la provincia con menos mora del país, con menos del 22%.


Fuente: MATE


Jóvenes y precarizados


En toda la Argentina, la deuda en mora de las familias en el sistema bancario ronda el 18%. El número crece si tenemos en cuenta a los proveedores no financieros y billeteras virtuales, donde la cifra supera el 30%, según informes recientes del Centro de Economía Política Argentina (CEPA). Se trata de los niveles más altos desde la crisis de 2001.


En cantidad de personas, se trata de cerca 6 millones de argentinos con deudas atrasadas, de un total de 20 millones de endeudados, lo que representa 1 de cada 4 en situación de mora.


Fuente: MATE


Según el Mapa de la Deuda publicado por el del Centro de Estudios para la Ciudad junto a la fundación alemana Friedrich-Ebert-Stiftung, la situación se agrava en los más jóvenes, donde casi 4 de cada 10 menores de 25 años registran atrasos en el pago de su deuda. Se trata también del sector poblacional más alcanzado por la informalidad laboral. De acuerdo con MATE, en el sector de 15 a 24 años la informalidad ya alcanza al 39,2%.


“La demografía de la mora y la del empleo se vinculan íntimamente: la precariedad laboral avanza sobre los jóvenes y sobre las provincias olvidadas por este modelo económico y la distribución de la mora refleja esta situación”, analiza el instituto liderado por los economistas Diego Kofman, Lavih Abraham, Marco Kofman, Natalia Pérez Barreda y Sergio Arelovich.


La informalidad crece en línea con la pérdida de empleos formales. Según el relevamiento del MATE, la economía argentina pierde más de 370 empleos formales por día.


“El sector privado ya expulsó a 265.765 trabajadores registrados: la industria y la construcción son los sectores que más puestos de trabajo destruyeron”, detallan. Por su parte, el sector público perdió 89.620 puestos, contabilizados desde diciembre de 2023. Se trata, en total, de 375.016 empleos formales menos desde la asunción de Javier Milei.

title: Trump Says Nationwide Outages Are “Fine” as More Systems Go Down
content:
Two additional outages occurred after Trump’s comments, affecting the NSA and Apple products.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

President Donald Trump appeared to downplay the nationwide outages that have affected millions of Americans over the past week, suggesting they aren’t anything to worry about.

In remarks to reporters in the Philippines on Tuesday, Trump indicated that he had spoken to Chase executives about one of the latest outages, which affected banking services for Chase, U.S. Bank, and Wells Fargo. When reporters asked Trump whether he was concerned about the outages, the president said he wasn’t worried.

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful, and you have all of the money, things like that happen. It’s fine,” he said.

Q: Have you spoken tothe banks regarding the outage at Chase?TRUMP: I haveQ: What are they saying?T: It's going to be very much under controlQ: Are you concerned about these outages?T: No. It's life. When you're big & powerful & have all the money, things like this happen. It's fine

Trump’s response is unlikely to calm the fears of millions of Americans, some of whom may be wondering if the outages are connected in some way. So far, there is nothing to indicate that, or that any of the outages are the result of cyberattacks.

Shortly after Trump’s comments, another outage was reported, this time affecting the National Security Agency (NSA). According to sources speaking to CNN, the agency’s internal communications system used to transmit classified information, called NSA Net, had gone down. The sources added that there was no reason to believe the outage had been caused by a cyberattack, and that it did not affect the NSA’s ability to continue informing Trump about national security matters.

Another source told The New York Times that NSA Net has been unstable for weeks.

Beyond the banks and the NSA, other outages have included problems with Microsoft products reported by users worldwide, which occurred on Thursday. Perhaps most notably, on Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all domestic flights for several hours, citing communications and radar errors that were later revealed to have been caused by the replacement of a copper-wired router connection at a facility in Arkansas. Flights have yet to resume at normal operating speeds at airports across the country, with some delays and cancellations still occurring.

Later on Tuesday, thousands of users worldwide reported problems accessing Apple services, including iCloud, Apple Pay, the App Store, and Apple Support. The issue with those products was ongoing as of 2 pm Eastern Time, according to reporting from DownDetector.

Donations are down for Truthout at a time when media is under immense pressure. Google’s AI search has driven our traffic down by 15 percent, Trump is arresting journalists, and many independent media organizations face heartbreaking cutbacks and closures.

At the same time, movement media is vital in the fight against Trump’s authoritarian reign. Our mandate to tell the truth, share strategies for resistance, and speak against fascism is ever more urgent in this deluge of political censorship and misinformation. Yet, we are struggling to meet our publishing costs when our work is so urgently needed.

We are fundraising right now for those basic operating expenses — we need $23,000 in the next 48 hours. If you can support Truthout with a one-time or monthly donation, you will make a significant impact on our work. Anything you can do makes a difference.

title: Sebahat Tuncel: Silencing the guns is not enough; rights must be guaranteed
content:
The relationship between militarism, the climate crisis and ecological destruction was discussed during a session titled “Combating Militarism from a Climate Justice Perspective” at the Peoples’ Climate Summit in Antalya. The session addressed the environmental impact of military spending and armed conflicts, as well as opportunities for cooperation between the climate justice movement and antimilitarist movements.


Speaking at the session, Free Women’s Movement (TJA) activist Sebahat Tuncel highlighted the links between the climate crisis and the capitalist system, policies of exploitation, wars and repressive practices.


Tuncel stated that while government representatives at COP31 were discussing ways to maintain capitalism and the system of exploitation, the Peoples’ Climate Summit was exploring how to build an alternative way of life in opposition to these policies.


Sebahat Tuncel stated that the situation in Palestine could not be considered separately from the policies of repression and violence faced by peoples in other parts of the world. “The injustice, climate crisis, policies of war and policies of genocide we are witnessing in Palestine actually affect all peoples. Replace Palestine with Kurdistan. Similar policies are being pursued in Kurdistan as well. Think of the Alawites in Syria, or all the peoples in the Middle East who face repression because of their identity, faith or culture. Therefore, the struggle for climate justice is a struggle that concerns us all,” she said.


Emphasizing that wars cause not only loss of life but also ecological destruction, Tuncel stated that the situation in Palestine, Kurdistan and Lebanon concerned all of humanity. She said that policies of war and conflict devastated living environments and that the effects of the ecological crisis were not limited to those living in conflict zones.


‘Solidarity alone is not enough’


Sebahat Tuncel stated that policies of war erected barriers between societies and alienated peoples from one another, calling for a united struggle against these policies.


“The policy imposed on us by states is one of divide and rule. What we must do in response is unite and struggle together. Solidarity alone is not enough. We need to go beyond solidarity and build a common internationalist struggle to change and transform the male-dominated capitalist system. Only an organized society can achieve this,” Tuncel said.


Referring to the LGBTI+ movement’s slogan, “We exist, and we will continue to exist,” Tuncel stated that Kurds, women and people of different identities would also continue their struggle for existence. Describing the denial of peoples, identities and beliefs as fascism, she said that it brought with it repression, oppression, exploitation and marginalization.


‘Turkey has been turned into a giant prison’


Addressing prison policies in Turkey, Sebahat Tuncel stated that there were 16 prisons of various types in Antalya. She criticized the government for presenting the construction of new prisons as good news, describing it as a continuation of policies of repression and punishment.


Recalling the arrest of Kurdish politicians in 2009 as part of the KCK investigations, Tuncel said that those demanding rights, freedom, democracy and peace faced the threat of prosecution. Arguing that the law had been turned into a political instrument, Tuncel said, “They have turned Turkey into a giant prison.”


Tuncel argued that the isolation imposed on Abdullah Öcalan in İmralı had spread throughout Turkey and its prisons. “In fact, it has spread across the whole of Turkey and into every prison. There are not only prisons being built physically, but also prisons being constructed in our minds. We cannot achieve freedom without dismantling all these policies of isolation,” she said.


Tuncel emphasized that freedom could not be achieved without overcoming the policies of isolation, stating that freedom required a social order in which people could express their thoughts, organize and live with dignity.


Time to build positive peace


Addressing the Peace and Democratic Society Process, Sebahat Tuncel said that a struggle had been waged for many years to resolve the Kurdish question through democratic means rather than war and conflict.

title: Oil exports begin through Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline
content:
Iraq’s Ministry of Oil issued a statement announcing the resumption of oil exports through the Kirkuk–Ceyhan pipeline.


The statement confirmed that crude oil would be exported through the old pipeline between Iraq and Turkey, with an initial export volume of 120,000 barrels per day.


Export capacity is expected to increase gradually in the coming period, with plans to reach 500,000 barrels per day.


The ministry described the reactivation of the pipeline and the resumption of exports as a “strategic step,” stating that it would strengthen Iraq’s oil export capacity and help diversify the country’s oil export routes.


The statement emphasized that reopening this export route would provide an important source of additional revenue and support the Iraqi economy.

title: Women’s Justice and Memory Vigil in Amed: Stories of seven women shared
content:
At the “Women’s Justice and Memory Vigil” organized by the Network Against Violence outside the courthouse in Amed (tr: Diyarbakır), participants carried photographs of women who had been killed. Representatives of numerous political parties and civil society organizations attended the demonstration, chanting slogans including “Jin, Jiyan, Azadî” (Woman, Life, Freedom), “Femicide is political” and “Stop protecting and exonerating perpetrators, prosecute them.”


Reading the statement on behalf of the organizers, Nermin Unat, a member of the Rosa Women’s Association, said that the stories of seven women who lost their lives in different cities between November 9 and 15 had been added to the collective memory. Unat emphasized that women who had been killed despite filing complaints and requesting protection, as well as those whose families were still seeking justice, would not be forgotten.


The women whose stories were shared this week included Pelin Pınar and Nuran Tay, who died after falling from balconies in Istanbul, Rukiye Demirel, who lost her life in Niğde, and Sema Gündüz, who died in Uşak. The stories of Aysel Sakaldaş, who was stabbed to death by her former husband in the Bayramiç district of Çanakkale; Ayşen Güneş, who was found dead in her home in the Elbistan district of Maraş; and Hanife K., who was shot dead by her husband in the Suluova district of Amasya, were also read aloud.


Speaking at the vigil, Amed Metropolitan Municipality Co-Mayor Serra Bucak said that activities organized as part of the November 25 International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women aimed to prevent further femicides.


Calling on the government to review its policies and take into account the efforts of local administrations to prevent violence against women, Bucak stated that 16 femicides had been officially recorded in Amed in 2026. She also drew attention to suspicious deaths of women, emphasizing the need to investigate these cases and hold those responsible accountable. “We will never give up demanding accountability,” Bucak said.


The vigil concluded with chants following a silent protest.
